title: Scam-Alert
description:
Scam Alert is a crypto-focused intelligence and reporting platform designed to combat the growing threat of fraud across the digital asset ecosystem. As blockchain adoption accelerates, so does the sophistication and scale of scams, ranging from phishing attacks and impersonation schemes to rug pulls and social engineering. Despite the transparency of blockchain, victims often lack accessible tools to report incidents, verify threats, or recover lost funds. Scam Alert addresses this gap by creating a unified, user-driven platform that empowers individuals and organizations to detect, report, and prevent crypto-related fraud in real time.


At its core, Scam Alert enables users to submit verified scam reports, flag suspicious wallet addresses, domains, and social media accounts, and access a continuously updated database of known threats. The platform aggregates and analyzes this data to identify patterns, high-risk actors, and emerging scam trends. Through this intelligence layer, users—including retail investors, compliance teams, and investigators—gain actionable insights that improve decision-making and risk mitigation.


In addition, Scam Alert aims to integrate with wallets, exchanges, and Web3 applications via APIs, enabling proactive alerts before users interact with malicious entities. This shifts fraud prevention from reactive to preventative. The platform also supports collaboration with law enforcement, compliance professionals, and blockchain analytics providers to enhance investigation workflows and improve asset tracing outcomes.


Beyond technology, Scam Alert is driven by a mission to increase transparency and accountability in crypto. By lowering the barrier to reporting scams and making threat intelligence openly accessible, the project contributes to a safer and more trustworthy digital asset ecosystem. Ultimately, Scam Alert is not just a tool—it is a collective defense layer against crypto crime, built for the community and powered by shared intelligence.

title: ERCx: Property Testing for ERC Token Standards
description:
ERCx is a free, open-source library of handcrafted Foundry tests for ERC token standards. It checks smart contracts against an extensive property-based test suite, measuring conformance, security properties, and behavioral risks for token implementations. Any developer can install it with forge install, point it at their source code or a deployed contract address, and get a detailed report of how well their token conforms to the standard in minutes.


ERCx currently covers ERC-20, ERC-721, ERC-1155, and ERC-4626, with over 900 individual tests across standard conformance, security properties, and implementation features. Each test suite is available in "Light" (fixed addresses) and "Heavy" (fuzzed addresses) versions for different levels of assurance, all open-sourced under https://github.com/runtimeverification/ercx-tokens.


Why this matters

Token standards are the most fundamental building blocks of the Ethereum ecosystem, since every DeFi protocol, vault, NFT marketplace depends on tokens behaving as the standard says they should. But ERC specifications are written in natural language, and implementations routinely deviate in subtle ways (see d-xo/weird-erc20), potentially breaking composability and enabling exploits. 


ERCx helps catch those issues automatically, using the test suites they are written by hand by engineers who have spent hundreds of hours reading EIP specifications, and then validated using mutation testing to ensure the tests actually catch the bugs they claim to catch.


How ERCx has been used

ERCx is used by token developers for pre-deployment testing, by auditors as a first-pass conformance check, and by protocol teams evaluating tokens for integration. For example, Rheo (formerly Size Credit) uses ERCx's ERC-4626 test suite alongside other test suites to test their Very Liquid Vaults. The test library is designed to be imported directly into any Foundry project as a dependency, and a VSCode extension provides inline results in the IDE. In addition, it is used by the ERCx web interface that allows anyone to test deployed tokens by address or paste in source code for evaluation.


What's next

The immediate priorities are maintenance and responsiveness to user feedback: merging community contributions, fixing issues reported by users, and keeping the test suites current with Foundry updates. Beyond that, extending coverage to additional ERC standards and expanding the depth of existing test suites. Longer-term, we see significant potential in AI integration: building AI skills and MCP tooling that let developers and AI agents run ERCx checks as part of automated security workflows, interpret results in context, and get actionable guidance on how to fix failing tests.


Why your support matters

Every token that ships without proper conformance testing is a composability risk for every protocol that integrates it. ERCx makes it trivial to check token conformance using the free and easy to integrate test suites. Funding keeps them maintained, expanding, and increasingly automated.


Funding breakdown 


All donations fund open-source ERCx Test Token Library development. The library is and will remain freely available under its open-source license. No portion of donations will support commercial services.


$0 - $5,000: Maintenance and community contributions. Merging pending contributions, addressing issues reported by users, keeping test suites compatible with the latest Foundry releases, and general upkeep. This tranche funds the baseline work that keeps ERCx reliable for the teams already using it.


$5,000 - $15,000: Extending test coverage. Deepening the existing test suites by introducing more security properties, better edge case coverage, expanded heavy (fuzzed) versions for standards beyond ERC-20, and improving documentation and onboarding for developers integrating ERCx.


$15,000 - $30,000: Supporting additional ERC standards. This tranche funds development of test suites for new standards based on ecosystem demand, with candidates including ERC-2612 (permit), ERC-3525 (semi-fungible tokens), and other standards seeing growing adoption. 


$30,000+: AI integration and automated workflows. Building AI skills and MCP tooling that enable developers and AI agents to run ERCx as part of automated security workflows: running conformance checks, interpreting results in context, and surfacing actionable fixes. This turns ERCx from a library you run manually into a tool that can be woven into CI pipelines and agentic coding workflows.

title: Plamen AI Security Researcher
description:
Web3 depends on open infrastructure, but security is still too expensive, too slow, and too concentrated. Many public-good projects cannot afford deep security review, and many users only discover weaknesses after funds, governance systems, or communities are already at risk.


Plamen exists to change that.


Plamen is an open security-audit system that helps find vulnerabilities in blockchain projects before attackers do. It combines automated analysis, specialist security agents, verification steps, and human-readable reporting to make high-quality security review more accessible to the projects that need it most.


The goal is simple: help public-good protocols, infrastructure teams, and open-source builders ship safer systems without wasting resources on a manual audit that will waste time on the same classes of bugs that LLMs can find and will instead help the manual review focus on the deep research.


Why This Matters

Security failures in crypto do not only hurt teams. They hurt users, donors, DAOs, public-good funding pools, and the broader trust in open financial infrastructure.


A single missed bug can lead to stolen funds, halted networks, broken governance, or loss of confidence in projects doing valuable work. At the same time, many public-good teams are priced out of traditional audits, especially early in their lifecycle.

Plamen focuses on closing that gap by building an audit pipeline that can repeatedly inspect large codebases, search for known and novel bug patterns, verify findings, and produce reports that developers can act on.

This is not meant to replace expert auditors. It is meant to give more projects a strong first line of defense, reduce obvious risk before expensive review, and help human auditors spend more time on the hardest problems.


What Donations Support

Donations help improve and operate Plamen as a public-good security tool.


Funding will support the development of:

 - Better vulnerability detection across smart contracts, L1 clients, bridges, DeFi protocols, and Move-based

  ecosystems.

 - More reliable verification so real bugs are preserved and false positives are filtered responsibly.

 - Better reports that developers can understand and fix quickly.

 - Open methodology improvements based on real audit misses, postmortems, and public vulnerability research.

 - Testing Plamen against large real-world codebases so the system improves from practical evidence, not theory.

 - Making security knowledge reusable across audits instead of locked inside one-off private engagements.


Impact


 A donation to Plamen helps create more accessible security coverage for the Web3 ecosystem.


 With more support, it could:

 - Run more benchmark audits against real protocols.

 - Improve recall on critical vulnerability classes.

 - Reduce false positives and noisy reports.

 - Add methodology for new ecosystems like Sui Move.

 - Publish clearer guidance for projects and auditors.

 - Help open-source teams identify dangerous issues earlier.


Even small improvements in security tooling can have large impact. If Plamen helps one project catch a critical bug before launch, the value protected may be far greater than the cost of building the tool.


Milestones


 Our near-term milestones are:


 1. Stabilize the audit pipeline so findings are not lost between discovery, verification, and reporting.

 2. Improve report quality so developers receive clear, actionable findings instead of noisy technical dumps.

 3. Expand coverage for recurring missed bug classes across L1 clients, smart contracts, and Move projects.

 4. Benchmark against known ground-truth audits and publish what improved, what failed, and what still needs work.

 5. Make the system easier for public-good projects to use as a pre-audit or continuous security review layer.

title: Firefly, open-source hardware wallet
description:
Firefly is a crypto-native device for Ethereum founded by Ricmoo, creator of EthersJS.

  • Human-readable transaction verification: our goal is to support decoding calldata on-device,so you see exactly what you are signing before you sign it
  • Open source hardware, all the way to the chip: built on the ESP32-C3 (32-bit RISC-V, 160MHz). Schematics and PCB design files are fully public
  • Open source firmware: every line of code is public, readable, and verifiable
  • Build or customise your own firmware: fork it, flash it, make it do something new
  • $10 target price: hardware security accessible to everyone, not a $80-$300 luxury device


Firefly is an open source hardware wallet for Ethereum. The hardware designs, schematics, and firmware are all public. Built on the ESP32-C3 with a 1.3" display, BLE, and USB-C. Anyone can read it, audit it, fork it, and build on it. Just visit github.com/firefly for more info.


As well as using open hardware, Firefly firmware is open-source. More than that, we want you to be able to modify and customise the firmware to suit your needs. Security is not one-size-fits-all. Someone protecting a multisig treasury has different needs to someone managing their on-chain identity or signing into decentralised apps. With Firefly, you can build or modify your own firmware to match your use case. Display what matters to you. Add the context you need. The goal is that by the time you press "sign", you are confident in exactly what you are approving.


Hardware security should not be a luxury. That is why the target price for a Firefly Pixie is $10. The most basic Ledger costs $79 and the more recent models are $400+. For most of the world, that is a real barrier. At $10, you can put a secure signing device in the hands of every developer, every student, and every user who needs one. Or even better, work with donors to subsidise devices for users in need.


Funding goes toward firmware development, hardware iteration and continued free devkit distribution.


In case you were wondering if you can run Doom on a Firefly (because we have been asked many times by security researchers) the answer is YES!

You can watch the demo on X.

title: Simbolik: Security Toolkit for Solidity
description:
Simbolik is a VSCode and Cursor extension that brings engineering tools for smart-contract security and quality assurance into the IDE, including:


Test explorer


See all your Foundry tests at a glance, run them individually or in batches. The test explorer makes it easy to understand your test suite's structure and quickly iterate on complex test scenarios.




Test coverage


Understand exactly which lines of your code are covered by tests, and which aren't. Systematically improve your test coverage and ensure that critical edge cases are not overlooked.




Static analysis


Simbolik continuously runs Foundry's native static analysis detectors on your code, surfacing warnings and potential issues right in your editor as you type.




Simbolik is built and maintained by Runtime Verification, the team behind KEVM — the formal specification of the EVM, maintained continuously since 2017 — and Kontrol, our Foundry-native formal verification engine. Simbolik is in daily use across hundreds of individual developers, protocol teams, and security researchers.


For transparency, we note that Simbolik also includes a proprietary Solidity debugger that is only partially open source. None of the raised funds is used for closed-source development or operations. All work funded by this round ships under BSD-3 to our public GitHub repository.


Roadmap


The five deliverables below ship *consecutively, in priority order*, as funding accumulates. Each ships with marketplace distributions of the VSCode and Cursor extensions, and published documentation. Anything funded ships in full; anything underfunded does not start. Budgets cover engineering, documentation, and release operations.


1. Kontrol formal verification, integrated — $0 - $15,000


Kontrol (Runtime Verification’s Foundry-native formal verification engine) becomes a built-in Simbolik feature. Where a Foundry test exercises only random inputs, a Kontrol proof exercises every possible input the path condition admits, surfacing nuanced bugs and providing stronger guarantees.


In Simbolik, the test explorer gains a “Prove” action that runs symbolic execution on any test, with results reported alongside conventional pass/fail status. Because proofs do not always terminate quickly, timeout and partial-proof states are reported explicitly rather than hidden behind an indefinite spinner; when a property fails, the offending input is shown as a concrete counterexample. A tutorial accompanies the integration, walking developers from “I write Foundry tests” to “I write formal specifications” through a sequence of working examples.


2. Stack-too-deep detector with auto-fix — $15,000 - $25,000


Stack-too-deep is one of Solidity’s oldest and most-criticized rough edges; the annual Solidity developer surveys have repeatedly ranked it among the language’s top compiler frustrations. The error occurs when a function’s local variable footprint exceeds the EVM’s 16-slot stack window.


A new static analysis detector flags the condition in realtime as code is being written, with quick-fix actions for the standard refactors, so the rewrite happens at design time rather than at deadline.

Importantly, this allows tools such as code coverage and debuggers that rely on disabled gas optimizations to run without manual refactoring of the codebase.


3. AI-assisted, coverage-guided test synthesis — $25,000 - $40,000


Simbolik gains a test-synthesis feature that uses an LLM to generate Foundry tests, informed by its existing test coverage reports. Simbolik renders line coverage in the editor gutter today; the new “Generate test” action prompts the LLM with an uncovered code path and the existing test suite as context, then validates each test candidate against the current code.


The deliverable is regression prevention: a generated test pin current behavior as the baseline, so its value compounds in the *next* edit rather than the present one. A growing share of Solidity is now produced by agentic workflows, where developers iterate alongside a coding agent rather than writing each line themselves; the result ships faster but is often under-tested, and the next agent-driven edit has nothing to push back against. A coverage-pinned test suite, generated alongside the code, captures an executable specification of what the contract is supposed to do, reducing the rate at which subsequent agent edits silently introduce regressions.


4. Web-hosted Simbolik for browser-based source review — $40,000-$55,000


A hosted, browser-based Simbolik makes any on-chain-verified contract or transaction auditable directly from a URL, with sources resolved via Sourcify and no local installation required.


Two entry points are supported: by contract address (`simbolik.dev/contract/<chain>/<address>`) and by transaction hash (`simbolik.dev/tx/<chain>/<tx-hash>`). The transaction-hash entry point loads every verified contract touched by the transaction into a single workspace: an auditor pastes a suspicious tx hash and sees, in seconds, every contract that participated, opened together — replacing the multi-step manual reassembly through a block explorer that this workflow currently requires. For deeper analysis, a clone-to-disk action in the desktop VSCode and Cursor extensions pulls the verified source into a standard Foundry project layout, so the auditor can keep editing locally with the full toolchain available.


5. Interactive symbolic execution — $55,000+


Kontrol already exposes the full internal state of a proof, but only through a terminal UI and only at the level of raw KEVM configurations — word stacks, memory regions, 256-bit storage keys, path conditions over symbolic words. For developers fluent in Solidity, that is a steep barrier between writing a specification and understanding why it does or does not go through.


This milestone closes the gap on two axes: the TUI is replaced by a graphical interface in the Simbolik test explorer, with breakpoints, single-step and step-over controls, and call-stack navigation; and every paused state is lifted from KEVM back to its Solidity meaning — storage slots as their declared mappings and arrays, packed bytes as struct fields, the symbolic word stack as named locals, path conditions as predicates over Solidity expressions. The engineer reasoning about a proof sees the contract they wrote, not the bytecode it compiled to.


This milestone is also where any excess funding lands. Because the final round size is unknown, we are not committing to a specific scope here: every dollar above $55,000 goes toward this deliverable, in priority order — graphical interface first, then progressively wider Solidity-level state lifting. What ships is determined by what is raised; nothing in this section is promised in full.

title: CuEVM: Accelerate EVM execution on GPUs
description:
CuEVM


CuEVM is a CUDA implementation of the Ethereum Virtual Machine that uses GPU parallelism to execute transactions at millions of TPS. Since my presentation on the preliminary results of CuEVM v1 at Devcon SEA (see link below), the project has progressed significantly to CuEVM v2, which now reaches over 8 million TPS on a single NVIDIA RTX 5000 (ERC-20 transfers). We originally aimed it for fuzzing to test thousands of transactions in parallel. Other potential use cases include large-scale parallel transaction testing, or customized L2 with proper concurrency control.


Current State:

  • Support Shanghai EVM, and multi-GPU execution.
  • Passed ~96% of eth-tests (ethereum/tests/GeneralStateTests)
  • We achieved up to 8 millions TPS on a single Nvidia GPU device and 13 million TPS on two GPUs (ERC20 transfer workload).
  • Show case fuzzing use case with in-house fuzzer and a fork from Medusa fuzzer from Crytic.


Project Plan (long term development and maintenance):

  • Upgrade to support new GPUs and new EVM (Pectra)
  • Maintain the codebase and review PRs from open-source contributors
  • Fix bugs and corner cases
  • In the long term we hope to be included in the official ethereum github.


Talk at Devcon SEA : https://app.devcon.org/schedule/PQBKHF


Project Links:

  • https://github.com/sbip-sg/CuEVM (existing repository)
  • https://github.com/minhhn2910/CuEVM (personal fork - future maintenance and syncs)
  • https://github.com/minhhn2910/medusa-cuevm (fuzzing tool interfacing CuEVM)


Core Developers:

  • https://github.com/minhhn2910 (active)
  • Previous developers https://github.com/sdcioc and https://github.com/cassc


Disclosure: The project was part of the Ethereum Foundation Research Grant "Massively Parallel Smart Contract Fuzzing on GPUs" and ETH Ranger project "Enhancing CuEVM: GPU-Accelerated EVM".

title: TID Research Risk Ratings
description:
TID Research: Independent Risk Ratings to Protect Ethereum Users from the Next Hack

It's 2026, and Ethereum users are getting drained at a pace the ecosystem hasn't seen since 2022. rsETH depegged after a contagion event ripped through Aave and Spark. Resolv's USR broke. Drift was exploited. WLFI left bad debt across Dolomite. Bridged DOT got siphoned. Every week another protocol, another asset, another set of users who didn't realize what they were holding until it was already too late.

The uncomfortable truth is that most of these hacks were foreseeable. The risk vectors — unaudited bridge contracts, concentrated admin keys, fragile collateral structures, oracle manipulation surfaces — were visible to anyone willing to do the work. But retail users don't have the time, the tooling, or the technical depth to do that work themselves. And the protocols that hold their funds have every incentive to downplay the risks rather than surface them.

That gap is what TID Research exists to close.

What we do

At TID Research (Today in DeFi), we publish independent risk ratings for DeFi assets and protocols on Ethereum and its L2s. Our goal is simple: give users the diligence layer they need to protect themselves before the next exploit hits, not after.

Our existing reports are live at https://tidresearch.com/reports, alongside dashboards at https://tidresearch.com/dashboards/ that let users monitor exposures across the protocols they actually use.

For assets, our risk reports systematically cover:

  • Smart contract risk — audit history, code maturity, upgradeability patterns, and the actual surface area an attacker would target. The kind of analysis that would have flagged rsETH's contract dependencies before the contagion.
  • Bridge risk — for any wrapped or cross-chain asset, we trace the bridge architecture, validator set, and failure modes. Bridges remain one of the largest categories of value lost in Ethereum history.
  • Admin key risk — who controls upgrades, who can pause, who holds the multisig keys, and what the real decentralization story is versus the marketing.
  • Economic and collateral risk — the category that took down Terra UST, that's currently driving questions around MicroStrategy-backed instruments, and that will take down the next wave of yield-bearing assets if users don't understand what's actually backing them.

For protocols, our risk analysis covers smart contract attack surfaces, admin key control structures, oracle dependencies, and economic attack vectors like manipulation, governance capture, and liquidation cascades.

Why this matters for Ethereum security

When most people hear "Ethereum security" they think about audits, formal verification, and core protocol research. Those matter. But there's another layer of security that determines whether ordinary users actually keep their money: the layer of information asymmetry between protocols and the people using them.

A user can hold an asset that's economically broken without knowing it. A user can deposit into a vault whose admin key is held by a single EOA without knowing it. A user can stake into a protocol whose oracle can be manipulated for the cost of a flash loan without knowing it. Every one of those scenarios ends in the same place: users lose funds, trust in Ethereum erodes, and the ecosystem absorbs another reputational hit.

Independent, rigorous, free-to-read risk research is public goods user protection infrastructure. It's the layer that turns audit reports and on-chain data into something a regular user can actually act on. And it's exactly the kind of work that markets systematically underfund, because the people who need it most can't afford to pay for it, and the protocols being analyzed have an interest in not paying for it.

That's why this round exists, and why we're applying.

Why us

TID Research has been operating in DeFi research and farming for years. We're not academics theorizing about risk — we're practitioners who've actively managed leveraged positions across Aave, Euler, Hyperlend, Velodrome, and others, watched liquidity crises play out in real time, and traded through multiple cycles of contagion. That hands-on experience is what lets us look at a protocol's docs and immediately spot the gap between what's promised and what's actually true on-chain.

We've covered breaking security stories as they happened, including the Drift exploit, the WLFI/Dolomite bad debt situation, rsETH contagion across lending markets, and the Aave/Spark 100% utilization spiral. Our subscriber base has come to rely on us for the kind of unvarnished, technically-grounded analysis that doesn't exist in mainstream crypto media.

We also publish openly. Our core risk reports are free. Our dashboards are free. The vast majority of what we produce is public goods — distributed widely so that the maximum number of users benefit, not gated behind paywalls only institutions can afford.

What funding will support

A grant from this round will directly fund expansion of our independent security and risk research:

  1. More asset risk reports, covering a wider range of LSTs, LRTs, stablecoins, yield-bearing tokens, and structured products on Ethereum mainnet and major L2s (Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, Hyperliquid, etc.).
  2. Protocol-level risk reports, going deeper than asset coverage into the lending markets, DEXes, perps platforms, and structured product venues where most user funds actually sit.
  3. Faster post-incident analysis — when the next exploit happens, we want to publish technical breakdowns within hours, not days, so users on related protocols can act before contagion spreads.
  4. Improved dashboards and monitoring, so users can track the risk profile of their actual on-chain positions in real time, not just read static reports.
  5. Open methodology — funding lets us document and open-source our risk frameworks so other researchers, DAOs, and risk teams can build on top of them.

Conflicts and transparency

We take editorial independence seriously. TID Research operates with disclosed conflicts of interest, and we're actively formalizing our entity structure, conflict-of-interest policies, and subscription terms modeled on the standards set by Blockworks Research and Delphi Digital. Any protocol we have a commercial or operational relationship with is disclosed in the relevant report. Funding from this round will be deployed exclusively toward independent research outputs published as public goods.

The ask

If you've ever lost money to a DeFi exploit, or watched a friend lose money, or held an asset that broke and wished someone had warned you sooner — that's the gap we're trying to close. Every dollar matched in this round goes directly toward more reports, faster coverage, and more users protected before the next hack happens.

Ethereum's security story isn't just about hardening contracts. It's about making sure the people who use those contracts actually understand what they're standing on. We'd be honored to be part of this round.

Read our work: https://tidresearch.com/reports Track risk: https://tidresearch.com/dashboards/

title: soldb - Open-Source Solidity Debugger
description:
What. An open-source, CLI-based debugger for Solidity, inspired by lldb. Built as a foundation other tools plug into — Foundry, Hardhat, Tenderly, block explorers. We're already in discussions with most of those teams.



Why. Solidity Surveys consistently flag debugging as the ecosystem's biggest gap. Despite being the most-used smart contract language, Solidity has no canonical CLI debugger the broader tooling can integrate. soldb fills that.


Who. Walnut — three years building blockchain compilers and debuggers:

  • Working with Argot on ETHDebug integration into solc, the canonical Solidity compiler. That uniquely positions us to build the client that consumes solc's debug info.
  • Starkware partnership: walnut.dev, a web-based transaction debugger and simulator
  • Miden partnership: midenc compiler and CLI debugger
  • Offchain Labs: stylusdb, the debugger for Stylus


Where. The Solidity / EVM ecosystem — usable on Ethereum L1 and every EVM L2.


How. soldb consumes ETHDebug-format debug info from solc and exposes a stable CLI other tools wrap. Open-source, integration-first, no lock-in.


What's next.

  • Foundry integration (Q2 2026) — soldb usable directly from forge workflows.
  • Tenderly proof-of-concept — early discussions underway on how Tenderly can integrate soldb.
  • lldb-inspired feature work: conditional breakpoints, storage watchpoints, pretty-printers for mappings/structs/arrays, multi-contract stepping across delegatecall, and Debug Adapter Protocol (DAP) support — so any DAP-compatible IDE (VS Code, Neovim, etc.) gets soldb for free.

title: Coalition to Change Crypto Freezes and Recovery
description:
Freezing stolen crypto is hard. Recovering it is even harder. The Coalition to Change Crypto Freezes and Recovery is bringing the industry together, from DeFi and VASPs to lawyers and regulators, to try to better address our response to stolen fund activity without solely relying on law enforcement to mitigate risks.


Crypto hacks, especially those from North Korea, highlight the inadequacy of current approaches to freezing and recovering stolen funds: despite good intentions, existing processes are too slow, fragmented, and reliant on law enforcement court orders. If the industry continues in its current state, its ability to support victims will continue to erode, ultimately undermining trust in crypto as a whole.


But together we’re finding ways to get stolen funds off of services’ books in a legally backed way that does not require additional internal resources. Some key areas include:


  • Engaging with geographically dispersed law enforcement bodies
  • Standardising processes and information, including evidence quality with the Trusted Investigator Recognition
  • Recovering funds via Indemnity or Hold Harmless Agreements, Arbitration, and DeFi fee sequestration
  • Better data sharing with private entities
  • Advocating for better response infrastructure through the private and public sectors


Since our start in Fall 2025 we have brought together hundreds of people within the ecosystem. We’ve seen progress in DeFi’s response and Hold Harmless Agreements, but there’s still more work to be done. Support the Coalition to continue to give hope to victims of crypto thefts.

title: Wallet Security Ranking
description:
What it is

The Wallet Security Ranking is an objective, transparent, and reproducible evaluation of crypto wallet security across iOS, Android, and browser extensions. Built and maintained by Coinspect since 2024, it scores wallets across four checklists — dApp Permissions, Intent Verification, Physical Access, and Threat Prevention — using a methodology that anyone can review and reproduce.

The ranking now covers 77 wallet builds — iOS, Android, and browser extensions tested independently, even for the same wallet. We re-test periodically as wallets ship improvements, with all changes tracked in public repositories.

Why it matters

Users lose funds every day to phishing, wallet drainers, and malicious dApps, and they have no objective way to tell which wallet would have protected them. Marketing claims and paid listicles dominate; independent evaluation is rare. The ranking changes that. By making security measurable and public, it creates pressure for wallets to ship real protections — and gives users and the security community a shared source of truth.

Real impact

Wallet Security Ranking is a working project used by the ecosystem, examples:

  • MetaMask's security page links to the ranking as a reference for users evaluating wallet security — a strong signal of industry recognition.
  • Wallet vendors discuss with us after shipping improvements — turning the ranking into a feedback loop that drives real security gains.
  • Other projects in the wallet-security space build on our data, integrating Wallet Security Ranking results into their own evaluations (e.g., Walletbeat).
  • Maintained continuously since 2024, with three published editions to date (Oct 2024, Apr 2025, Jan 2026) — each expanding scope and refining methodology, with re-tests in between.
  • Mainstream media is starting to cite our results. Money.com's crypto wallet methodology, for example, names Coinspect as a trusted security assessment source.

Open Resources

The Wallet Security Ranking is built on years of research, but the ranking website itself is only the visible output. The methodology, the dataset, and the checklist behind it are all open, versioned, and reusable

Wallet Security Ranking — Public Dataset:

Every score we've ever published, with evidence, fully reproducible.

https://github.com/coinspect/wallet-security-ranking

Per-wallet, per-platform check results with evidence, plus the configuration (categories, weights, included wallets) for each round. Round folders are immutable snapshots so any past ranking is fully reproducible. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

Wallet Security Framework

https://github.com/coinspect/wallet-security-framework

The versioned checklist, MIT-licensed and decoupled from WSR scoring so it can be reused independently. 


What funding would support

1. Continued maintenance and expansion. Periodic re-tests, new wallets, and new security checks as threats evolve — from phishing patterns to wallet drainers and dApp interaction risks.

2. More open-source tooling. We've built several tools internally to scale testing and automate parts of it. Releasing them publicly takes additional engineering work to make them reusable by anyone.

3. Open the scoring weights to community votes. Checklist weights are set by experts using an Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) — rigorous but tedious. A public web app would let Ethereum Security Badge holders and other experts vote directly, broadening who shapes the criteria.

title: Safe OpenSig: Eliminating Blind Signing
description:
Safe OpenSig

Eliminating Blind Signing for Ethereum's Multisig Signers


In February 2025, three Bybit signers reviewed a transaction carefully. Each used a hardware wallet. Each approved it. $1.5 billion was gone.


They did nothing wrong. Attackers had compromised the frontend interface months earlier, injecting JavaScript that silently replaced the transaction payload. What each signer saw looked correct. What their hardware signed was a delegatecall handing the attacker full control of the implementation contract. Their Ledgers showed two hashes. Hardware wallets cannot decode complex transactions. They faithfully sign whatever calldata they receive.


This is blind signing. And it affects every multisig signer on Ethereum.


Every major protocol you interact with, Aave, Arbitrum, ENS, GnosisDAO, Optimism, Compound, is managed by elected stewards approving treasury transactions through Safe. So are the corporate and enterprise treasuries entering Ethereum today. Verification is technically possible but requires expertise most signers don't have. The common approaches are circular: simulating via a browser tool or decoding calldata from the same interface means using the potentially compromised interface to verify the potentially compromised interface. On April 1, 2026, Drift Protocol on Solana lost $285 million the same way.


Security Council signers blind signed admin key transfer transactions. Hardware wallets rendered the instructions as raw hex. The admin key to the entire protocol was handed to the attacker. Different chain, same root cause.


What Safe OpenSig does


Safe OpenSig is a mobile app that runs on your phone, isolated from your desktop and browser, before you touch your hardware wallet.


It simulates the transaction locally using a native Rust EVM implementation (REVM), entirely on-device. It verifies onchain state against multiple independent nodes using Merkle Patricia Tree proofs checked locally. And it generates a pixel-accurate reconstruction of what your Ledger screen will display, so you can confirm the hashes match before committing to anything.


Three properties make this different from simulation tools that run in the browser:


Isolation. The app runs on a separate device. A compromised browser cannot reach it. A malicious Safe UI cannot feed it altered calldata, because the app fetches transaction data independently.


Cryptographic proof. State is not taken on faith from a single RPC endpoint. Merkle proofs are verified locally against multiple nodes. If nodes disagree, you see it before signing.



Hardware parity. You see exactly what your Ledger will show before you touch it. The hashes you verify on screen match the hashes the hardware will present. The moment of signing becomes confirmation, not discovery.




If Bybit's signers had used this workflow, the simulation would have shown: Operation: DELEGATECALL. New implementation: attacker-controlled address. A signing-ending discrepancy. The transaction stops there.


Here it is on a real transaction for Frax Finance, $35M Safe multisig, 3-of-5 threshold, one signer pending on a 17k frxUSD transfer. This is what verifying that transaction looks like, without blind signing.


Why it belongs in the Ethereum security stack


Safe OpenSig is fully open source. The code is on github. The app is free for everyone, available on iOS and Android. We built it with the World Foundation for their signing operations and launched in April 2026. No token. The tool exists because the problem is real and the ecosystem needed it.


The app is free. The verification protocol is open source. Anyone can bring their own RPC nodes and run the full stack independently. For teams who want reliable managed node infrastructure without running their own, Candide offers that as a service. That funds ongoing development. The verification layer itself is and will remain free.


Your support helps sustain the core: expanded hardware wallet coverage, broader transaction type support, and the independent audit work required to give signers confidence in the tool they are relying on.


The people managing Ethereum's most important assets deserve to know what they are signing. This is the tool that makes that possible.

title: Quick Intel
description:
The free, open token security scanner protecting Web3 traders across 60+ chains.


Quick Intel is a free, public good token security scanner that protects everyday users from rug pulls, honeypots, and malicious smart contracts before they trade.


Anyone can paste a contract address into app.quickintel.io, pick a chain, and get a real-time, AI-driven breakdown of exactly what that contract can do, whether it can mint, blacklist, pause transfers, set arbitrary fees, drain liquidity, steal tokens from your wallet, or hide behind a proxy. No wallet connection. No paywall. No signup. The same scan a professional auditor would run, available in seconds to anyone, anywhere.


Why this matters and why I built it

I started Quick Intel after losing money to scam tokens in 2022. That experience made one thing painfully clear: most users have no way to read a smart contract, and the tooling that could protect them was either paywalled, closed-source, limited to one or two chains, or hidden behind APIs only big platforms could afford. Meanwhile, scammers were industrializing and deploying thousands of malicious tokens a day across every new EVM chain that launched.


Token level scams are still one of the largest sources of preventable user loss in crypto. Phishing sites, drainer approvals, and social engineering get most of the attention, but the contract itself is often the weapon. If we can show users the weapon before they pull the trigger, most of these scams stop working. That's the entire mission of Quick Intel, to make sure no one ever has to lose what I and many others lost, because the information was right there if only someone had built the tool to surface it.


What Quick Intel does today

  • 60+ blockchains supported — Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Optimism, Polygon, BNB Chain, Avalanche, Solana, and every major L2/L3, plus long-tail and niche chains most scanners ignore.
  • 60M+ tokens scanned across the ecosystem.
  • 4M+ scams detected and flagged — honeypots, hidden mints, allowance bypasses, transferFee backdoors, tx.origin wrappers, SafeMath manipulation, proxy traps, and more.
  • 15M+ API calls per week served to developers, wallets, bots, and trading platforms.
  • Free public scanner at app.quickintel.io, no wallet, no account, no fee.
  • Developer APIs documented at developer.quickintel.io so any builder can embed token security into their own product.


Who already relies on Quick Intel

Quick Intel powers token security on platforms used by millions of traders every day, including DexTools, DexScreener, GeckoTerminal, and Gate.io, plus a long list of bots, wallets, and dashboards. When a chart screen warns you that a token can mint or has a buy/sell tax, there's a good chance that signal came from Quick Intel.


I've also been pushing the frontier on detection itself: advanced allowance-bypass scam detection (catching tx.origin wrappers, SafeMath manipulation tricks, transferFee backdoors), worker-thread-parallelized honeypot simulation, and a fully self hostable detection pipeline. The goal is for the next class of scam to get caught the same week it appears, not six months later after thousands of users have already lost funds.


Why this is a public good for Ethereum

Ethereum's promise is a permissionless market, but a permissionless market only works if users can verify what they're trading. Closed, paywalled, or single chain scanners create an information asymmetry that scammers exploit. Quick Intel exists so that every trader, on every EVM chain, has the same level of protection that institutional players have, for free.


How donations will be used

100% of QF funds go directly into keeping Quick Intel free, fast, and ahead of attackers:

  • Subsidize free scans for end users — every API call costs money. Donations directly offset the cost of keeping the scanner free for the traders who need it most.
  • Expand chain coverage — onboarding new EVM chains, L2s, and emerging ecosystems as they launch (often before scammers arrive).
  • Improve scam detection — funding ongoing R&D into new detection signatures (allowance bypasses, novel proxy traps, MEV-aware honeypots, and the next class of scam we haven't seen yet).
  • Free security education — articles, threads, and developer guides on how to read a contract and recognize red flags, so users can protect themselves long-term.
  • Open developer access — creating a developer tier free for indie builders and public-good projects so wallets, dashboards, and trading tools can integrate security by default.


Founder

I'm Ninja Dev, solo founder and developer of Quick Intel. I build it, run the infra, ship the integrations, and answer the support tickets. Quick Intel has grown from a personal project, born out of getting scammed myself with no clear tools at the time, into critical security infrastructure used across the EVM ecosystem, entirely on user trust and word of mouth. Your support helps keep it that way.

title: EVVM
description:
Have you ever thought of Ethereum as a hypervisor for virtual blockchains?


The next layer of Ethereum security and scalability isn't another chain. It's a substrate where many independent virtual blockchains run as smart contracts on top of the EVM, each with its own rules for accounts, gas, tokens, permissions, signatures, and compliance. No new infrastructure, no sequencers, no bridges, no liquidity fragmentation. That's EVVM.



Security work

Most security tooling on Ethereum operates on top of the chain: audits, monitors, incident response, governance security. EVVM extends the design space inside it. Gates, signature schemes, compliance rules, privacy layers, and post-quantum research can be deployed and iterated as virtual blockchains, without disrupting the host chain.


What's missing on plain EVM today, and where EVVM fills the gap:

  • Chain compliance: KYC/AML and access control as native onchain primitives.
  • Token incompatibilities: e.g. x402 payment-required flows for the agent economy and new ones.
  • Complex privacy solutions: zk + FHE, composable with the public chain.
  • Post-quantum resistance: signature scheme migration without losing identity, at account level.
  • Gas and account abstraction: without external alternative-mempool stacks/new infra.
  • Multi-chain composability: virtual blockchains can be deployed across host chains without each becoming an isolated environment.



How it works

EVVM is as decentralized as each deployer wants and as closed as each purpose needs. Core contracts and admin functions are renounceable, so a deployment can be fully immutable. Fishers (relayers) are optional helpers that improve UX, run markets, and can be configured to emulate sequencers or sharded execution; users can also be their own relayers, if permitted by the deployer. This makes EVVM a substrate that adapts to use cases ranging from open DeFi to permissioned bank consortiums, all on the same protocol.


Signatures today use the EIP-191 standard. The architecture is built so signature schemes evolve cleanly, that's what makes the post-quantum migration tractable (see "What's coming" below).


The last changes

  1. Cryptographic primitive abstraction in Core: A single, centralized validation entry point in Core verifies signatures, nonces, and executor permissions atomically. This makes it possible to evolve signature schemes (passkeys, contract-account signatures, post-quantum) without rewriting downstream services. Signature abstraction is the load-bearing primitive for the next wallet UX and post-quantum migration.
  2. zkVVM: privacy for users, transparency for institutions. A zero-knowledge service for EVVM for private token transfers on Ethereum. Designed so fund movements among institutions remain auditable while transactions among compliant users can be 100% private (via zkProofs). MVP ready to deploy by anyone, new modular release on April 30th.
  3. KYC/AML/Whitelist gates as native primitives: Compliance is a security concern when the alternative is opaque mixers and unmonitored flows. EVVM lets each virtual blockchain define its own access control using KYC/AML gates, allowlists, token-gated access, custom delegatecall checks. Banks and institutions can experiment with compliance-aware environments without operating their own chain.
  4. x402: programmable payment-required middleware. TypeScript middleware for Express.js / Next.js that accepts EVVM payments via the HTTP 402 status code. Published on npm as @evvm/x402 v0.1.6. Enables AI agents, APIs, and machine-to-machine flows to pay-per-call with cryptographically verified payments, an important security primitive for the agent economy.
  5. Sandbox infrastructure for safer development: scaffold-evvm provides a complete dev environment with 30-second timelocks instead of production's 30-day timelocks, letting security researchers and developers iterate quickly on EVVM-based security designs locally before deploying. Now ships with a built-in block explorer, making it one of the most complete sandbox environments in the EVM tooling space.


🎥 video link


What's coming next: QR-EVVM (July 2026 target)

A working EVVM where accounts use post-quantum signature schemes instead of EIP-191. The novel part: users keep stable on-chain identity through usernames (already resolved by our NameService contracts today), so when key formats and signature algorithms migrate, users don't lose who they are.


Three primitives line up to make this practical:

  • Usernames as fixed IDs: already shipped in NameService.
  • Gas abstraction: already shipped on the current EVVM; in QR-EVVM it covers post-quantum signatures so the user flow stays gasless and identical.
  • Composability with the host chain: via abstraction services so QR accounts interact seamlessly with the rest of the EVM ecosystem, e.g. Uniswap, AAVE, Stablecoinns, Payments, RWAs, etc.


Adjacent work also on the active roadmap:

  • FHE-EVVM for confidential accounting on Ethereum.
  • Hyperledger Besu EVVM consortium for banks (treasury on Ethereum, public products listing), 30 minutes presentation made at Decentralized Trust Linux Foundation event, in exploration with NTT Data.
  • Abstractor Service and Storage Service as new on-chain services in the next-month roadmap.



Traction

  • 200+ EVVMs deployed across +10 chains by hackers, developers and our team: open source experimentation across the EVM landscape (Sepolia, Base, Arbitrum, Monad, Mantle, Astar, Celo, BNB, Scroll, Zircuit, Optimism, Polygon).
  • testnet-Contracts v3.1.2 "Kitsuragi" released April 1, 2026: 6 core contracts, 623 commits, dual-platform CLI.
  • @evvm/x402 v0.1.6 published on npm.
  • 11 public repos in the EVVM organization.
  • Quip.Network confirmed as our first formal PoC partner for QR-EVVM.
  • NTT Data in exploration for the Hyperledger Besu Banks consortium use case. 30 minutes demo in Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust event January 29th 2026 in NJ.
  • Academic collaboration on the privacy/compliance layer of QR with PhD research groups at top global universities (currently under NDA), organized by NTT Data.
  • Talks delivered at EthCC, The Graph Devs, ETHGlobal Pragma, ETH Cluj, EthereumZuri.ch, ECH Institute, Ethereum Privacy Gathering, ETH Denver, including security and privacy framing.



Why this round for EVVM?

The Ethereum Security QF round explicitly funds: security tooling & infrastructure, cryptographic primitives, ZK & circuit security, post-quantum research, secure development tooling. EVVM hits four of those at once and extends the Ethereum security space inside the chain A platform where new compliance, privacy, and post-quantum primitives can be built, tested, and shipped without launching new chains.


This is also the first round of TheDAO Security Fund, the same fund whose reactivation depended on careful on-chain assertions and batched transactions. EVVM's primitives, typed signatures, async nonces, batched execution, central transaction validation, are exactly the building blocks the next generation of those careful operations will rely on.


What your support funds:


Current monthly burn is ~$13.5k USD (core team salaries+average company expenses). Audit quote is $50k to $70k confirmed by the listed companies. New-hire scenario adds ~$10k/month.


License

EVVM is free and open-source for individuals, researchers, hackers, public-good projects, and any open-source commercial use. Closed-source commercial deployments require contacting MATE Labs for licensing, making the open core as public infrastructure.


Team

  • German Abal, CEO and founder. Leads EVVM's internal security audits across code, in charge of the core logic and architecture. Builder since 1996, with deep EVM, protocol, and cryptography expertise. Co-founder of ETH Cinco de Mayo, one of LATAM's largest non-profit Ethereum onboarding initiatives.
  • Jistro, CTO and founder. Full-stack dev, in charge of the EVVM Core contracts and Services coding, maintenance, fuzz and unitary tests, Arbtirum Ambassador, co-founder of ETH Cinco de Mayo.
  • Artur Vargas, zk-dev and founder. In charge of zk/FHE privacy solutions research, planning and implementation, co-founder of ETH Cinco de Mayo.
  • Manu, Full-stack dev. In charge of maintenance x402 middleware, zk-VVM service, EVVM.dev tooling, EVVM-js project and new services implementations.
  • Oucan, AI dev. In charge of Scaffold-EVVM implementations and maintenance, EVVM documentation, evvm-full-docs-llms.txt and new services exploration and implementation.
  • Victor, Communication and Design.


Investors backing the EVVM work include Cameron and David the founders of Burner Wallet (burner.pro) and Kevin Jones (Edge & Node senior DevRel, BuidlGuidl DevRel, Spritz & 1claw.xyz founder), people who've been building privacy and UX-first crypto tools for years.

title: Roundabout: Static Analysis for Solidity
description:
Certora is building an open source static analysis tool based for Solidity. Our goal is to use syntax tree analysis and abstract interpretation to build a series of inter-procedural, flow sensitive static analyses that detect common security vulnerabilities in Solidity smart contracts. Our first target is rounding errors, and we have released the Roundabout tool here: https://github.com/Certora/wala-solidity


Unlike code scanners and other syntax tree analyzers, Roundabout is based on the concept of abstract interpretation. Abstract interpretation guarantees that the static analyzer collects a safe approximation of actual program behavior. The result is a precise and sound analysis, meaning it can report false positives but it will not miss bugs.


Such a tool is ideal for detecting security vulnerabilities where even a single missed bug can lead to a financial disaster. Roundabout detects inconsistent rounding directions, and clearly illustrates to a developer the rounding direction of each fixed point value used within a Solidity smart contract. We have already built a simple, local HTML-based UI for analyzing results and Claude skills to ease the adoption of Roundabout.


Certora would like to extend this open source tool to include new analyzers that build on top of our work with Roundabout. Such analyzers could include a static analysis for unit conversion errors, an analyzer for access control checks, and more. All funds raised through the DAO vehicle would be used directly to build out this tool for the community.


You can learn more about how roundabout works from our co-founder and Chief Scientist, Mooly Sagiv's, presentation at EthCC: https://www.youtube.com/live/1KR0GnxhNz4?si=PqzpyvBNtUMzGVQt

Zero Cool is built by security researchers (devtooligan and i-am-phaze) with a proven record in public security competitions and bug bounty work. The tool has found dozens of confirmed severity bug bounties and achieved seven top-10 finishes in public audit contests, including two 1st-place finishes and one 2nd-place finish, and is currently ranked in the top 25 on the HackenProof all-time leaderboard.


What?

This fund will support the continued development of Zero Cool and help provide free security scans to early-stage protocols. It will also help pay security researchers to use the tool on real targets, validate results, improve detection quality, and submit valid bug bounty findings where appropriate.


Where?

The project is focused on crypto protocols and blockchain infrastructure, with an emphasis on early-stage teams that need better security insight before they have mature security programs, large treasuries, or outside funding.


When?

Funding will be used on a rolling basis to improve the Zero Cool platform, support researcher-led testing, and provide free scans to eligible early-stage protocols. As part of this initiative, ZeroCool plans to provide 100 free scanning runs to early-stage teams.


Why

Zero Cool exists to make vulnerability discovery faster, cheaper, and more scalable. By combining AI-powered scanning with human security expertise, the project helps teams identify risk areas earlier and gives researchers better tools for finding serious issues.


How

Funds donated to this project will be used to improve the Zero Cool scanning platform, including the AI agents, verification workflow, infrastructure, benchmarking, and researcher feedback loops that make the tool more effective over time.


Donations will also help pay security researchers to test Zero Cool on real protocols, validate findings, reduce false positives, identify missed bug classes, and contribute feedback that improves the platform. This creates a practical cycle: researchers use ZeroCool in real security work, the tool improves from that work, and the ecosystem benefits from better vulnerability discovery.

title: AgnopraxLab
description:
Our Vision
Making Ethereum’s communication system safer, stronger, and more trustworthy.

Why This Matters

Ethereum is not only a blockchain. It is also a living network of computers constantly talking to each other.

If this communication is unreliable or vulnerable, the whole system can suffer:

  • nodes may crash
  • messages may be misunderstood
  • attackers may find hidden weaknesses
  • the stability of the network may be put at risk

Today, most security testing looks at only one part of this communication system at a time. But in reality, problems often appear between different parts working together. These “in-between” gaps are exactly where dangerous issues can remain unnoticed.

If the network is not safe, the protocol is not truly safe.


What We Want To Do

We want to build a new security testing framework that looks at Ethereum’s network communication in a more complete and realistic way.

Instead of checking isolated pieces one by one, our approach will simulate how a peer behaves over time:

  • how it joins the network
  • how it exchanges messages
  • how it reacts to changing conditions
  • how different communication layers affect each other

This helps us find problems that traditional tools are likely to miss.


Why This Is Important

Our goal is simple:

Find hidden weaknesses earlier

Before attackers or real-world failures expose them.

Test the system more like the real world

Because real networks are dynamic, messy, and full of interactions—not neat isolated steps.

Protect the broader Ethereum ecosystem

A stronger network layer benefits:

  • client teams
  • node operators
  • developers
  • users
  • the long-term reliability of Ethereum itself


What This Project Will Deliver

Open-Source Security Tooling

We will release an open-source toolkit that others can use, extend, and integrate into their own testing workflows.

Practical Security Improvements

We will work with client teams to help turn findings into real fixes, patches, and improvements.

Public Knowledge for the Ecosystem

The project will also produce:

  • research publications
  • vulnerability advisories
  • public writeups that help the wider community learn and improve


What Makes This Project Different

Most existing efforts check only limited parts of the network.

Our project focuses on the whole communication journey, not just isolated moments.

That means we are not only asking:

“Can this single message break something?”

We are also asking:

“What happens when many steps unfold together over time, the way they do in the real network?”

That broader perspective is where many important security problems can be discovered.


Early Proof That This Works

We are not starting from zero.

Our earlier work already produced:

  • a working security-testing prototype
  • real bug discoveries in major Ethereum clients
  • direct engagement with development teams
  • a strong engineering foundation for this next step

This gives us confidence that the new project can create practical value for the ecosystem.


Codebase

  • GitHub Repository: AgnopraxLab / D2PFuzz

Selected Bugs We Found


  • go-ethereum issue #31471
  • reth issue #15255
  • erigon issue #13931
  • besu issue #8445
  • besu issue #8339


What We Will Do With Funding

Our current work has built a strong foundation in testing Ethereum’s network layer — the part of the system that allows nodes to communicate, exchange messages, and stay connected.

With funding, we want to take the next step: moving from testing how Ethereum nodes talk to testing how they agree.

This is important because Ethereum’s security does not depend on communication alone. At its core, Ethereum relies on many independent nodes maintaining a shared view of the chain and reaching agreement under complex, changing conditions. If this agreement process fails, the consequences can be far more serious than a simple networking error.

From a technical perspective, this means extending our fuzzing framework from network-layer behavior into consensus-state and consensus-algorithm testing. Compared with network message fuzzing, consensus fuzzing is more demanding because it must reason about:

  • how protocol state evolves over time
  • how different clients handle the same sequence of events
  • how edge cases affect agreement, finality, and fork choice
  • how unexpected inputs or timing conditions may expose hidden implementation differences

The funding will be used primarily for two core needs:

  • Engineer salaries
  • To support the research, development, implementation, testing, and maintenance required to extend the framework from network-layer fuzzing to consensus-focused fuzzing.
  • Server rental and computing infrastructure
  • To run large-scale fuzzing campaigns, long-duration experiments, multi-client validation, regression testing, and continuous security testing workflows.

title: claudit
description:
claudit - 20,000+ audit findings as prior art for your AI


What

Claudit is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that connects AI coding agents (such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor) to Solodit's corpus of 20,000+ real-world audit findings.


Through a simple set of tools, AI agents can search across the entire history of disclosed smart contract vulnerabilities, filter by severity, audit firm, protocol, language or tag, and pull the full details of any specific finding on demand.


In short, Claudit gives AI agents access to the Ethereum security community's collective memory.


Who

Built by Martin Marchev, a Senior Security Researcher at Certora and one of 200 recipients of the ETHSecurity Badge from TheDAO Security Fund. Open source, MIT-licensed, developed in the open on GitHub.


Why

AI-assisted auditing is becoming a reality but the agents keep rediscovering the same bugs in slightly different shapes. They have the reasoning ability but they lack the prior art.


Every year, millions of dollars in smart contract exploits are lost to bug patterns that were already documented and fixed elsewhere in the ecosystem. The knowledge exists - it just is not reaching the tools that developers and auditors are actively using.


claudit closes that gap. Whether you are writing a new protocol, auditing an existing one or running an AI-powered security agent, the lessons from thousands of previous audits become searchable context inside your coding environment.


This is a public good project. Better prior art awareness means fewer repeat bugs, safer deployments and more secure protocols on Ethereum.


Where

  •  Source code: github.com/marchev/claudit (MIT licensed)
  • Distribution: npmjs.com/package/@marchev/claudit
  • One-line install for Claude Code, Codex CLI and Cursor
  • Used by security researchers and smart contract developers globally


How

claudit implements various MCP tools that the agent can call during a coding or audit session to search for prior art findings.

title: zkbugs <> AI
description:
zkSecurity is building open-source public-good infrastructure for Ethereum and L2 security through better security for zero-knowledge circuits, proving systems, and tooling used across the Ethereum ecosystem. We maintain zkbugs (https://github.com/zksecurity/zkbugs/), a public dataset of real ZK vulnerabilities, and will expand it from ~110 to 200 bugs, starting with Circom and Plonky3. We will also create an open ZK security skills repository for auditing ZK circuits and proving systems, inspired by pashov/skills (https://github.com/pashov/skills), to help developers, auditors, researchers, and AI tools understand bug patterns, reproduce issues, and use the right tools. Finally, we will build a public benchmark for ZK tools and AI auditors, including evaluations of frontier models with and without the skills layer. This builds on our active, verifiable work in Ethereum security and will remain openly accessible, with public progress updates and a post-round report. Funding will support bug curation, reproducibility, skills creation, and benchmark infrastructure.


Repo: https://github.com/zksecurity/zkbugs/

Website: https://zkbugs.com/


Use of Funds


  • <$5,000: expand and curate the zkbugs dataset by identifying, validating, and documenting additional real-world ZK vulnerabilities, improving metadata quality and coverage across Ethereum- and L2-relevant ZK ecosystems.
  • $5,000–$10,000: reproduce a first set of Circom bugs, creating working proof-of-concept environments and public documentation so developers and auditors can understand and learn from real vulnerabilities.
  • $10,000–$25,000: reproduce as many Circom and Plonky3 bugs as possible, turning zkbugs into a stronger public benchmark with reliable, reusable reproduction setups across two important ZK DSLs/frameworks.
  • $25,000–$50,000: build and open-source a ZK security skills repository for auditing ZK circuits and proving systems, and develop ZKBugs Arena infrastructure: a benchmark environment containing both real historical bugs and intentionally introduced bugs in otherwise secure code, to reduce bias and improve evaluation quality.
  • >$50,000: run continuous, multi-turn evaluations of frontier and open-source AI models on ZK security tasks using zkbugs, the skills repository, and ZKBugs Arena, publishing results and maintaining the benchmark for as long as funding allows.

title: Guild Academy
description:
Guild Academy is a public-goods Web3 security training program.

About Us

Guild Academy trains developers, cybersecurity professionals, and blockchain builders into capable smart contract security researchers through a 16-week intensive bootcamp that runs twice a year — combining deep technical education with real-world auditing practice.

What makes us different is our dedicated physical training facility with stable power, internet, devices, and accommodation — removing the infrastructure barriers that prevent talented individuals in emerging regions from accessing high-quality security education. We also run a full online track, reaching participants across Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas.


We are not a course platform. We are a security talent pipeline — training people to think adversarially, break real systems, and ship verifiable output.


Our Impact (5 Cohorts)

Talent: 300+ security researchers trained across 5 cohorts spanning multiple continents. 48 researchers in the most recent cohort alone. 221 applications from 22 countries received for a single cohort cycle.


Vulnerabilities: 200+ vulnerabilities reported (High, Medium, Low) across Code4rena, Sherlock, Codehawks, Cantina, and Immunefi. Several alumni ranked in the top 10 on global audit leaderboards. 25+ competitive audits participated in.


Research: 55+ technical articles published. 40+ real-world hacks replayed and analyzed. Student-led EIPs proposed. AI-assisted security tools built by students (Blocksploit, Solvra).


Ecosystem: Pro-bono audits delivered for open-source projects including Coinsafe, SIR Protocol, Fractal Visions, Paynode, and PayCrypt. Open-source hack labs and training repos maintained on GitHub. StarkNet Cairo security bootcamp partnership. Formal Immunefi training partner.


Recognition: Selected as one of 17 recipients of the Ethereum Foundation's ETH Rangers Program — a public-goods security stipend alongside Secureum, The Red Guild, and the Security Alliance (SEAL). Founder recognized as Ethereum Foundation Next Billion Fellow .


Student-Built Security Tools

One of our most impactful outcomes has been students building their own security tooling:

Blocksploit — an AI-powered smart contract analysis tool for automated vulnerability detection and code behavior explanation.

Solvra — a security research assistant that combines static analysis with AI-driven pattern recognition to accelerate audit workflows.

These tools demonstrate that our graduates are not just consumers of security methodology — they are builders of next-generation security infrastructure.


Community & Ecosystem Building

We organized the Web3 Security Summit Africa — a landmark event held in Lagos on November 8, 2025, bringing together security researchers, developers, auditors, and ecosystem leaders for workshops, technical presentations, and panel discussions on smart contract vulnerabilities and the future of decentralized security. It was the first event of its kind on the continent, and we are committed to making it a recurring institution.

Our alumni are active across major audit platforms — ranking on leaderboards, contributing to private audits and public contests, earning from bug bounties, building security tools, and returning to mentor new cohorts. Each cohort strengthens the next.


Why Support Matters Now

Web3 continues to grow, but security talent remains critically limited. Exploits cost the ecosystem billions, often due to preventable vulnerabilities.

Guild Academy addresses this at the root: by training people who can identify, understand, and prevent these vulnerabilities before they become exploits.

Support at this stage is not about starting something new. It is about scaling what is already working: training more researchers, expanding physical infrastructure and tooling, supporting participants who otherwise would not have access, increasing open-source security contributions, and growing the Web3 Security Summit Africa into a permanent institution.

We are building critical security infrastructure through people. And we intend to keep going.

title: LLZK Maintenance & Verification Infrastructure Grant
description:
Project Overview

LLZK is an open-source compiler framework for zero-knowledge (ZK) circuits that enables analysis, optimization, and formal verification across multiple ZK ecosystems. Built on top of MLIR, LLZK provides a modular intermediate representation that supports multiple frontends (e.g., Circom, Halo2, Plonky3) and multiple verification backends (e.g., PCL, Lean, R1CS).


The project is publicly available at: https://github.com/project-llzk


LLZK is designed not just for circuit construction, but for security-critical reasoning about circuits, including determinism, soundness, and constraint correctness.


Existing Functionality and Usage

LLZK is already a working system with the following capabilities:

  • Frontends: Circom, Halo2, and Plonky3 circuits can be translated into LLZK
  • Backends: LLZK can lower circuits into:
  • PCL (for determinism verification via Picus)
  • Lean-based verification representations (including zkLean)
  • R1CS
  • Analysis & Optimization Passes:Degree lowering
  • Interval analysis
  • Unconstrained signal detection
  • Redundant constraint elimination


Real-World Usage

LLZK is actively used internally at Veridise as part of our verification pipeline:

  • We use LLZK + Picus to analyze circuits from zkVM systems such as:
  • RISC Zero (SP1)
  • Other zkVM-style architectures
  • LLZK serves as the intermediate layer enabling these circuits to be checked for determinism and soundness properties
  • We also run custom static analyses over LLZK representations to detect circuit-level issues


Ecosystem Adoption and Contributions

LLZK is beginning to see adoption and contributions beyond its original authors, reflecting its role as emerging shared infrastructure for ZK circuit verification.

  • Galois has contributed support for a Lean-based verification backend (zkLean), enabling integration with formal verification workflows in the Lean ecosystem.
  • The Noir ecosystem is actively developing a frontend from Brillig (Noir’s intermediate representation) into LLZK.

These contributions indicate that LLZK is evolving into a common intermediate layer for interoperability and verification across ZK frameworks, rather than a project tied to a single toolchain.


Motivation

Modern Ethereum scaling systems (zk rollups, zkVMs) rely on increasingly complex ZK circuits. However:

  • Circuit implementations span multiple frameworks (Circom, Halo2, Plonky3, emerging zkVM IRs)
  • There is no unified infrastructure for verification across these ecosystems
  • Subtle bugs (e.g., underconstrained circuits, nondeterminism) can lead to critical security vulnerabilities


LLZK addresses this gap by providing a common compilation and verification layer, enabling:

  • Translation of circuits into formal verification backends (PCL, Lean)
  • Application of uniform analysis passes across ecosystems
  • Reuse of verification tooling across different proving systems


Scope of This Grant (Maintenance Focus)


This proposal focuses on maintenance, stabilization, and ecosystem integration of LLZK—not new project creation.


The goal is to make LLZK a usable, reliable public good for Ethereum security researchers and developers.


Priority Areas

  • Stabilization & Usability (Primary)Improve documentation and onboarding
  • Provide clear workflows for verification use cases
  • Package existing functionality into accessible interfaces
  • Verification & Analysis ImprovementsMaintain and extend existing analysis passes
  • Improve support for real-world circuits encountered in audits and research
  • Infrastructure Hardening and Issue ResolutionExpand the testing infrastructure for LLZK, especially the core analysis passes.
  • Resolve open issues in the public issue tracker, particularly technical debt tasks and bugs.
  • Upgrade MLIR/LLVM versions for LLZK to take advantage of upstream changes — SMT dialects in MLIR 21.


Deliverables

1. End-to-End Verification Pipelines

We will deliver fully documented, runnable verification workflows for ZK circuits, along with a unified interface for executing them. While many of the underlying components already exist, end-to-end pipelines have not yet been fully integrated, stress-tested, or made easily usable by external developers, and current documentation is limited.


This effort will focus on building complete workflows that take circuits from supported frameworks (e.g., Circom, Halo2, and zkVM-style systems) through LLZK and into verification backends such as PCL/Picus and Lean. In addition, we will provide a unified CLI and supporting scripts to ingest circuits, run LLZK passes, and export verification artifacts in a consistent and user-friendly manner.


Comprehensive documentation and tutorials will accompany these workflows, enabling users to reproduce results and apply LLZK to their own circuits with minimal setup.


Artifacts:

  • Public repo examples with step-by-step instructions
  • One-command or scripted execution of pipelines
  • Tagged releases with working tooling


Timeline/Cost

  • 8 weeks, $80,000


2. Expanded Verification Backends

We will extend LLZK’s verification support to better match real-world needs:

  • Bitvector-based SMT encodings for circuits over small primes
  • Finite field–aware encodings
  • Improvements to current integer-based encodings


Artifacts:

  • New SMT lowering passes which use different encodings: bitvector, finite field, optimized integers.
  • An evaluation of the lowering on real world benchmarks, demonstrating that users can leverage SMT solvers to check properties of their circuits out-of-the-box.


Timeline/Cost

  • 3 weeks, $30,000


3. Core Infrastructure Hardening & Issue Resolution

We will systematically address open issues in LLZK to improve the correctness, stability, and usability of the framework. This includes resolving bugs in dialect implementations and lowering passes, strengthening validation of IR invariants, and ensuring reliable translation across supported frontends and backends.

This work will be guided by and transparently tracked through the project’s public issue tracker: https://github.com/project-llzk/llzk-lib/issues.


In parallel, we will improve the developer experience by refining error reporting, simplifying APIs, and reducing friction when integrating LLZK into external tooling. We will also expand test coverage and CI workflows to prevent regressions and ensure the reliability of end-to-end verification workflows.


Timeline/Cost:

  • 8 weeks, $80,000


Importance

This project directly strengthens Ethereum’s security ecosystem by:

  • Providing shared infrastructure for verifying ZK circuits across frameworks
  • Enabling detection of critical bugs such as nondeterminism and underconstrained signals
  • Supporting auditing of zk rollups and zkVMs, which are central to Ethereum scaling
  • Lowering the barrier for applying formal verification techniques to real-world circuits


About the Team

Veridise is a blockchain security firm specializing in the analysis of smart contracts and ZK systems, with deep expertise in formal methods and verification.


We have audited critical infrastructure including zkVMs, rollups, and DeFi protocols (e.g., RISC Zero, Linea, Succinct, Mina), and have developed internal tools such as Picus for circuit verification.


LLZK builds on this experience to provide general-purpose verification infrastructure for the ecosystem.

OpenSense is a free Web3 security education project.

https://www.youtube.com/@opensensepw


OpenSense exists to help more people get good at Web3 security.
