title: Dedaub Decompiler: From Bytecode to Solidity-Like Code
description:
Dedaub Decompiler: From Bytecode to Solidity-Like Code

Free EVM bytecode decompilation infrastructure for Ethereum security research.

The problem

In the last 12 months, approximately 83M smart contracts deployed across Ethereum, Binance, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, Avalanche, Optimism, and Blast, have no verified source code.

When one of these contracts holds value, is exploited, or interacts with another project, the only way to understand what it actually does is to decompile its bytecode.

Why this matters for Ethereum security 

A large portion of onchain activity relies on contracts with no publicly available source code, creating blind spots in security and risk assessment. Understanding behavior and responding to exploits, therefore, depends on analyzing raw bytecode rather than developer-provided sources.

Hack response. This becomes critical during exploits. Every time a major hack happens, researchers need to inspect the attacker’s contracts immediately. Attackers usually do not publish source code, so decompilation is often the only way to understand the exploit path, identify copied infrastructure, and support real-time incident response.

Bots and MEV. The same constraint applies beyond hacks. Bots and MEV strategies are routinely deployed without verified source code, often deliberately to obscure behavior. As a result, assessing risk, detecting malicious patterns, and understanding interactions in real time also depend on reading and decompiling bytecode.

How Dedaub Decompiler addresses this security visibility issue

Because understanding smart contract logic without source code is critical for security, the Dedaub Decompiler has become widely used over the years. It enables researchers to reconstruct and analyze contract behavior directly from bytecode at scale.

Today, the Dedaub Decompiler has over 12,000 registered users. Any registered user, including free users, can search smart contracts deployed on Ethereum, Binance, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, Avalanche, Optimism, Blast, and visualize a Solidity-like version to understand the logic.

Fast and comprehensive. Contracts are indexed and decompiled within minutes across major chains.

High-quality reconstruction. Recovers most contract logic, enabling meaningful analysis without source code.

Accessible and real-time. Free access removes friction during incidents and supports immediate investigation.

The Dedaub decompiled smart contract database spans back to the very early days of the Ethereum ecosystem. The oldest block in the database is 47205, timestamped 7 August 2015 at 08:26:34 UTC. Just 8 days after the Ethereum mainnet genesis block (30 July 2015). See the decompiled view: https://app.dedaub.com/ethereum/address/0xc669eaad75042be84daaf9b461b0e868b9ac1871/decompiled-yul and the corresponding Etherscan page: https://etherscan.io/address/0xc669eaad75042be84daaf9b461b0e868b9ac1871

Sustaining an Almost Public Good: Ongoing R&D and Infrastructure Investment

Although the Dedaub Decompiler operates as an almost public good with free access for any registered user, the cost of sustaining the service is completely self-funded. Maintaining and improving it requires continuous investment in both research and infrastructure, with an estimated annual cost of around $500K, including researcher support and the infrastructure needed to host and maintain the database. 

Over the years, Dedaub has advanced EVM decompilation through a combination of peer‑reviewed research and production engineering.

Core areas include:

Core EVM decompiler research in progress: improvements to reconstruction quality and scalability.

Static analysis algorithms: Contributions to function boundary reconstruction and EVM‑tuned context sensitivity (e.g., The Incredible Shrinking Context… in a Decompiler Near You https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3728935).

Storage layout recovery. Precise static identification of Ethereum storage variables (e.g., Precise Static Identification of Ethereum Storage Variables https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20690).

Engineering features: AI-based source reconstruction, additional representations such as Yul, and continuous expansion to new networks.

Because reconstructing contract logic without source code is critical, the Dedaub Decompiler is widely relied upon across the ecosystem. If Dedaub were to stop operating, access to large-scale decompiled data could disappear; community funding helps reduce this risk.

Technical strengths of Dedaub’s decompilation approach

The EVM exposes only low-level bytecode with no explicit functions, types, or structured control flow, making reliable reconstruction inherently hard. Traditional decompilers rely on symbolic execution, which does not scale to real-world contracts due to path explosion and compiler optimizations, resulting in low coverage.

Dedaub takes a different approach: advanced static analysis that over-approximates all executions while remaining scalable through context sensitivity. Its core innovation, introduced in Gigahorse and formalized in Elipmoc, treats calls and returns asymmetrically, recording context on entry and discarding it on exit, achieving precision without exponential blowup.

Elipmoc enables recovery of function boundaries, control flow, and storage layout at scale, delivering significantly higher accuracy than prior tools. The result is a near-complete reconstruction of deployed contract logic, enabling dependable analysis even when no source code exists.

  • If you want to go deeper, check out: https://dedaub.com/blog/gigahorse-thorough-declarative-decompilation-of-smart-contracts/
  • https://dedaub.com/blog/elipmoc-advanced-decompilation-of-ethereum-smartcontracts/
  • https://youtu.be/fZUzBGA37Hs 

Why are we asking for your support?

We have submitted a funding request via Giveth (giveth.io) under the umbrella of The DAO Fund (thedao.fund) to do even more for the community. With proper financial support, we can expand the Dedaub decompiler database both vertically and horizontally. 

Expand chain coverage. Increase the number of supported chains from 8 (Ethereum, Binance, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, Avalanche, Optimism, Blast) to cover up to 95% of EVM activity, including for instance Monad, Hyperliquid, and Tron.

Extract more information from bytecode. Expand the use of AI to reconstruct cleaner, more readable Solidity-like representations from decompiled output, reducing low-level artifacts and bringing them closer to developer-intended logic.

Connect the dots between smart contracts. Expand the ML-powered “find similar public function” feature to help security researchers identify similar behavior across contracts using LLM-based function-level pattern detection.

What donations fund

Delivering the three expansions below over 12 months adds approximately $100,000 to $150,000 to the infrastructure Dedaub already runs. Dedaub continues investing its own resources throughout.

Under $25k: Remove AI analysis limits.

Scales the LLM-assisted analysis layer, raising or removing the current cap on daily contract analysis for free users. Researchers can run full AI-assisted inspections across large contract sets without interruption, including during active incidents.

$25k to $75k: Full coverage for more chains

Funds infrastructure to onboard additional EVM chains: indexing pipelines, storage, and continuous analysis. Brings mainnet-level decompilation and static analysis to L2 ecosystems where exploits are increasingly concentrated.

$75k+: Similarity analysis at ecosystem scale

Expands the ML-based “find similar” feature across all contracts and supported chains. Detects reused code patterns, forks, and previously exploited logic at scale using LLM-derived embeddings over decompiled bytecode.

Commitments

The free tier at app.dedaub.com remains free for the duration of the funded period and beyond. No previously free feature will be paywalled. If the community demonstrates clear backing, Dedaub will open-source components of the decompiler codebase. A public retrospective on fund allocation and measurable outcomes will be published within 60 days of the round closing.

The Platform

title: Blockchain Security Incentives: Research + OS PoC dev
description:
Project Description: Blockchain Security Incentives in a Changing Threat Environment


Who

This project is led by Dr Kelsie Nabben, an established researcher in blockchain security and digital ethnography, with a demonstrated track record of contributions to the Ethereum security ecosystem. This includes the book on blockchain security from a social science perspective (see: https://manchesteruniversitypress.co.uk/9781526187086/), and prior funded collaborations with organisations such as Shield3, zeroShadow, and BlockScience. The project builds directly on existing, publicly available research outputs and practitioner collaborations, including an ETH Rangers security grant to open access publications and an academic grant to R&D an open-source red-teaming library.


What

This project delivers an open, public-good research and tooling framework for analysing and improving blockchain security incentives within Ethereum and EVM-compatible ecosystems. It focuses on three domains:


  1. Incentives for protocol cooperation in incident response (e.g., fund freezes, coordination requests)
  2. Incentives shaping white-hat behaviour (e.g., responsible disclosure, rescues, fund returns)
  3. The transformation of incentives under AI-driven and automated adversarial conditions


Outputs will include:

  • A comparative framework for analysing how incentive mechanisms operate across public, decentralised blockchain ecosystems
  • Practitioner-oriented guidelines to inform incentive-aware incident response design
  • (open access)
  • Annotated case studies of Ethereum security incidents


Why

Security in Ethereum is not solely a technical problem but an incentive alignment challenge. As articulated by Vitalik Buterin, the goal of security is ‘to minimise divergence between user intent and system behaviour’—yet current incentive structures remain fragmented and insufficiently coordinated.


Ethereum security increasingly depends on the alignment of economic, social, and reputational incentives across diverse actors, including protocols, white hats, and incident responders. Meanwhile, AI-enabled adversaries and automation are accelerating exploit discovery and execution, undermining traditional mechanisms such as bug bounties.


This project addresses a critical gap: there is no systematic, publicly available framework for understanding or designing incentive-compatible security coordination in Ethereum ecosystems. By producing open, actionable qualitative knowledge, the project contributes directly to Ethereum’s security ecosystem formation and resilience as a public good.


Where

The research is grounded in Ethereum and L2 ecosystems (including EVM-compatible chains), ensuring strong ecosystem alignment. Empirical cases will focus on Ethereum-based incidents. Fieldwork will be conducted in public and semi-public coordination environments (e.g., Discord, governance forums, Telegram) and through established practitioner networks spanning industry, non-profit security collectives, and policy organisations.


How

Using a digital ethnographic methodology, the project combines participant observation, semi-structured interviews, and case study analysis of security incidents. These qualitative insights will be complemented by document analysis (e.g., post-mortems, governance proposals, an announcements) to trace how incentives are articulated and enacted in practice. The project will synthesise findings into a practical framework and set of design recommendations for incentive-aligned security coordination.


The final deliverable will be a practical, written framework and set of design recommendations that can be used by Ethereum developers, security teams, and governance actors, to be disseminated by the researcher.


When

The project will run over 12 months:(in-depth, long-form qualitative research takes time).


Initial phases will focus on mapping the current incentive landscape and conducting fieldwork (Months 1–6), followed by analysis and framework development (Months 7–10), and publication and ecosystem dissemination of findings through Open Access reports, practitioner briefings, and workshops (Months 11–12).


This research directly contributes to strengthening blockchain security by identifying actionable pathways to align incentives for cooperation, ethical behaviour, and rapid response in an increasingly automated adversarial environment.


Use of Funds Disclosure

Funding will be used to support research time, data collection, analysis, and the production of open-access public goods for the Ethereum security ecosystem. Outputs will scale in depth, scope, and ecosystem engagement depending on the level of funding secured.


<$5,000 — Baseline Output (Minimum Viable Public Good)


  • Produce a short open-access blog mapping the current Ethereum security incentive landscape
  • Analyse a limited set (2–3) of recent Ethereum security incidents
  • Disseminate through existing networks (e.g., practitioner forums, social media)


Impact: Establishes an initial, publicly available synthesis of incentive dynamics and considerations in Ethereum security.


$5,000–$10,000 — Expanded Analysis


  • Extended case study analysis.
  • Conduct a small number of targeted expert interviews (security practitioners, protocol teams)
  • Develop a structured analytical framework for comparing incentive mechanisms and analysing gaps
  • Produce a more detailed open-access report and practitioner briefing.


Impact: Moves beyond descriptive mapping toward a comparative and actionable framework.


$10,000–$25,000 — Core Research Output


  • Conduct systematic digital ethnographic fieldwork across Ethereum security coordination spaces
  • Expand interviews and stakeholder engagement across white hats, incident responders, and developers
  • Produce a comprehensive comparative framework for Ethereum security incentives
  • Deliver practitioner-oriented design recommendations for incentive-aligned incident response


Impact: Generates a robust, ecosystem-relevant public good with direct applicability to Ethereum security practices.


$25,000–$50,000 — Ecosystem Integration

  • Develop practical tools or templates to inform ecosystem coordination efforts on security-forward incentive design (e.g., incentive design checklists, incident response coordination frameworks) released under an open-source license
  • Host an industry workshop or roundtable with Ethereum security practitioners and protocol teams to inform findings
  • Increase dissemination through presentations, webinars, and ecosystem channels


Impact: Translates research into actionable resources embedded within Ethereum security workflows.


>$50,000 — Advanced Research & Infrastructure Contribution

  • Contract a third-party technical research partner to expand research to include AI-driven security dynamics and automation impacts on Ethereum ecosystems
  • Develop open-source prototype tooling or dashboards for analysing incentive structures in incident response


Impact: Positions the project as a long-term public good infrastructure contributing to Ethereum’s security resilience in an AI-mediated threat environment.


Public Goods Contribution & Impact


All outputs will be released under open, permissive licenses and actively disseminated by the lead researcher.

This project addresses a structural gap in Ethereum security: the absence of a shared understanding of how incentives shape coordination under real-world conditions. By bridging empirical research with operational security practices, it equips the ecosystem with practical, evidence-based mechanisms to improve incentive design, and thus incident response and resilience.


This project contributes directly to Ethereum and L2 security as a public good by:


  • Enhancing white-hat incentive design: Clarifying and advancing best practice incentives for responsible disclosure, rescue operations, and post-incident fund returns in a way that is legible and actionable across the ecosystem
  • Advancing security research and standards: Delivering empirically grounded insights into incentive alignment, contributing to shared knowledge, emerging standards, and more coherent security practices across Ethereum
  • Strengthening incident response coordination: Producing openly available frameworks and guidance that improve how protocols, security teams, and ecosystem actors structure incentives during exploits

title: OSs Security - Hardening for macOs, Linux & Windows
description:
OSs-security: Open-source device hardening for Linux, macOS & Windows

Who

Opsek is a Web3 operational security firm. We audit smart contracts, run OpSec training for crypto founders, investigate compromises, and protect treasuries for DeFi protocols and high-net-worth individuals. We've responded to enough incidents to know one thing: most Web3 hacks don't start on-chain. They start on someone's laptop.


What

OSs-security is a free, open-source toolkit of hardening scripts and factory reset guides for Linux, macOS, and Windows. Run a single script and your machine moves from a default consumer config to a security-conscious baseline: firewall tightened, telemetry reduced, attack surface cut, logging enabled, unnecessary services disabled. If you suspect compromise, the factory reset guides walk you through safe recovery.

The scripts have been audited by Sigma Prime and are currently being audited by Coinspect — report lives in the repo.


Where

  • Repo: https://github.com/Opsek/OSs-security
  • Opsek: https://opsek.io
  • Audit report: PDF in repo


How

Fully open-source. Bash for Linux/macOS, PowerShell for Windows. Modular and auditable — every control is readable. PRs welcome. No telemetry, nothing phoning home. Built for solo devs, multisig signers, validator operators, and anyone who handles funds from a personal machine.


When — and what your donation unlocks

Live today: 100+ commits, audit complete, in active use by Opsek clients and the broader community. Matching funds will let us:

  • Expand OS coverage (more Linux distros, older macOS/Windows builds)
  • Add threat-model-specific profiles (solo dev, multisig signer, validator, high-value target)
  • Ship video walkthroughs for non-technical users
  • Fund continuous re-auditing as operating systems evolve
  • Localize guides (ES, PT, ZH, RU)

If you sign Ethereum transactions on a laptop, this is the layer most people forget. Help us keep it free, audited, and in more hands.

title: Rescue-Lifeboat
description:
Operation Rescue - Lifeboat

Free, Open-Source NFT Rescue Tool for Compromised Wallets


In February 2026, my MetaMask wallet got compromised. A sweeper bot was deployed on the address, monitoring it 24/7, draining any ETH the moment it arrived. My NFTs were still there. I could see them. But I couldn't move them because every attempt to fund gas got swept before the transaction landed. I was watching my collection through a glass wall I couldn't break through.


Every "whitehat" recovery service I found wanted thousands of dollars to even look at the problem. So I built what I wished had existed, tested it on myself, and rescued 413 NFTs across Ethereum mainnet, Polygon, and Base, plus my Manifold creator contract and my ENS domain. The compromised wallet was drained to zero. The bot had nothing left to take.


Operation Lifeboat is the tool that made that happen, now open-source and free for anyone in the same situation.


It's a local application. Not a website, not a browser extension. You download a folder, double-click a launcher, and your browser opens to localhost:3000. Your private keys never leave your machine. On Ethereum mainnet, transactions route through MEV Blocker so the sweeper bot never sees the funding or transfers in the mempool. The bot doesn't know you're there until your NFTs are already gone.

The tool scans compromised wallets across Ethereum, Polygon, Base, Optimism, and Avalanche. It estimates gas per token individually, which matters because flat gas limits fail on roughly 20% of non-standard contracts. It scans and sweeps ERC-20 tokens. It shows native balances across all chains. It handles Manifold contract transfers. And it has a scan-only mode so you can assess a compromised wallet without entering any keys. Just look before you commit.


Every feature in this tool exists because I hit that wall during a real rescue, at 2am, under real pressure. The gas estimation logic, the MEV protection, the session persistence so you don't lose progress if your browser crashes mid-rescue, the burn button that wipes your keys from memory when you're done. None of this was theoretical. It was all tested live on 413 real tokens with a real bot watching.


Nobody should have to go through this without a tool built for exactly this scenario. Free. No catch. No percentage. Just help.


Funding would go directly toward continued development. Solana support is next, which is essentially a second engine since it's a completely different architecture. Beyond that: improved UX around gas funding so the tool better explains what to do when the compromised wallet is empty, public address read-only scanning so people can assess a situation before touching any keys, and better documentation for non-technical users who are finding this tool at the worst moment of their crypto experience. Everything stays open-source. Everything stays free.


Not from a business... im a neighbor.

title: SCAR: AI Retrieval for Smart Contract Security
description:
TL;DR — SCAR is an open-source AI retrieval system that helps smart contract auditors (and the AI tools they use) find relevant vulnerability precedents in 114 milliseconds. R@10 = 0.901 across 232,000 real Ethereum contracts. Independent research. Apache 2.0. Built for Ethereum security.


🎯 The Problem

Balancer: $128M. Cetus: $223M. Drift: $285M. Smart contract exploits drained $1.2B+ from DeFi in 2025 alone — and most involved vulnerability patterns that had been caught before in past audits, if only auditors could surface them fast enough.

When an auditor sees a suspicious pattern, they need to know: has this vulnerability class been caught before? Where? How? Existing retrieval tools fail here. BM25 keyword search doesn't know that "price oracle manipulation" maps to getReserves() and swap() calls. Dense embeddings like CodeBERT score barely above random (R@10 = 0.109) on real audit findings.


🛡️ What SCAR Does

SCAR is a sparse latent retriever that lets auditors semantically search the full body of past Ethereum audit findings. Given a natural-language query, it returns ranked vulnerable contracts from a corpus of 232,000 real Solidity contracts in 114ms.

It introduces SAE-LoRA, the first published application of low-rank adaptation to Sparse Autoencoder encoder weights — a novel technique that transforms reconstruction-oriented SAE features into retrieval-discriminative ones.

  • R@10 = 0.901 on full 232,000-contract corpus retrieval (BM25 collapses to 0.308)
  • Validated on EVMBench (OpenAI + Paradigm + OtterSec, 2026) — hybrid beats BM25 on all three metrics
  • Trained on 7,552 real auditor findings from Trail of Bits, OpenZeppelin, Sherlock, Code4rena (via Solodit)
  • 6× faster than dense retrieval · Interpretable: 7 of top 10 features map to security-critical Solidity patterns (transfer, call, owner, auth, burn, lock)


⚡ Why SCAR ≠ another audit AI

AI audit tools are shipping fast in 2026. They share the same weakness: their AI reasons about vulnerabilities in a vacuum, producing hallucinated findings disconnected from real precedent. SCAR is the retrieval infrastructure underneath — the component that grounds AI-assisted audits in the 7,552 audit findings already out there. SCAR doesn't compete with audit AIs; it's what makes them stop hallucinating.


🔬 Why this funding matters right now

The paper is complete. The system works. What separates research from infrastructure audit firms adopt is second-backbone validation on the models that just released:

  • Qwen 3.5-8B (Alibaba, Feb 2026) — outperforms the previous-gen 30B on most benchmarks
  • Gemma 4 26B (Google DeepMind, April 2026) — built on Gemini 3 research

Validating SAE-LoRA on both proves generalization across architectures (dense → MoE) and labs. This is the #1 reviewer concern — and I've exhausted my self-funded compute budget (~$280 on Modal plus 800$ on pre-runs and pipeline configs) after the initial training runs. This is the exact gap funding closes.


💰 Where your donation goes

Cumulative tiers — higher unlocks broader work. Everything stays Apache 2.0.

  • Under $5K — Qwen 3.5-8B validation, arXiv preprint, full weights release on HuggingFace
  • $5K–$10K — Above + Gemma 4 26B A4B validation, reviewer-requested ablations
  • $10K–$25K — Above + production API + CLI for audit firms, Slither/Mythril integration
  • $25K–$50K — Above + multi-chain expansion (Arbitrum Stylus, Solana, Move)
  • $50K+ — Above + 6–12 months sustained research, audit firm partnerships (Trail of Bits, OtterSec, OpenZeppelin)


🔗 Links

  • Dataset (live): https://huggingface.co/datasets/Farseen0/scar-corpus
  • GitHub: https://github.com/FarseenSh/scar
  • Paper: EMNLP 2026 submission in ARR, available on demand
  • Contact: farseenshaikh20@gmail.com


Built by Farseen Shaikh, independent researcher. No institutional affiliation. No company. No monetization plans. Just research the Ethereum security community can freely build on.

title: Forge Proposal Simulator - FPS
description:
Forge Proposal Simulator (FPS) is an open-source framework built on top of Foundry that gives developers and signers a standardized way to simulate governance proposals before they touch the chain. It covers the full proposal lifecycle: deployment scripts, calldata generation, proposal simulation throughout the governance lifecycle, and post proposal state validation. The framework runs your existing test suite against the post-proposal state of the protocol, catching bugs that unit tests and auditors miss. When governance proposals contain bugs, protocols break. Funds get locked, markets get frozen, users experience cascading liquidations on healthy positions. The Compound V2 WETH incident is a perfect example of this: the governance proposal was not tested against the live state of the protocol before execution.


FPS supports four governance models out of the box: OpenZeppelin Timelock Controller, Gnosis Safe multisig, Compound Governor Bravo, and OpenZeppelin Governor. The architecture is loosely coupled. If your protocol uses a different governance model, FPS is flexible enough to accommodate it.

OlympusDAO made FPS mandatory for all governance proposals. Other top rollups and DeFi protocols use concepts this tool pioneered to secure their governance process. This tool has been used in production, helping govern protocols with a combined TVL of over a billion dollars.


This project is the culmination of years spent building smart contracts for DAOs and watching governance security be treated as an afterthought. I have deployed, written, reviewed, and debugged proposals that broke in production. Almost every protocol I worked with had the same blind spot: there wasn’t a standardized way to test a governance action and contract deployment against the real state of the system before it executed. FPS was born from years of direct exposure to the problem, building with teams that needed this tool and didn't have it. At DeFi Security Summit (DSS 2024), we presented how FPS can be used to find hard-to-catch bugs in deployment scripts (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UU4wkD4hXUY).


The framework is MIT licensed, free to use, and has been open source since 2023. It is a public good. There is no token, no revenue model, and no paywall.


Funding tiers are cumulative, with each funding level enabling us to do more to secure the ecosystem:


Under $5k: Ongoing maintenance. Bug fixes, Foundry version compatibility, triaging GitHub issues from teams integrating FPS. This would enable me to survey users, and understand their pain points.


$5k–$10k: Better documentation and onboarding. Dedicated guides for each governance model, video walkthroughs, a standalone project site, more mainnet examples covering Uniswap Governor, Aave governance, and a migration guide including intuition for teams currently testing proposals with bespoke tooling. At this level, I would prioritize implementation of features identified in the user survey.


$10k–$25k: Community outreach and adoption. A dedicated FPS Twitter/X account, regular content, integration case studies, regular conference workshops on governance testing, a library of real governance bugs FPS would have caught, and a Tenderly integration for visualizing simulation output. CI integration runner and an expanded set of features to enable seamless onchain verification of governance proposals within CI.


$25k–$50k: Feature development. A proposal diffing feature that shows exactly what state changes a proposal will make in human-readable format. FPS already has parts of this, but it could be a lot more ergonomic and communicate storage slot changes in a human-readable format. At this level of funding, I would dig in and figure out native support for L2-specific governance patterns like cross-chain proposals and L1-to-L2 timelocks. I would also host a small prize pool at EthGlobal to have hackers try FPS and give feedback.

title: OWASP Smart Contract Security Framework by CredShields
description:
CredShields is the creator of OWASP SCS Framework, an open source risk-prioritization framework built from real-world exploits observed across Ethereum and EVM chains in 2025.


OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 | CredShields Open Source Project

The OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 2026 is an authoritative standard awareness document for smart contract risk. Published under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 as a sub-project of the OWASP Smart Contract Security (OWASP SCS) initiative, it gives every Ethereum developer, auditor, and protocol team a free, community-owned reference for the vulnerabilities actually causing losses on-chain.


We led the structured incident aggregation and impact-weighted pattern analysis behind the 2026 ranking, powered by our exploit intelligence platform Web3HackHub and our AI-powered auditing platform SolidityScan. The 2026 edition is anchored in 134 deduplicated smart contract incidents from 2025, representing ~3.6B in on-chain losses, the most data-driven edition of the Top 10 ever released.


SCWE (Smart Contract Weakness Enumeration)

A catalog of common security and privacy weaknesses in smart contracts, modeled after MITRE's CWE and acting as the bridge between SCSVS controls and SCSTG tests. Each weakness is categorized under SCSVS control groups and documents an overview, impact, modes of introduction, and mitigations with the important distinction that a weakness is a condition that can contribute to vulnerabilities, not a vulnerability itself.


https://scs.owasp.org/SCWE/


SCSVS (Smart Contract Security Verification Standard)

The requirements standard: a list of specific security requirements and tests for Solidity/EVM smart contracts used by architects, developers, auditors, and tool vendors to define and verify secure dApps and DeFi protocols. It is organized into 11 control groups covering the most critical areas of the smart contract attack surface.


https://scs.owasp.org/SCSTG/


SCSTG (Smart Contract Security Testing Guide)

The testing counterpart to SCSVS: a methodology manual for developers, auditors, and security professionals that describes technical processes for verifying the controls listed in the SCSVS through the weaknesses defined by the SCWE, with detailed detection methods, examples of common flaws, and remediation strategies. Together, SCSVS defines what to verify, SCWE defines what can go wrong, and SCSTG defines how to test it.


https://scs.owasp.org/SCSVS/



Why This Matters for Ethereum Security

Most Ethereum and L2 exploits in 2025 weren't novel, they were variants of failure classes the community already knew about but hadn't standardized against.


The OWASP Smart Contract Top 10 closes that gap by turning real breach data into a shared vocabulary the entire ecosystem can align on, and it sits on top of a deeper stack: the SCSVS (verification standard - 11 control groups covering architecture, access control, oracles, bridges, DeFi logic, etc.), the SCWE (weakness enumeration - the smart-contract analogue of MITRE's CWE, with ~150 catalogued weakness classes), and the SCSTG (testing guide - concrete methodology to verify each SCSVS control through the weaknesses SCWE defines).


The 2026 Top 10 introduced Proxy & Upgradeability Vulnerabilities as a new category and elevated Business Logic Vulnerabilities to #2, changes that directly reflect where Ethereum capital is actually being lost, and that flow through into corresponding SCSVS controls (ARCH-2, GOV) and SCWE entries (e.g., SCWE-099 Storage Layout Collision on Upgrade, SCWE-101 Flash-Loan-Fueled Governance Manipulation).


The Feedback Loop We Operate

Every exploit logged in Web3HackHub (a dataset of on-chain incidents going back to 2011) feeds OWASP's methodology, which in turn shapes SolidityScan's 700+ detectors scanning Ethereum and every major EVM chain (Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, zkSync, and more). That loop real-world exploits → Web3HackHub → OWASP categorization → detector coverage → developer workflows is what makes the Top 10 a living standard.


The framework is designed to be used alongside the OWASP SC Weakness Enumeration (SCWE), the OWASP SCS Checklist, and the Alternate Top 15: Web3 Attack Vectors together forming a layered defense for Ethereum builders.


The Top 10 is free, open-source, and used by auditors, enterprises, and solo devs around the world. Supporting this round supports the public-good layer of Ethereum security: the taxonomies, datasets, and standards everyone else builds on top of.


Framework, methodology, and data sources: scs.owasp.org/sctop10


CredShields: An Overview

CredShields is a security company specializing in blockchain and traditional security headquartered in Singapore, founded in 2021 by Indranil Roy and Shashank. SolidityScan is CredShields' flagship product an automated auditing and vulnerability scanning platform built specifically for Solidity, Ethereum's native smart contract language. It ships with 700+ vulnerability detectors and delivers an average scan time of just 6 seconds, making it one of the fastest automated auditing tools in the Ethereum ecosystem. SolidityScan has done over 7M+ scans so far.


QuickScan is a specialized free-to-use security tool designed for the rapid analysis of deployed smart contracts to identify vulnerabilities and potential "rug pull" scams. 


Web3HackHub is CredShields' exploit intelligence platform a curated collection of past and present Web3 security incidents designed to help developers, researchers, and security teams learn from real-world attacks.

title: CrossBar Open Source Security Hardware Wallet
description:
1. Project Description

CrossBar Inc, registered in DE, headquarter in Santa Clara, CA. Founded 16 years ago, CrossBar owns more than 200 patents in security hardware technology. CEO Mark Davis, PHD; CTO Sung-Hyun Jo, PHD; Chairman Ker Zhang, PHD; Chief Business Officer Elaine Wang, PHD; Chief of Hardware Security Andrew Huang, and more than 50 team members including hardware, software and cryptography experts, collaborating partners includes TSMC and Foxconn.


One of crossbar's team member Andrew Bunnie Huang, is a world famous open source hardware hacker, his IRIS project use infraded camera to inspect semiconductor chips, emphasizing the importance of open hardware. (https://media.ccc.de/v/38c3-iris-non-destructive-inspection-of-silicon) (https://baochip.com/)


Crossbar (https://www.crossbar-inc.com/) is building the world’s first truly open source security hardware wallet — from the silicon chip level all the way up to the application software. Unlike every existing hardware wallet on the market, which relies on proprietary, NDA-protected secure elements that users cannot inspect or verify, CrossBar’s approach opens the entire security stack for public scrutiny.


Our custom security processing unit combines the protection of a traditional Secure Element with the functionality of a modern microcontroller. The core cryptographic engine and data access controller are published under the CERN-OHL-W open hardware license, with source RTL available for anyone to review, test on FPGA, and verify against the physical chip. The chip features both an ARM Cortex-M7 and a RISC-V core, giving the community a verifiable execution environment from boot0 through the application layer. The chip utilizes resistive-based memory technology (ReRAM), enabling secure firmware updates without the vulnerabilities of traditional floating-gate flash, increasing durability, significantly enhancing performances such as processing power, memory size. It is the most powerful chip ever built, with 150 years of key retention, non-capacitive no scanning can extract stored secrets. Our chip developed on this ReRAM technology remains physically unbreakable, will self-destruct when sensing physical attacks in all forms.


This matters for Ethereum security because today’s self-custody is built on a contradiction: users choose hardware wallets to avoid trusting third parties, yet they must blindly trust opaque chip vendors whose designs are hidden behind. CrossBar eliminates this “security by obscurity” foundation by enabling genuine, verifiable self-custody.


Our hardware wallet ships as a compact USB-C dongle with a full feature set: OLED display, fingerprint biometric authentication, FIDO2 support, and has the optional to integrate MPC (Multi-Party Computation) capability. MPC splits cryptographic keys across multiple devices — the hardware wallet and a companion mobile app — eliminating the single point of failure that plagues traditional seed-phrase wallets.


The project has moved well beyond the concept stage. We have published chip-level RTL on GitHub, developed a working prototype with integrated hardware and software, and are participating in the IRIS project for unprecedented chip inspectability using low-cost laser interferometry. Our production chip incorporates Resistive Memory (ReRAM) technology, enabling secure firmware updates without the vulnerabilities of traditional floating-gate flash.


CrossBar directly strengthens Ethereum’s security ecosystem by providing open source security tooling and infrastructure, advancing supply chain security through chip-level transparency, implementing cryptographic primitives in verifiable hardware, and establishing new security standards and best practices for hardware wallet design and user security.


All development outputs are and will remain open source. We are committed to ongoing public access and will provide post-round impact reporting.


2. Eligibility Criteria 

2.1 Open Source & Public Goods

Open Source / Public Benefit

All core security components of CrossBar’s hardware wallet are open source for scrutiny. Firmware and companion software will also be released under open source licenses. Anyone can construct, inspect, or test an FPGA system that performs the same logical security operations as our production chip, and build the product that fits the most of their need.

2.2 Ecosystem Alignment

Ethereum-Focused (Required)

CrossBar’s hardware wallet primarily supports Ethereum and EVM-compatible L2 security. Our software implementation targets Ethereum transaction signing, and is designed for Ethereum-native workflows. The hardware supports EIP-712 structured data signing for safe transaction verification. We are open to implementing additional Ethereum-specific features as guided by the community and the Ethereum Foundation. We focus on Ethereum clear signing for all critical applications (Safe, governance councils)

2.3 Verification & Compliance

Applicant Type

CrossBar is a registered corporation. Team includes semiconductor engineers, cryptography specialists, and embedded systems developers with deep experience in chip design and blockchain security with decades-long experience. 

Not in Sanctioned Countries

CrossBar is not located in any OFAC-sanctioned jurisdiction.

2.4 Track Record & Maturity

Contribution Track Record (Required)

Active, verifiable contributions to Ethereum security within the past 12 months:

  • Published chip-level RTL (Secure Crypto Engine, Data Access Controller, RISC-V core) on GitHub under CERN-OHL-W (https://github.com/Cramiumlabs/daric-sdk ).
  • Developed and demonstrated working wallet hardware + software prototype at major conferences (Token2049, Proof of Talk, Devconnect 2025)
  • Published comprehensive whitepaper on open source foundations for cryptography hardware, analyzing the security-by-obscurity problem in existing secure elements
  • Ongoing collaboration on the IRIS chip inspectability project

Beyond Concept Stage (Required)

This project has substantial working output:

  • Production chip with published open source RTL
  • FPGA test environment allowing independent verification of cryptographic operations
  • Published whitepapers and technical documentation on open source SE challenges and solutions
  • Active participation in IRIS inspectability project with published research

3. Use of Funds Disclosure

As required, here is how CrossBar can allocate funds at different funding levels.

Funding Level

Planned Use

< $5,000

Documentation improvements and community engagement: update developer guides, improve GitHub repository documentation, and create onboarding tutorials for developers wanting to verify or build upon our open source RTL.

$5,000 – $10,000

Developer tooling: build and publish improved FPGA test scripts and verification frameworks so that independent researchers can more easily replicate and test our cryptographic engine on commodity FPGA hardware.

$10,000 – $25,000

EIP-4337 and enhanced transaction decoding as EIP-712 should be part of the common feature set.

$25,000 – $50,000

Production of first Ethereum wallet prototype: Integrating Ethereum-based software design, hardware wallet design, connecting to the supply chain capacity of Taiwan Semiconductor Company (TSMC) and Foxconn to produce the first prototype of Ethereum wallet.

> $50,000

Full production acceleration: fund the final engineering sprint toward the production USB dongle hardware wallet for Devcon 8, including PCB finalization, firmware hardening, independent security audit of the full stack, and manufacturing of an initial batch for community distribution at Ethereum events. It will be an open finalized product and a development board for hackers.


4. Impact on Ethereum Security Ecosystem

Target Security Areas Addressed

CrossBar’s work directly contributes to multiple target areas of the Ethereum Security QF Round:

  • User Protection & Wallet Safety: Eliminates the single point of failure in seed-phrase wallets. Open hardware enables users to verify the security of their own custody solution rather than blindly trusting vendors.
  • Security Tooling & Infrastructure: Provides the first open source secure element that any wallet developer can integrate, inspect, and build upon. Our FPGA test framework is reusable infrastructure for the entire hardware security community.
  • Supply Chain Security: Participation in the IRIS inspectability project enables physical verification that manufactured chips match the published open source design — addressing a fundamental supply chain trust problem for all hardware wallets.
  • Cryptographic Primitives & Implementations: Open source implementation of ECDSA and secure key storage in verifiable hardware.
  • Security Standards & Best Practices: Establishing new standards for transparency in hardware wallet design, moving the industry away from security-by-obscurity.

Why This Matters Now

The Ethereum ecosystem is maturing rapidly. More value, more users, and more institutional adoption mean that the security of self-custody infrastructure is more critical than ever. Yet the hardware foundation of that security — the secure element — remains a black box across the entire industry. Certified chips have known-but-unpublished vulnerabilities hidden by NDAs. Users choosing self-custody are, paradoxically, transferring trust to an opaque platform with undisclosed flaws.


CrossBar addresses this structural problem at its root. By open-sourcing the silicon, we enable the kind of community scrutiny and continuous improvement that has made open source software the backbone of internet security.


CrossBar aims to be ready for production by November 2026.


Measurable Impact Metrics

  • Number of independent FPGA verifications of our cryptographic engine
  • GitHub: stars, forks, contributors, issues, pull requests on the RTL repository
  • Number of hardware wallet projects integrating our open source SE
  • Developer documentation page visits and tutorial completions
  • Security audit findings published and resolved

title: Fight Human Trafficking and Crypto Fraud With dobs
description:
Background


Romance scams (sometimes called “pig butchering”) aren’t just fraud - they’re human trafficking operations. Behind countless fraudulent cryptocurrency investment schemes that drain a victim’s wallet, there are often trafficked workers inside fortified compounds across Southeast Asia, forced to run the scam under threat of violence. The crypto industry talks about protecting users from fraud. I’m working to dismantle the infrastructure that makes the fraud possible in the first place.


I’m Joe “dobs” Dobson - a security researcher and incident responder with over 20 years of experience, including work with Mandiant, Google, and the US Military. I have been doing pro-bono work at the intersection of human trafficking and cryptocurrency fraud: investigating scam compound operations, helping secure anti-trafficking NGOs, and tracing the on-chain infrastructure that these networks rely on. None of this work is paid. I do it because the problem is urgent, the crypto community is uniquely positioned to help, and not enough folks with the right skills are showing up.


I’ve conducted firsthand field research at Myanmar-based scam compound sites - including KK Park, Tai Chang, and Shwe Kokko - documenting how these operations work on the ground and presenting findings to the Web3 security community at conferences like darkMode (SEAL). I also participated in the recent documentary from ChainPatrol, “Lights In Dark Rooms”.


This work supporting NGOs on the front lines - from cybersecurity best practices to cryptocurrency investigations - has been self-funded and pro-bono.

Close-up views of two scam compounds in Myanmar.


What I do


My work spans three areas that are rarely connected but need to be:


On-chain investigation - Tracing fraud infrastructure across blockchains, identifying wallet clusters, mapping laundering flows, and linking on-chain activity back to the compound operations behind it.


NGO security - Anti-trafficking organizations operate in dangerous environments with limited resources and are frequent targets themselves. These groups are doing incredible work on tiny budgets. I help these groups harden their infrastructure, improve their operational security, and protect the people doing rescue and advocacy work on the ground.


Detection research - I’m establishing techniques that identify patterns specific to compound-run romance scam operations, methods I share carefully to build awareness without tipping off operators. The goal is to turn these into tools and intelligence that exchanges and protocols can act on.


What funding supports


Every dollar raised goes directly toward this pro-bono work:


Research and investigation - Deep-dive analysis of fraud campaigns, wallet forensics, attribution work, and tracking compound operations as they adapt and relocate.


Open-source tooling - Building and releasing detection and analysis tools that help the broader Web3 security community identify and respond to trafficking-linked fraud infrastructure.


Field work - Travel to affected regions to gather ground-truth intelligence, build relationships with local partners, and validate on-chain findings against physical operations.


NGO support - Hands-on security assessments and hardening for anti-trafficking organizations that can’t afford to hire help.


How funding would be spent:


$10k and less: Building and releasing some detection and analysis tools to assist with identifying and tracking fraudulent trading platforms and investment scam infrastructure. This would be geared towards feeding data into tools such as EthPhishingDetect to warn cryptocurrency users before visiting such malicious sites.


There is a lot that can be done in this range - if possible, I would also build automated processes to flag malicious cryptocurrency job ads that are used to recruit and traffick victims.


$10k-$25k: This supports field work/on-the-ground investigations and security work for NGOs. This includes supporting debriefs of trafficking victims to understand how cryptocurrency was used by their captors, what platforms were used, and informing how to trace it.


Investigatory work also includes in-person meetings to unmask their on-chain activity, determine offramps, and work with local authorities to cut the flow of funds.


While in the local areas, I will meet with NGOs to assist them in growing their cybersecurity posture - from educating them on passkeys to hunting for malicious activity in their networks.


$50k+: On top of everything else, this helps to secure NGOs and provide safety to their personnel. I would sponsor/hire someone in SE Asia - likely a refugee from Myanmar living in Thailand - to assist with in-person research and work. I would personally mentor this individual, sharing my 20+ years of cybersecurity experience with them so they can convey it in-person in local languages with NGO workers.


Why this matters to Web3


This problem is a direct threat to crypto’s legitimacy. Tens of billions in stolen funds flow through DeFi protocols and centralized exchanges, and behind those flows are real people - both the victims who lose their savings and the trafficked individuals forced to execute the scams. The Web3 community has the tools, the talent, and the on-chain transparency to make a meaningful difference here. I’m asking you to fund the work that connects those capabilities to impact.


Construction can be seen at a scam compound in Myanmar during a supposed government “crack-down” on compounds.

title: Northscan by Heiner
description:
Hey! I am Heiner, an independent cyber threat intelligence researcher specializing in on-chain investigations. Since 2024, my work has concentrated on two closely related threat vectors: crypto fraud infrastructure and North Korean state-sponsored IT worker operations. My methodology combines on-chain fund flow analysis, open-source intelligence, and Human Intelligence evidence-based reports. All findings are published openly and made freely available to the security community.


Since early 2024


I began following Omega Pro which is a Ponzi Scheme linked to an Ethereum address that later was flagged by OFAC as connected to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force (IRGC-QF): https://medium.com/coinmonks/omegapro-funds-flow-linked-to-ofac-sdn-address-associated-with-the-irgc-qods-force-irgc-qf-948fd569af46


Around that same time, the crypto ecosystem was getting hit hard by drainers. Names like Monkey Drainer, Pxssy Drainer and Pink Drainer were everywhere. That is where my Pink Drainer investigation comes in. I followed the money, mapped the fraud-as-a-service infrastructure they were running, and through on-chain evidence managed to identify an individual strongly connected to the organization: https://medium.com/coinmonks/scam-as-a-service-pink-drainer-5b4165371916


On the North Korean IT worker side, what started as a curiosity turned into a full research track


My interest in DPRK IT Workers started when i was approached multiple times by recruiters through LinkedIn, and something felt off. That curiosity turned into research. The following investigations form a growing body of research into North Korean IT workers operating in GitHub as a platform for persona construction, social engineering, and job infiltration


• Fraud Alert: Fake Recruiters on GitHub and LinkedIn. This investigation revealed a fraud campaign involving fake recruiters operating on GitHub, making use of LinkedIn Premium accounts: medium.com/coinmonks/fake-recruiters-in-github

• Suspicious Activity in GitHub Associated with DPRK IT Workers. An investigation mapping suspicious GitHub patterns tied to DPRK IT Workers targeting developers and companies: medium.com/coinmonks/suspicious-activity-in-github

• The SuperStar Campaign: Reviewing GitHub Accounts Linked to DPRK IT Workers. This report documented a coordinated network of GitHub personas used for social engineering, named the SuperStar Campaign. It mapped the cluster's reach, account construction patterns, and tactics used to build credibility within open-source communities: medium.com/coinmonks/reviewing-github-accounts-lazarus

• Summary of Findings on Suspicious GitHub Activity Linked to DPRK IT Workers. A consolidated intelligence summary drawing together findings from multiple investigations, structured for use by security teams, OSS maintainers, and policy researchers: https://medium.com/coinmonks/recap-of-findings-regarding-suspicious-lazarus-activity-on-github-cc361074bdc2

• Unmasking Suspicious GitHub Activity: The Wagemole Campaign and Its Links to DPRK Threat Actors. An investigation into a DPRK-linked cluster of GitHub accounts engaged in systematic identity construction and job infiltration across open-source communities, named the Wagemole Campaign for its method of embedding operatives as legitimate contributors: https://medium.com/coinmonks/unmasking-suspicious-github-activity-the-wagemole-campaign-and-its-links-to-dprk-threat-actors-248e7901de38


As the interest grew, so did the methods


The continued findings on DPRK IT workers pushed the research further, leading to deeper investigations and, eventually, to collaborating with other researchers who were following the same thread


• Ketman.org: Understanding DPRK IT Worker Activity: Conversations and Insights. A collaborative initiative bringing together researchers to share knowledge and build a broader understanding of DPRK IT worker activity, to which I contributed directly: ketman.org/understanding-dprk-it-workers

• CoinTelegraph: North Korean spy slips up, reveals ties in fake job interview. A feature article in which my investigative findings were cited, covering a North Korean operative who inadvertently exposed their identity during a fraudulent job interview: cointelegraph.com/features/north-korean-spy-reveals-ties

• ANY.RUN: PyLangGhost RAT: Rising Stealer from Lazarus Group Striking Finance and Technology. Sharing a malware sample to analysis report on a newly identified Lazarus Group remote access trojan targeting the finance and technology sectors, to which I contributed threat intelligence findings: any.run/cybersecurity-blog/pylangghost-malware-analysis

• SEAL: From North Korean IT Workers to IT Recruiters. An active collaboration with SEAL, contributing to an investigation tracking the evolution of DPRK IT worker operations from individual job seekers to organized recruiter networks: https://radar.securityalliance.org/from-north-korean-it-workers-to-it-recruiters/

• ANY.RUN: Smile, You're on Camera: A Live Stream from Inside Lazarus Group's IT Workers Scheme. A collaborative investigation conducted alongside other companies, providing a real-time look inside Lazarus Group's IT worker infiltration scheme: any.run/cybersecurity-blog/lazarus-group-it-workers-investigation


Why Northscan.co ?


The activity around this threat vector kept growing, thus I decided to build something more permanent. That is how Northscan was born. Northscan is the platform I created to publish structured, evidence-based threat intelligence on DPRK IT worker operations. All reports are public and free, and the platform runs entirely as an independent effort, without institutional backing or commercial sponsorship.


Why donate?


By contributing with your donations to this project, you are directly funding an independent researcher working to keep this type of differentiated, original intelligence work going


Specifically, your support enables:


• New published investigations into DPRK IT worker campaigns, covering GitHub, freelance platforms, Financial Intelligence and emerging vectors.

• Continued production and public release of indicators of compromise for use by security teams and automated detection pipelines.

• On-chain analysis reports covering new fraud schemes targeting the crypto ecosystem, including drainer operations and Ponzi schemes

•  Ongoing collaboration with the wider intelligence community, contributing to joint investigations and shared knowledge initiatives.


Every report published to date has been a personal effort to generate content that serves the intelligence community rather than any single company or agenda!


Heiner.

title: Symproof by BlockScience & Shield3
description:
Symproof: Uncovering Hidden Axioms in Ethereum Protocol Design by Formalizing the "Math Layer" of Ethereum Security


A project providing essential Infrastructure for institutional-grade security and identifying "unknown unknowns" before they become multi-million dollar exploits, Symproof is an extension of BlockScience’s longstanding work in creating, distributing, and stewarding Ethereum security public goods. The Symproof repo is a modular extension, working prototype, and functional automation of the existing, widely-adopted cadCAD, MSML, and Token Engineering tools, frameworks, and practices we have stewarded since 2017. It codifies both our longstanding open-source and proprietary work in the underlying math and security logic that has protected billions in TVL and refined grant programs by flagging and reducing fraud. It enables the automation and scaling of this security work as a public good and the formal proof-checking extension for the cadCAD modeling ecosystem.


Project Overview


Ethereum security currently operates at primarily two layers: manual auditing and formal code verification. Symproof is an open-source library built on SymPy that adds a third layer - verifying that the mathematical formulas underpinning a protocol have their claimed properties before any code is written. 


Tools like Certora verify code correctness, while tools like Slither find common vulnerability patterns in code. Neither is designed to verify that the specification's math is correct in the first place. A class of security failures involves mathematical invariant violations that were present at the specification level - conditions that downstream tools inherit as assumptions rather than check.


Symproof allows researchers to write small, focused, hashed proofs about formulas. Each proof answers one question: does this formula have this property, given these assumptions? It uses SymPy's simplify(), ask(), and refine() for symbolic verification, and srepr() for deterministic serialization of expressions into proof hashes. Assumptions are explicit and hashed into the proof identity - changing an assumption changes the hash. Inherited axioms (conditions forced by an external theorem rather than chosen by the proof author) must carry a Citation (source="..."). The full chain from a protocol's proof back to the academic result it depends on is traceable by design. This allows for surfacing, documenting and testing the mathematical underpinnings of DeFi, ZK, and other protocols. 


As Symproof is built on SymPy, auditors are one step from numerical evaluation. SymPy expressions can be passed directly to lambdify() to produce numerical Python functions and test vectors, moving from a symbolic proof to concrete validation without leaving the tool. Where SymPy's verification is heuristic rather than complete, the proof says so. The result carries an advisory flagging the specific concern and the step it applies to.


Proof bundles are permanent and composable. Instead of mathematical facts about a formula pattern being re-derived independently for each audit, a verified bundle can be published and imported by hash into future work. This makes security research cumulative across engagements rather than within them and allows for further Public Goods development across protocol security domains. Future projects could import these bundles (e.g., "Uniswap v3 Tick Arithmetic Invariants") rather than re-deriving them, raising the security floor for the entire ecosystem.


The Gap & Our Proposal


The Problem: The "Hidden Axiom" Gap


In practice, teams often cite mathematical theorems without verifying whether Ethereum's operational constraints satisfy the theorem's implicit conditions. The knowledge produced by each audit then lives in static PDFs, where every auditor re-derives the same facts independently, and errors propagate through every downstream layer until they surface as exploits. No practical tool exists for making formula-level claims machine-checkable and reusable before code is written.


High-reliability systems fail when their environment violates their mathematical assumptions. If an engineer cites a theorem without checking its preconditions against Ethereum's constraints, the proof is incomplete, while the gap may not be visible until it is expensive.


The Solution: Machine-Checkable, Cumulative Security


Symproof makes mathematical assumptions explicit, hashed, and independently verifiable. It introduces three properties to the security workflow that do not currently exist together in any available tool:


  • Assumption Transparency. All axioms are explicit and hashed. If an assumption changes, the proof hash changes. Hidden simplifications become hard errors, as the framework refuses to proceed if a proof depends on a condition that isn't declared.
  • Decomposition. Complex protocols are broken into focused Proof Bundles. Rounding Direction, Overflow Bounds, Entropy Leakage - each reviewable independently. Specialists can verify one property without reading the rest.
  • Honest Confidence. When verification reaches a known limitation of the underlying symbolic engine, Symproof attaches an Advisory rather than passing silently - explicitly flagging where human review is still required. Beyond advisories, seal() actively rejects provably false axioms, contradictory axiom pairs, and proofs where lemma assumptions contradict the declared axiom set. The framework is designed to fail loudly rather than pass silently.


Together these properties address a structural problem in Ethereum security: research is not always cumulative. By automating the derivation of mathematical ground truth, Symproof allows human auditors to focus on genuinely novel risks, reducing the cost of thorough security review across the ecosystem and creating a multiplier effect on auditor productivity. This is especially valuable as the complexity of deployed protocols continues to outpace the supply of qualified reviewers. Symproof additionally ships with structured LLM guidance (as a Claude Code skill.md file) that lowers the barrier to writing correct proofs, making the framework accessible to security engineers who are not specialists in symbolic mathematics.


What This Is vs. What It Is Not


What Symproof Is

  • A Pythonic framework built on SymPy for making the mathematical assumptions of DeFi and ZK protocols explicit, hashed, and independently verifiable
  • A design-phase tool - it operates before Solidity is written, on the formulas themselves
  • A growing library of reusable, pre-proved components for common Ethereum formula patterns: AMM arithmetic, ZK circuits, fixed-point rounding, vault invariants
  • Accessible to security engineers who are not specialists in symbolic mathematics - the repo ships with structured LLM guidance that assists in writing correct proofs
  • Equipped with falsity and consistency guards - seal() rejects self-contradictory axiom sets and proofs that depend on undeclared load-bearing assumptions, before verification runs


What Symproof Is Not

  • A replacement for Certora, Halmos, or Slither - it sits beneath them, ensuring the specification those tools verify is itself sound
  • A Solidity verifier or runtime monitor
  • A full theorem prover - it is less rigorous than Lean or Coq, more rigorous than auditor inspection, and designed for the workflow of practicing security engineers


In short: Symproof tells you what properties to prove and verifies the math behind them - formal verification then checks that the code delivers those properties, and fuzzing finds edge cases at runtime. Each layer depends on the one below it being sound.


Applications


AMM Mathematical Audits

Symproof allows auditors to verify AMM formula properties at the design stage: swap output positivity under declared reserve and fee conditions, rounding direction at each step of an execution pipeline, uint256 overflow safety under realistic reserve sizes, and correct cross-decimal normalization (e.g., USDC at 6 decimals against WETH at 18). Each property is a separate, independently verifiable proof bundle. As such, a finding on overflow safety does not depend on the rounding proof being read first.


ZK Circuit Security & Soundness

Symproof supports verification of R1CS witness satisfaction and symbolic analysis of output entropy. An AND gate provably leaks more information about its inputs than an XOR gate - symproof can quantify this difference as a Shannon entropy bound. This gives researchers a symbolic handle on information leakage that complements but does not replace cryptographic soundness proofs.


Protocol Specification & Hidden Axioms

When a protocol cites an external theorem to justify a security property, it inherits that theorem's preconditions. If those preconditions are not explicitly declared, the proof has a gap. The theorem holds in the abstract but may not hold under the protocol's specific constraints. Symproof surfaces these hidden axioms by requiring every assumption to be declared and hashed into the proof. A proof that depends on an undeclared condition is a hard error, not a warning. Where an axiom is inherited from an external theorem, it must carry a Citation naming the source. The assumption chain is traceable from the protocol's proof bundle back to the named academic result. Not just declared, but attributed.


Rounding Pipeline Integrity

Multi-step DeFi pipelines accumulate rounding errors across deposit, swap, fee, and withdrawal operations. The direction of each rounding (whether it favors the pool or the user) determines whether the protocol is sound or leaking value. Symproof proves the net rounding direction across an entire pipeline symbolically, identifying directional errors before the code is written. Rounding bugs in this class have been exploited in production; catching them at the formula level is substantially cheaper than catching them after deployment.


Working Output & Further Technical Details


The project is not just a proposal, but already has a functional, installable, Apache 2.0 licensed codebase with a test suite, domain libraries, and runnable examples.

Repository: BlockScience/sympy-proof

License: Apache 2.0 (currently MIT, see Issue #10) 

Dependencies: SymPy ≥ 1.12, Pydantic ≥ 2.0, Python ≥ 3.12


The library in its current form includes:

  • A proof engine (seal(), verify_proof(), verify_lemma()) that enforces assumption transparency, hash binding, and honest confidence via the advisory system
  • Domain libraries covering AMM arithmetic, ZK circuits, fixed-point rounding, convex optimization, linear programming, control systems, and Shannon information theory
  • Runnable audit examples: including a full AMM swap audit producing eight independent proof bundles and a DIP routing case study that surfaced seven hidden axioms across three proof pairs
  • A ProofBuilder chainable API for constructing proof scripts without boilerplate
  • Structured LLM guidance for assisted proof writing, lowering the barrier for security engineers who are not specialists in symbolic mathematics

All proofs are deterministic: running the same proof twice produces the same SHA-256 hash. The codebase is managed with uv and linted with ruff.


Roadmap & Further Work: From Core Engine to Ecosystem Standard


We consider the Symproof core engine as functional and the foundational design decisions as proven, but a working research tool and a usable public library are different things. The roadmap describes the sequence of work required to close that gap, and to build the domain coverage that makes the tool valuable beyond the team that built it. The three phases follow a deliberate dependency order.


Phase 1 is a prerequisite for everything else. An open-source library that external contributors cannot install, understand, or extend reliably is not a public good. The provenance infrastructure (citation tracking, inherited axiom marking, foundation enforcement) is stabilized here as the documented backbone that all domain libraries build on.


Phase 2 establishes credibility and accessibility through application. Domain libraries built on an unvalidated tool are unconvincing. A public, reproducible analysis of a nine-figure incident (the Balancer V2 rounding exploit) demonstrates what the tool can actually catch, where its scope ends, and how it connects to the broader verification stack. This is the reference case that makes Phase 3 libraries trustworthy rather than theoretical.


Phase 3 is where the compounding effect begins. Each domain library published as a hashable proof bundle is a permanent contribution to the ecosystem. An auditor reviewing a Uniswap v3 fork two years from now can import a verified tick arithmetic bundle rather than re-deriving the mathematics. The value accumulates across every subsequent audit that uses the same formula patterns, where audit by audit, the baseline rises.


The extent of Phase 3 scales with available funding. The priority order is listed in the Use of Funds section. The measure of success is not components shipped but whether a practicing Ethereum security engineer can reduce their mathematical re-derivation work drastically for the covered patterns.



Use of Funds


This grant funds the transition of Symproof from a specialized internal tool to a public-grade security standard. Each tier of funding unlocks a more complex "Domain Library," expanding the safety net for Ethereum developers and auditors.


Tier 1: Open Source Foundation (<$25k)

Focus: Making the tool genuinely usable by external Ethereum security researchers (extent pending actual funding amount reached)

  • Resolution of known soundness issues prior to public release: order-independent axiom set hashing (Issue #5), lemma assumption justification enforcement (#4), INFERENCE lemma structural validation (Issue #3)
  • CI/CD pipeline with automated test and lint runs on every commit (Issue #9)
  • Documentation site hosted on GitHub Pages (Issue #7)
  • License corrected to Apache 2.0 (Issue #10)
  • API stabilization, dependency packaging, and clean pip install across supported Python versions
  • Comprehensive test suite expansion covering edge cases, adversarial axiom sets, and documented failure modes
  • Reference documentation for all public API surfaces and contribution guidelines for external domain library authors
  • Structured onboarding for security engineers without a symbolic mathematics background - including a worked mock audit walkthrough from whitepaper formula to sealed proof bundle
  • Stabilization of the assumption provenance API: Citation, inherited, foundations= documented and stable enough to build on


Tier 2: Case Study ($25k–$50k)

Focus: Demonstrating the tool against a real exploit with documented impact (extent pending actual funding amount reached)

Context: The Balancer V2 Composable Stable Pool exploit (November 2025, $94.8M) was not a code bug. The Solidity code executed correctly. The flaw was in the mathematical specification: the <_upscale> function rounded <amountOut> down through the exact-out path, causing <amountIn> to also round down, meaning callers systematically underpaid and the pool invariant decreased with every swap.

  • This is a formula rounding direction property. It is stateable as a symproof hypothesis and the directional chain proof through <_upscale → StableMath> would have failed pre-deployment, surfacing the gap before any code was written.


The deliverable is a fully public, worked Symproof analysis of the exploit:

  • Domain library correctness audit prior to case study publication: convex_hessian() (Issue #1) and lyapunov_stability() (Issue #2) fixes, plus a systematic review of all domain library functions for similar criterion errors
  • A complete proof bundle targeting the rounding direction property of the exact-out swap path
  • Explicit hidden axiom enumeration: what conditions the stable swap math implicitly requires that the V2 specification never declared
  • A documented finding in symproof's evidence format: hypothesis, axiom set, proof failure, and the corrected hypothesis that V3's architecture satisfies

The report will also sketch how simulation and formal verification would extend the finding: characterizing exploitability under different liquidity conditions, and asserting the corrected invariant in code. The case study will trace the full verification chain from symbolic proof of the formula flaw, through simulation of exploitability conditions, to formal assertion of the corrected invariant in code, demonstrating where symproof fits in that chain and what each subsequent layer adds, even where those layers are illustrated rather than fully executed.


Scope: symproof surfaces the formula flaw. Connecting it to the full attack path requires human judgment and additional tooling. The case study documents that boundary explicitly.

Outcome: a public, reproducible analysis of a nine-figure incident demonstrating exactly what formula-level verification catches and where it hands off to the next layer.


Tier 3: Domain Libraries (e.g.: DeFi, ZK, …) (+$50k)

Focus: Reusable proof components for the most common Ethereum formula patterns (extent pending actual funding amount reached)

Builds on Tier 1 infrastructure and Tier 2 Case Study. All work is greenfield mathematical formalization e.g.:

Uniswap v3 concentrated liquidity

  • Tick boundary arithmetic: 1.0001^tick encoding, square root price representation, boundary conditions at tick transitions
  • Token amount formulas: provable bounds on token quantities as a function of liquidity and price range
  • Price impact bounds: symbolic upper bounds on output shortfall as a function of input size and in-range liquidity depth

Generalized AMM invariants

  • Stable swap curves: invariant conservation under swap, rounding direction through the Newton iteration, output positivity under the Curve formula
  • Weighted pools: power function invariant conservation, rounding direction, output bounds as a function of weight parameters

Fixed-point arithmetic

  • Directed rounding proofs for WAD and RAY scale operations
  • Chained error bounds across multi-step pipelines
  • Overflow safety conditions parameterized by reserve size

Sandwich attack profitability bounds

  • Symbolic upper bounds on sandwich profit as a function of pool depth and input size — formula-level only
  • Does not model mempool ordering, gas competition, or partial fills

ZK circuit expansion

  • R1CS witness satisfaction for multi-constraint systems
  • Output entropy bounds for single and small composed gate circuits (larger circuits likely require research beyond SymPy's current capabilities)

We partner with organizations in healthcare, energy, finance, and government to develop and integrate new capabilities while maintaining reliable operations.
