title: The Obol Collective
description:
Obol builds Distributed Validator Technology (DVT) for Ethereum. Our flagship software, Charon, is a middleware client that enables any Ethereum validator to run across multiple independent nodes instead of relying on a single machine. It works by sitting between the consensus client and validator client, coordinating threshold signing across a cluster of nodes - so a validator can tolerate node failures, network partitions, and even compromised operators without going offline or getting slashed.


Charon clusters use Distributed Key Generation so the validator's private key never exists in one place - a threshold of independent nodes (e.g., 3-of-4) must agree to sign, eliminating single points of failure. This active-active redundancy replaces fragile failover setups that are the leading cause of double-signing slashing events on Ethereum. Because Charon is middleware, each node in a cluster can run different execution and consensus clients, reducing correlated failure risk from client bugs and improving Ethereum’s client diversity. And by distributing trust across multiple independent operators, DVT directly mitigates the concentration risk that forced the emergency exit of over 1.6M ETH from a single compromised provider in September 2025.


Obol currently secures billions in staked ETH across mainnet, trusted by protocols including Lido, EtherFi, and Liquid Collective, and more, as well as operators and traditional financial institutions including Blockdaemon, Bitcoin Suisse, New Zealand ETPs, and the even state of Lichtenstein. Obol actively decentralises and thus secures Ethereum with this technology.

title: KaiSign - Decentralized Clear Signing Registry
description:
What KaiSign is:

Every day, people approve blockchain transactions they do not fully understand.

Instead of seeing clear information like “Approve 1,000 USDC to Uniswap Router”or “Deposit 500 USDC into Aave”, users are often shown raw transaction data, unreadable contract calls, and long strings of hexadecimal code. This is one of the biggest usability and security problems in Web3. It makes phishing easier, creates avoidable mistakes, and forces people to trust what they cannot verify.

KaiSign is building decentralized clear-signing metadata infrastructure to solve this problem.

KaiSign helps turn opaque transaction data into human-readable information so users, wallets, and protocols can understand what is actually being signed before assets are put at risk.

Why people should care

Blind signing is not just a bad user experience, it is a serious ecosystem problem.

When users cannot clearly understand a transaction, they are more likely to:

  • approve malicious token allowances,
  • sign phishing transactions,
  • interact with contracts they do not trust,
  • and lose funds through confusion rather than intent.

This affects everyone in Web3: users who want safety, developers who want trust, wallets that want better UX, and protocols that want more transparent interactions.

If Web3 is going to reach mainstream users, signing a transaction cannot feel like guessing.

KaiSign exists to make signing safer, clearer, and more trustworthy.

Why KaiSign matters

KaiSign is not only building a product. It is building public infrastructure for safer blockchain interactions.

The project focuses on decentralized metadata curation for clear signing, so that contract actions can be described, reviewed, verified, and distributed in a way that does not depend entirely on a single centralized party.

That matters because security infrastructure for Web3 should be open, auditable, and useful across the ecosystem.

KaiSign is designed to support a future where:

  • users can verify what they are signing,
  • wallets can display meaningful transaction details,
  • protocols can make interactions easier to trust,
  • and autonomous agents can safely verify that a transaction matches user intent.

Current progress

KaiSign has already made real progress.

The project has:

  • a Chrome extension for previewing transactions before signing,
  • a builder for clear-signing metadata workflows,
  • documentation for the project’s architecture and workflow,
  • and an active focus on deploying the decentralized metadata submission and attestation registry.

KaiSign has also already communicated a clear use case to the ecosystem: transform unreadable blockchain interactions into understandable signing information.


What donations will support

Donations will help KaiSign move from an early-stage security tool into stronger, more decentralized public goods infrastructure for Web3.

Protocol and contract deployment

Advancing the deployment and reliability of the infrastructure behind decentralized clear-signing metadata.

Decentralization

Increasing participation and distribution so KaiSign can move toward minimum viable decentralization.

Developer tooling

Improving the builder, submission flows, documentation, and onboarding for projects that want to support clear signing.

Security and verification

Strengthening the review and validation systems that make metadata trustworthy and useful.

Adoption and ecosystem growth

Expanding the number of supported contracts, contributors, reviewers, protocols, wallets, and end users.

Wallet readiness

Helping make clear signing easier to integrate across wallet experiences, including future hardware-wallet support.

Goals

Short-term goals

  • Improve developer and protocol onboarding
  • Increase community participation in metadata review

Medium-term goals

  • Move toward stronger deployment and decentralization
  • Make KaiSign easier for wallets and protocols to integrate
  • Improve transparency, trust, and auditability
  • Support more common DeFi, NFT, and governance transaction types

Long-term vision

KaiSign can become foundational infrastructure for safe transaction signing in Web3.

The long-term goal is a decentralized system that helps users, wallets, protocols, and autonomous agents understand exactly what is being signed before approval happens.

Why donate

If you care about safer Web3 UX, phishing resistance, better wallet security, and open public infrastructure, KaiSign is worth supporting.

Crypto adoption will not scale if people are expected to sign transactions they cannot read.

Your donation helps fund infrastructure that can improve safety and trust across the ecosystem, not just for one app, but for users, developers, wallets, and protocols across Web3.

title: Zodiac
description:
🛡️ Zodiac: Open-Source Security Infrastructure for Onchain Entities


👥 Who We Are

Zodiac is an open-source project developed by Gnosis Guild, a team of smart contract engineers and DAO tooling practitioners building composable, non-custodial infrastructure for onchain organizations. Our work sits at the intersection of Ethereum security and decentralized operations. We build the permissioning primitives that DAOs, protocols, and treasury management teams rely on to stay secure while executing at scale. The Zodiac protocol is already trusted by some of the most consequential organizations in the Ethereum ecosystem, including Safe, ENS DAO, Balancer, Gnosis DAO, and kpk, collectively securing several billion dollars worth of onchain assets.


🔩 What We've Built

Zodiac is a collection of open-source smart contracts and tooling built according to a composable open standard, freely available at github.com/gnosisguild/zodiac. It extends systems like Safe with modular permissions, security controls, and governance execution, without sacrificing security or custody.

The core components of the open standard include:

  • Roles Modifier — Fine-grained, role-based access control enforced entirely onchain. Defines exactly which contracts can be called, which functions can be invoked, and what parameter constraints apply. Permissions are checked by the smart contract at execution time, not by operational trust or an off-chain service.
  • Delay Modifier — Enforces a configurable time delay between when a module initiates a transaction and when it executes, providing a critical window for intervention in the event of a compromised key or malicious proposal.
  • Scope Guard — Limits the set of addresses and functions that a module or signer can interact with, preventing unauthorized or out-of-scope transactions at the contract level.
  • Bridge, Reality, Governor, and Exit Modules — A suite of governance execution modules enabling cross-chain control, Snapshot-based on-chain execution, OpenZeppelin-style governance, and rage-quit mechanics, all built to the open Zodiac standard.

The library has 481 GitHub stars, 114 forks, and over 608 commits. It is licensed under LGPL-3.0 and has been independently audited by the G0 Group.


❓ Why It Matters for Ethereum Security

The dominant threat model for DAO and protocol treasuries isn't a smart contract exploit: it's operational risk. Multisigs with overly broad signer access, undocumented delegation practices, and a lack of onchain accountability are responsible for a significant share of value lost and governance failures across the ecosystem. When teams grow, when operations get routine, when signers become bottlenecks, the pressure to expand access increases. And expanded access without constraints means an expanded attack surface.

Zodiac's open-source permissioning layer addresses this directly. By encoding access rules as verifiable, auditable, onchain policies rather than relying on social trust or off-chain systems, Zodiac reduces the risk profile of complex treasury operations without requiring teams to sacrifice efficiency or decentralization. Security enforced by code is security that can be verified, audited, and trusted by anyone.

This is foundational Ethereum security infrastructure, protecting more than $2 billion in onchain assets. It is the kind of work that is easy to overlook when nothing goes wrong, and catastrophically visible when something does.


🌍 Where We Operate

Zodiac contracts are deployed across all major EVM-compatible networks where Safe is supported, including Ethereum Mainnet, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, Polygon, and Gnosis Chain. As an open standard, the protocol is framework-agnostic and can be used with any programmable account that implements the IAvatar interface, not just Safe. The tooling is permissionlessly available to any developer or organization in the ecosystem.


⚙️ How Funds Will Be Used

Support through TheDAO Security Fund's ETH Security grant will directly help sustain and extend Zodiac's open-source security infrastructure: continued maintenance of core contracts and SDKs, security audits for Roles and new modules, stronger developer documentation and integration support, and grants for external builders extending the standard.


📅 When — Status and Roadmap

The Zodiac library is live, audited, and in active production use. Near-term development focus includes expanded parameter constraint tooling in the Roles Modifier, additional audit coverage for new modules, and deeper integration support for teams building on the standard.

👉 Support open, auditable infrastructure for secure onchain operations.

Source code: github.com/gnosisguild/zodiac | Community: discord.gnosisguild.org

title: human.tech
description:
Protecting Users with Protected Self Custody.

Ethereum wallets have always been the target. Phishing, malware, malicious dApps, compromised key infrastructure and the attack surface has grown every year. What's changed is who, and what, is holding the keys.


There are ~250,000 AI agents active on-chain at the date of this writing, and that number is growing fast. By the end of 2026, most on-chain transactions are expected to be agent-driven. Agents are signing transactions, moving capital, and managing portfolios without any human directly in the loop.


The problem is not that agents are autonomous. This is a good thing. The real problem is that there is no native proof that a human — sometimes with certain attributes — ever authorized any of it. A signature is a signature, and anyone with access to a private key can generate it. So how do we tell agents from humans, and more specifically which agents are acting dutifully on behalf of true human authority?


 We have built two key primitives to solve this problem:

 1. Secure Secrets Management — keep humans in control of the loop by securing their keys (waap.xyz)

 2. Proof of Humanity — prove the human in the loop is likely human (passport.xyz)


 Wallet as a Protocol (waap.xyz) enforces what agents can do. Passport is the identity layer that proves who authorized them to do it. This maps directly to what ERC-8004 and the Ethereum Foundation's dAI team are building toward: an identity and validation standard for trustless agents that traces back to real humans.



WaaP: Who Needs Keys when you have Collaborative Signing?

https://docs.waap.xyz


Wallet as a Protocol (WaaP) is wallet infrastructure for autonomous agents, built on 2PC (Two-Party Computation) cryptography to shore up an aggressive security model:


  1. Don't trust the device (malware exists)
  2. Don't trust the user (makes errors at 3am)
  3. Don't trust the app embedding the wallet (can be malicious)
  4. Don't trust the smart contract (could be zero day r.i.p.)
  5. Don't trust the key infra (bug, collusion)
  6. And absolutely don't trust the agent with the private key.


How do we do this? The private key in practice doesn't exist. Instead it is split into two shares, the Sovereign Share (k₁) and the Security Share (k₂). The full key k = k₁ + k₂ is never reconstructed anywhere. Instead, when a transaction needs signing, both parties run an interactive protocol to jointly compute a valid ECDSA signature. Each party contributes their share to produce a signature (s) from a message (m): s = r⁻¹(H(m) + x·Rₓ) mod n, where x is the private key, r is the nonce, and n is the curve order.


This occurs without either share ever leaving its owner or needing to know x or r. The mathematics makes unilateral signing structurally impossible: a valid on-chain signature requires both parties to have participated.


The Sovereign Share is kept on the user's device and never exposed to any third party. The Security Share lives in a Trusted Execution Environment (for privacy) or on-chain (for censorship-resistance) with a verifiable programmable policy engine. Neither share can sign a transaction alone. Policies can be set by the user, the dApp, or both to keep the user safe against known or evolving threats.



The policy engine enforces daily spend limits, whitelisted contracts, and auto-approve rules for routine operations. An agent literally cannot exceed what the owner defined. When a transaction falls outside that scope, a one-tap approve or deny goes to Telegram, email, SMS, or a hardware wallet. In this flow, agents propose a transaction, humans approve it, and on-chain protocols enforce its settlement.


WaaP also includes Privileges: scoped, time-bounded capabilities enforced server-side (maximum two hours) that let agents operate within pre-approved bounds without interrupting the human for every transaction. Every transaction is simulated before signing to catch malicious payloads before they execute.


WaaP supports all EVM chains at runtime, plus Sui and Stellar, with Solana coming in Q2 2026. WaaP wallets work as signers for ERC-4337 Smart Accounts, enabling full account abstraction including gas sponsorship, batched transactions, and session keys, on top of 2PC security across chains. The SDK is a drop-in EIP-1193 replacement compatible with wagmi, ethers.js, and viem. A headless CLI gives agents wallet access with the same policy enforcement applied. Integration is free.


Passport: Who Is the Human Behind the Agent?

https://docs.passport.xyz


2PC solves what agents can do. Passport solves who authorized them to do it.


Human Passport is a ZK-powered proof-of-personhood system with over 2.4 million verified users, 43 million credentials issued, more than $512 million in capital protected from Sybil attacks, and 175+ partner projects. It is one of the most widely deployed proof-of-personhood systems in web3, originally built in Gitcoin to protect quadratic funding rounds and later folded into the human.tech stack by Holonym Foundation in December 2024.


Passport is how you prove a verified human exists at the root of every agent delegation chain. When an agent acts, the chain of authority traces back to a real person rather than a bot, a farmed wallet, or a Sybil. ZK credentials let users prove humanity, KYC status, and AML compliance on-chain without exposing raw identity data.


Security Program: Audits, Adversarial Testing, Bug Bounties, and Open Research


WaaP's 2PC architecture has already been independently audited four times, by Cure53, Hexens, Least Authority, and Halborn, with additional security consulting from Anderson Software and Distrust. That is the baseline we are building from, not where we stop.


Funds from this round go toward expanding and publishing that work. We will run adversarial testing across agent wallet interaction patterns, Agent Privileges edge cases, and policy engine attack surfaces, specifically targeting the failure modes that appear when agents operate at scale.


We will commission independent audits of new architectural components as WaaP moves more components on-chain and as we ship ERC-8004-aligned agent identity support. We plan to open a bug bounty program to bring the broader Ethereum security community into the process.


Perhaps most importantly, we will publish. Agent wallet security is an unsolved problem at the infrastructure level, and the research should be in the commons. Threat models, audit findings, and architectural decisions will be published as open source work so the ecosystem can build on what we learn.



Why Donate

VCs fund distribution. They do not fund the security research, public audits, and open tooling that the whole ecosystem depends on. This is that work. If human oversight of autonomous agents on Ethereum matters to you, this is a direct way to fund the infrastructure that makes it real.


Under $5k: Seed the dev bounty pool and publish our first open security research: threat model for the 2PC architecture and known attack surfaces for wallet interaction patterns.


$5k–$10k: Focused adversarial testing engagement on Privileges edge cases and policy engine bypass attempts. These are the attack surfaces most specific to agent-scale usage and least covered by our existing audits.


$10k–$25k: Commission an independent audit of the on-chain Security Share components as WaaP moves from TEE-only to on-chain censorship-resistant key management. This is new architecture that hasn't been audited yet.


$25k–$50k: Full adversarial testing engagement plus audit of ERC-8004-aligned agent identity support as we ship it. Expand the dev bounty to a level that actually attracts serious researchers. Begin publishing audit findings and architectural decisions as open research.


$50k+: All of the above, plus dedicated security researcher time to produce a comprehensive public report on wallet security: attack vectors, mitigations, and open problems. This becomes a public good for anyone building in this space, not just for us.


Why TheDAO

The original DAO hack happened because there was no human in the loop to catch what was going wrong. Ten years later, autonomous agents are executing billions in on-chain transactions daily with the same absence of human authority at the root. Human Tech is the infrastructure fix, and funding this work through TheDAO Security Fund is the right origin story.

title: Bitfinding
description:
We are a small Ethereum security team focused on one of the hardest problems in DeFi: stopping exploits while they are happening.

The project was started by @snfernandez and @feliam, and later joined by @0xlucca to continue and expand the mission. We have been doing this since 2024, with no recurring revenue beyond bounties paid by the projects we rescued.


What we do

Most crypto security work happens before or after the attack. We focus on the few seconds in the middle, when funds can still be saved.

Almost nobody operates in the narrow window where an attack is already live and funds can still be saved.﻿

We build and operate an automated whitehat security agent for Ethereum and L2s. The system monitors the chain in real time, detects exploit patterns, validates rescue paths, and executes protective transactions fast enough to secure vulnerable assets before they are stolen.

This is not a research idea or an unfinished prototype. It is working security infrastructure used in real incidents.


Progress so far

Since starting in 2024, our whitehat operations have rescued more than $1.5 million in user and protocol funds.

That includes $1 million in the Balancer rescue alone in less than 12 seconds after the attacker’s first move (writeup).

Other public incident reports also include multiple rescues on Ethereum, Arbitrum, BSC and Base showing the same live interception approach in production (blog).

We were also the first recipients of a confirmed Safe Harbor bounty, helping validate SEAL’s Safe Harbor framework through real exploit interception and fund return. Safe Harbor is SEAL’s framework for pre-authorizing whitehat interventions during active exploits.


Why this matters

Ethereum already has many strong auditors, researchers, and security platforms. That part of the ecosystem is active and well developed. What is still rare is active exploit interception.

Safe Harbor exists because live whitehat intervention is a distinct need: it gives protocols a framework to pre-authorize independent whitehats to step in during active exploits, rescue funds, and return them safely.


How it works

Our system continuously watches Ethereum for patterns associated with active exploitation.

When a high-confidence threat is detected, it reconstructs the likely attack path, checks whether a rescue transaction can succeed, and intervenes when the conditions are right.

Speed matters, but precision matters too. It is not enough to notice suspicious activity. The system has to act correctly, in real time, under pressure.

Each real incident also improves our heuristics and execution logic, making the system stronger as attack patterns evolve.


Why donate

Donations help us keep this system online, low-latency, and ready before the next exploit starts.

Your support helps fund:

  • real-time monitoring infrastructure
  • low-latency execution systems
  • continuous tuning of detection and validation logic
  • incident readiness and maintenance
  • public reporting and updates on results


This project has been sustained mostly through bounties, which means funding is unpredictable even though the work is continuous. Exploits do not wait for a business model.


Where we are going

Our goal is simple: keep building a reliable live-response security layer for Ethereum.

We want to prove that Ethereum security should not stop at passive monitoring or retrospective analysis. When an attack starts, there should be a real chance to intervene and save funds.

title: ECH Institute - EthCatHerders
description:
Who We Are

ECH Institute is a U.S. 501(c)(3) nonprofit and the institutional home of Ethereum's community-led protocol support group. We formally incorporated as a nonprofit in 2024, giving a legal entity to support the Ethereum ecosystem.


ECH Institute is uniquely positioned at the intersection of People, Process, and Protocol.


What We Do

Every protocol improvement passes through a rigorous, open governance process. We coordinate EIPs, support network upgrades, produce educational videos and podcasts, facilitate EIP Editing Office Hours, and run Women in Ethereum Protocol (WiEP) study group cohorts (in association with the Ethereum Foundation) to onboard technical women into Ethereum protocol development. Our work is credibly neutral and owned by the whole community. As a neutral public good, we bridge gaps by empowering individuals with blockchain knowledge, strengthening communities, and supporting the Web3 ecosystem with a strong focus on education and inclusion & diversity.

EIP Process Management

We support the full EIP and ERC lifecycle — from draft review through finalization. Weekly Editing Office Hours, monthly EIPIP governance meetings, and open GitHub stewardship keep proposals moving and the process transparent. We organized EIP Editors workshop & facilitated onboarding new EIP editor. Also, organized the first EIP Summit at Devconnect 2025 bringing EIP Editors, authors, contributors and implementers in one room.


Network Upgrade Coordination


We coordinate and livestreamed most Ethereum network upgrades since 2019. For each hard fork including Pectra and Fusaka (in 2025), ECH produces educational episodes for every included EIP, documents All Core Devs meetings, manages testnet post-mortems, runs community watch parties, and distributes author-recognition NFTs. 12+ upgrades supported; 200+ explainer videos produced.


PEEPanEIP & The Fusaka Files Podcast


PEEPanEIP (135+ episodes) is Ethereum's definitive EIP education series: hour-long conversations with EIP authors covering every major proposal. In 2025 we launched The Fusaka Files - a limited enterprise-focused series co-hosted with Paul Brody (EY Global Blockchain Leader and EEA Chairman), bridging protocol changes like EIP-7594 (PeerDAS), EIP-7825, and EIP-7917 to enterprise and institutional audiences. Guests have included Tomasz Stańczak, prev. Co-Executive Director of Ethereum, Tim Beiko, Alex Stokes, Justin Drake and other Ethereum Foundation researchers.


Women in Ethereum Protocol (WiEP)


Co-founded with the Ethereum Foundation at Edge City Denver on February 29, 2024, WiEP is the only program dedicated to onboarding technical women into Ethereum's core protocol development. In under two years: 4 cohorts completed, 36 women developers onboarded from 21 countries, with ongoing study groups, mentorship, and open-source contributions. Events held at EthCC, EthDenver, EthSingapore (ArtScience Museum, with Ethereum Foundation President Aya Miyaguchi), Devcon, EDCON, Devconnect. WiEP is an amaging opportunity to learn and contribute to the Ethereum ecosystem.


Enterprise Ethereum Education


Protocol changes are not optional background noise for organizations building on Ethereum — they directly affect smart contract compatibility, tooling, and infrastructure planning. ECH Institute provides the clearest window into Ethereum's governance process for enterprise teams. Through our EEA partnership and co-produced The Fusaka Files with Paul Brody, we translate governance proposals, scalability upgrades, and privacy standards into business-context education for teams at EY, JPMorgan, Microsoft, and beyond.


Community Partnership & Onboarding

ECH’s community partnerships focus on onboarding the next generation of contributors into Ethereum’s governance and protocol processes. Through initiatives like Road to Devcon and our collaboration with EthCluj, we create accessible entry points for learning, collaboration, and meaningful participation. Our Learn2Earn platform rewards users for learning Ethereum protocol concepts via quizzes and free NFTs - deployed across Dencun and Pectra upgrade cycles. Our open contributor program, bounty system, ACD Internship, and Discord community (20,000+ members) continuously lower the barrier to participation in Ethereum governance for developers, writers, and researchers worldwide.


Why This Matters

ECH Institute is not building a product. We are maintaining and expanding the public infrastructure that makes Ethereum's open governance work. No single company owns this work; which is exactly why it needs sustained community funding.


Our 2026 priorities reflect where the gaps are largest:

  • Strengthening EIP process research & security, alongside protocol coordination and public governance.
  • Enterprise education on Ethereum upgrades, protocol changes, and ecosystem projects
  • EIP Summit — bringing the global EIP community together
  • Expanding WiEP -scaling the only program onboarding technical women into Ethereum protocol
  • Continued podcast production & content creation.


ECH Institute makes Ethereum's evolution visible, accessible, and reliable, and through WiEP, ensures the next generation of protocol builders reflects the full breadth of human talent.


ECH Institute is a verified 501(c)(3) — U.S. donations may be tax-deductible.

title: K Stack: The Formal Verification Layer for Ethereum
description:
K is the engine behind Ethereum's most rigorous security tooling. It's a universal semantic framework that lets you define a programming language once, precisely and mathematically, and automatically derive a full suite of analysis tools from that single definition. Built and maintained by Runtime Verification over two decades, K is the foundation of an open-source infrastructure stack that secures Ethereum from the smart contract layer down to the clients and cryptographic libraries that run the network.

K powers KEVM — the first complete, executable formal semantics of the EVM. KEVM is a public good the ecosystem depends on: the reference point against which client implementations and zkEVM stacks are checked for correctness, and the foundation that makes formal verification of smart contracts possible. It was used to verify the Ethereum Beacon Chain deposit contract (today holding over 77 million staked ETH), uncovering a subtle compiler bug in the process. More recently, KEVM played a central role in EF-funded zkEVM verification work, proving equivalence with revm and the EVMYul model of EVM in Lean 4 (full report). KEVM has been actively maintained by RV for over eight years, tracking every major Ethereum upgrade through Pectra. 

Kontrol is the developer-facing layer: a free, open-source formal verification tool that lets Solidity developers write formal specifications as Foundry tests, using tools and languages they already know. It is actively used across the Ethereum ecosystem, with production deployments at some of the highest-stakes protocols. Optimism runs Kontrol proofs in CI, verifying Bedrock contract components before every deployment. In the Term Finance engagement, Kontrol proofs caught loop-related vulnerabilities that fuzzing and manual audits had missed. It has been used for pre-deployment formal verification of critical invariants across Lido, Zivoe, Cork Protocol, Levery, and other major protocols. 

As of March 2026, Kontrol is used by 70 projects building on Ethereum. As AI tools for bug-hunting advance and make black-hats ever more productive, the only defense is eliminating all bugs at launch, which only formal verification can achieve. For anyone already writing Foundry tests, Kontrol is the lowest-friction path to formal verification available today.

Beyond the EVM

KWasm provides formal semantics for WebAssembly, which becomes increasingly critical as Arbitrum Stylus, Wasm-based fraud proofs, and Wasm zkVMs become live infrastructure on Ethereum. KWasm is the foundation for Skribe, an open-source property-based testing and fuzzing tool for Arbitrum Stylus contracts.

KMIR brings formal verification to Rust, the language that Ethereum's consensus clients, cryptographic libraries, and ZK proving systems are written in. KMIR makes a deliberate choice to support all of Rust, including unsafe code. This matters because the most security-critical components, such as cryptographic primitives, memory management, and low-level protocol logic, are precisely where unsafe code lives.

RV collaborates directly with AWS on upstream Rust compiler improvements and on stable-mir-json, a tool RV developed that lets any verification tool extract MIR from the rustc toolchain, and toward contributing KMIR to the AWS/Rust Foundation initiative to formally verify the Rust standard library. Improvements to the public MIR interface and to stable-mir-json are public goods that benefit the entire Rust verification ecosystem.

Further down the stack, RV's KRiscV semantics for RISC-V brings formal verification to the instruction set underlying many zkVMs.

Every K-based tool shares the same backends, and any improvement to K benefits all of them simultaneously. This economy of effort is why K punches so far above its weight for a largely unfunded infrastructure project, and sustained support would multiply that leverage further.

A decade of public goods

All tools in the K stack are fully open source under the BSD-3-Clause license. K-related publications have accumulated thousands of academic citations, and the framework has been used to deliver practical security results for NASA, DARPA, Toyota, and Boeing beyond blockchain. 

RV also maintains ERCx, a free, open-source library of over 900 handcrafted Foundry tests for ERC token standards.

This infrastructure has been largely unfunded relative to its importance. RV maintains it because it underpins not just our own tools, but a significant part of Ethereum's formal verification and security ecosystem. Community support is what would help keep it sustainable long-term.

What's next

The immediate priorities are 

  • Keeping KEVM synchronized with Ethereum protocol upgrades
  • AI-assisted workflows for Kontrol that help developers onboard faster and diagnose stuck proofs, and
  • Performance improvements across the stack that benefit both human developers and AI agents driving verification workflows.

Longer-term investments fall into three categories:

  • Strengthening the core: hardening K's Lean 4 backend to benefit from the rapid progress in AI-assisted theorem proving, developing a Rust frontend for K (kframework-rs), and coverage-guided greybox fuzzing over K semantics
  • Expanding coverage: bringing KWasm up to date with the Wasm 3.0 specification for Arbitrum Stylus and emerging Wasm-based zkVMs, and expanding KMIR toward Ethereum client and cryptographic library verification, and
  • Scaling through AI: developing agent capabilities for writing K semantics and working with K-based tools, reducing the cost of both building new formal specifications and using existing ones for verification.

Why your support matters

Runtime Verification has maintained this infrastructure for over a decade, through every hardfork, every new EVM feature, every shift in the ecosystem. Every Kontrol proof, every zkEVM equivalence check, every hardfork-compatible verification engagement depends on someone keeping this stack correct, complete, and current. That work needs sustained community support, and every donation here goes directly toward it.

Funding Breakdown

All donations fund open-source development of RV's formal verification infrastructure. All tools are and will remain freely available under BSD-3-Clause. No portion of donations will support commercial services.

$0 - $15,000: AI-assisted onboarding and proof debugging for Kontrol. Building AI skills and tooling that guide teams using Foundry through setting up Kontrol, writing specifications, diagnosing stuck proofs, generating counterexamples, and suggesting concrete next steps, without requiring RV's direct involvement. This tier funds AI capabilities that can unlock teams that are getting started or stalled, and reduce the need for expert hand-holding on routine proof issues.

$15,000 - $45,000: KEVM hardfork tracking and core maintenance. Keeping KEVM current with Ethereum protocol upgrades is the single most critical ongoing cost, which amounts to about $150,000/year. This tier covers a substantial portion of 2026 maintenance, keeping the semantics synchronized with the chain for Kontrol's 70+ monthly active users and the broader ecosystem that depends on it.

$45,000 - $75,000: Hardening K Framework Lean 4 backend. Making the K-to-Lean extraction pipeline substantially more robust, expanding what can be verified with K-based tools and opening an alternative path for proofs where automated tools hit scalability limits.

$75,000 - $90,000: Agent-facing tooling and documentation for K. Bringing more advanced tutorials, onboarding guides, and structured APIs that lower the barrier for new users and AI agents working with K semantics, running proofs, and interpreting results.

$90,000 - $120,000: Symbolic execution performance improvements. Targeted engineering work on K's Haskell backend, focused on metrics that directly affect KEVM, Kontrol, and KWasm. Faster symbolic execution means more teams can run more challenging proofs in CI without prohibitive runtimes.

$120,000 - $180,000: KWasm Wasm 3.0 update and scaling. Bringing KWasm in line with the Wasm 3.0 specification, which is critical for Arbitrum Stylus and Wasm-based zkVMs, and scaling it to handle larger programs. Newer stable rustc releases are already emitting post-1.0 Wasm instructions that KWasm doesn't yet support, making this increasingly urgent.

$180,000 - $210,000: kframework-rs and greybox fuzzing. A Rust frontend for K modernizes how external tools interact with the framework, replacing the legacy Java frontend with something faster and more ergonomic across every tool in the stack. Coverage-guided greybox fuzzing over K semantics delivers coverage-guided fuzzing across all K language semantics simultaneously.

$210,000+: KMIR, AI skills for K, and Rust infrastructure verification. This tier funds upstream rustc improvements and stable-mir-json hardening, expanding KMIR's language coverage guided by real verification targets, and introducing further AI agent capabilities for writing K semantics, reducing the cost of building new formal specifications and K-based tools.

title: WiiMee | Wallet Security Education
description:
Users need to feel safe to act confidently in crypto.

And still, every day, users lose funds not because of sophisticated smart contract exploits but because of simple, preventable mistakes. Signing malicious transactions, exposing seed phrases, interacting with compromised websites or falling for social engineering attacks.


The education gap is massive, and I'm here to help make wallet security more understandable and actionable for everyday users. Since 2021 I've been focused on closing the gap with content in written and video form around security education.


The content is designed to meet users where they are, on social platforms like X and YouTube.

My goal is to simplify complex security concepts into clear insights. The variety of topics goes from wallet hygiene to approval risks, seed phrase security, malware threats, smart account risks (EIP-7702) to emerging scam patterns.


The end goal is to prevent losses before they happen. Because this is really the biggest weapon we have. I hate to be the guy to break it down to a person that got scammed, that they will never see their funds again.


I'm deeply invested in the security ecosystem and I'm currently working with Revoke.cash, Boring Security and ChainPatrol to elevate and distribute education even further.

title: Bluechip
description:
Stablecoins are the backbone of DeFi, but most users still can't answer a basic question: is my stablecoin actually safe? Terra showed what happens when that question goes unasked. Bluechip exists to make sure it never goes unanswered.


Bluechip is the first, independent stablecoin rating agency built as a public good for the Ethereum ecosystem. Our security research benefits stablecoin holders, DAO contributors, and DeFi protocols by allowing them to make informed decisions. All ratings are available via our website (bluechip.org) or API.


Our SMIDGE framework is the first publicly available, factor-based risk model for rating stablecoin safety. We score six factors (Stability, Management, Implementation, Decentralization, Governance, and Externals) and assign letter-grade ratings (from A+ to F). These factors cover what actually matters: reserve composition, redemption rights, smart contract risk, and more.


We also host an annual conference dedicated to crypto safety that draws a curated audience of institutional users. The Bluechip25 edition was hosted in partnership with the Ethereum Foundation. Your support helps us rate more stablecoins, and develop frameworks to expand beyond stablecoins.

title: Tool Against Price Manipulation Attacks in DeFi on EVM
description:
Automated Price Manipulation and Flash Loan Attack Discovery for Composable DeFi Systems

Prepared and submitted by Martin Derka, Head of New Initiatives @ Quantstamp and Co-Founder @ Zircuit, ETH Security Badge #29.


Most DeFi attacks no longer exploit isolated bugs, but behaviors emerging across protocol compositions. Exploits driven by asset price manipulation, with or without flash loans, are a prominent cause of losses arising from carefully orchestrated interactions between lending markets, AMMs, and oracles.

This proposal aims to advance the state of DeFi security by modernizing and making accessible to the broader Ethereum community FlashSyn (2024, Z. Chen et al.), a research tool developed at the University of Toronto that has already demonstrated strong effectiveness in discovering real-world flash loan exploits.


We propose to improve its usability and reliability by addressing the currently known drawbacks that prevent FlashSyn from wider adoption, extend it into a continuous monitoring system for EVM-compatible chains, and release the result as an open-source tool for the ecosystem.


Motivation


Modern DeFi exploits are increasingly compositional: attackers construct multi-step strategies that span multiple protocols and exploit assumptions that only break under composition.


A canonical attack pipeline looks as follows:

  1. An attacker enters with capital, potentially obtained via a flash loan
  2. Manipulate price or liquidity in one protocol
  3. Exploit mispriced collateral or accounting in another
  4. Extract back the capital, possibly repay the flash loan, and extract profit


Each step is valid in isolation; the protocols operate as they are intended to, but the systemic vulnerability emerges only when actions are composed.


This shift is well documented and relevant for Ethereum in 2026:

  • Industry data confirms the trend: flash loan and manipulation attacks account for a large share of DeFi losses, often involving multiple protocols: https://www.halborn.com/reports/top-100-defi-hacks-2025
  • Ethereum alone saw 92 incidents and ~$470M in losses in H1 2025, many tied to pricing and logic flaws in composable systems: https://thedefiant.io/news/research-and-opinion/ethereum-hit-by-most-security-incidents-in-h1-2025-slowmist
  • FlashSyn models attacks explicitly as "sequences of actions across DeFi protocols" : https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.10708
  • Prior work shows flash loan attacks rely on atomic composability and cross-protocol interactions → https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.03810
  • Recent examples such as KiloEx (April 2025), Moonwell (November 2025), and Silo Finance (June 2025) reinforce that these exploits often rely on cross-protocol price manipulation and liquidity feedback loops.


The ecosystem has responded to smart contract security threats primarily by embedding audits into the development process. Yet the numbers demonstrate that audits can fail to surface vulnerabilities of this kind. This is precisely where automated tooling can close the gap.


Background: FlashSyn in Practice


FlashSyn is an open-source research tool, released under the Apache 2.0 license, developed by Z. Chen et al. at the University of Toronto. It is the first automated end-to-end program synthesis tool for detecting flash loan attack vulnerabilities.


FlashSyn models potential exploits as parameterized sequences of actions across multiple DeFi protocols, where each action represents a valid interaction (e.g., swaps, borrows, approvals) with placeholder parameters. It systematically generates and executes combinations of these actions, identifying sequences that do not revert and produce measurable changes in the attacker's balance.


To efficiently search this space, FlashSyn approximates the resulting profit as a multivariate polynomial function over the action parameters using sampled executions. It then analyzes this approximation to find profitable extrema and validates them through concrete EVM execution, confirming whether a true exploit exists.


Using FlashSyn requires several expert steps, primarily: extracting relevant protocol actions, defining pricing relationships, and occasionally mocking infrastructure dependencies. The tool's authors and Quantstamp (also the current maintainers of the repository) have proceduralized these steps. Quantstamp actively uses FlashSyn in its security offering, and it has successfully and reliably rediscovered exploits including bZx, Eminence, Harvest, Value DeFi, CheeseBank, Warp, Yearn, InverseFi, bEarnFi, AutoShark, ElevenFi, ApeRocket, WDoge, Novo, OneRing, and Euler.


See the following resources for more details:

  • Automated Flash Loan Attack Synthesis (DeFi Security Summit, 2023)
  • FlashSyn: Flash Loan Attack Synthesis via Counter Example Driven Approximation


Proposed Work


Despite the apparent strength of the tool and its open-source license, community-wide adoption remains limited. We believe this is caused by the following shortcomings:

  • Manual, expert-heavy action definition to guide the search
  • Non-trivial setup and protocol-specific configuration


We propose to transform FlashSyn into a practical, automated, and extensible security tool for the broader Ethereum community.


1. AI-Augmented Action Extraction

The overhead that necessitates expert use is primarily action extraction and protocol setup. We believe that an LLM can effectively substitute an expert by inferring actions from the codebase, ABIs, transaction history, test suite, and documentation. It can also iteratively refine those actions based on execution feedback from subsequent steps.


2. Tooling, Optimization, and Usability

The goal is to refactor FlashSyn into a clean codebase with a simple interface and smooth developer experience, targeting a workflow as straightforward as:


git clone ...

flashsyn run ...


3. Continuous Monitoring

To date, FlashSyn has only been used for one-time analyses of protocols. The techniques it employs are, however, well-suited for continuous post-deployment monitoring. This opens up valuable new directions: detecting vulnerabilities triggered by changes in protocol integrations or configurations, and alerting to risks introduced by shallow liquidity pools. These directions have not been explored in prior work.


4. Reusable Protocol Artifacts

Using FlashSyn for protocol analyses inherently produces reusable artifacts, including protocol deployment configurations and action definitions. We intend to collect these artifacts in the repository and make them available for future reuse and more advanced analyses across the community.

title: Soldeer
description:
Soldeer is a lightweight package manager for Solidity that focuses on fixing one of the most painful and underdeveloped parts of the ecosystem: dependency management.


Today, most Solidity projects depend on a mix of Git submodules, manual imports, or npm-based setups. In practice, that leads to brittle builds, unclear versioning, and a lot of time wasted debugging dependency issues instead of writing contracts. Soldeer introduces a clean, native approach to handling dependencies in a way that actually fits how smart contracts are built and deployed.


With Soldeer, developers can install and manage dependencies in a deterministic way. For example, instead of adding a Git submodule for a library like OpenZeppelin and hoping everyone on the team keeps it in sync, you can simply declare it as a dependency and lock its version. That means every developer and every CI run uses the exact same code, eliminating “it works on my machine” issues.


It also supports pulling dependencies from multiple sources. You can install a package from a registry, a GitHub repository, or even a zipped release. For instance, if you want to depend on a specific commit of a protocol, you can pin that exact version and be confident it won’t change underneath you. Updating is just as straightforward — bump the version, review the diff, and move forward without manually reconfiguring your repo.


Another key improvement is reproducibility. Soldeer introduces proper lockfiles, so builds are deterministic by default. This is especially important in smart contract environments, where even small changes in dependencies can have security or financial implications.


The tool is written in Rust and integrates seamlessly with Foundry, so it fits naturally into existing workflows without adding overhead. You don’t need to switch ecosystems or adopt heavy tooling — it’s designed to stay lightweight while solving a real problem.


Overall, Soldeer brings structure and reliability to Solidity dependency management. Instead of relying on ad-hoc Git setups and implicit assumptions, it gives developers a clear, consistent way to define, share, and reproduce their dependencies — closer to what mature ecosystems already take for granted.

title: Phylax Systems
description:
Phylax is a security and risk infrastructure company. Our circuit breakers are already deployed and operated by Linea, protecting over $16.3M and supporting protocols including Euler, Malda, Lagoon, Kyber Swap, and 0x. Phylax is building the Credible layer, a module that allows network operators to enforce security rules set by dapp teams. This means the circuit breaker is trust-minimized, highly customizable, deterministic and nearly impossible to bypass as transactions are validated during block production.


How it works:

The Credible Layer is security infrastructure that enables developers to link security rules to their smart contracts on-chain. Then, the network validates every transaction that interacts with their smart contracts against their security rules, dropping any invalidating transaction.


How to use it:


1) Define rules in Solidity

Write assertions; security rules that define states your protocol should never reach. No contract modifications required.


2) The network validates every transaction

The network checks each transaction against your assertions before inclusion in a block.


3) Invalid transactions are dropped pre-finality

Transactions that violate your rules are dropped by the network and never execute.

title: WEBCAT
description:
Freedom of the Press Foundation and Tor are developing WEBCAT (Web-Based Code Assurance and Transparency), a tool that protects users from tampered or malicious code when they visit websites. This is a standard security mechanism used in app stores that is missing from the open web. WEBCAT, which will initially be bundled with Tor Browser but is intended to inform integrity verification standards implemented in every major web browser, makes it possible for developers of security-sensitive software to digitally sign the software itself. Without WEBCAT, when a user opens a website, there's no way to verify the version of the site that's delivered to their computer hasn't been maliciously altered. WEBCAT keeps users safe by checking that the site's code matches the manifest signed by its developer. This keeps users safe before any data is processed or displayed, further strengthening the protections of encryption. 


WEBCAT is built with every use case in mind, which is why we will enable any application developer to use the WEBCAT plugin, first for regular websites, and eventually for anonymous websites accessible only in Tor Browser network as well. This kind of code verification is important for a wide range of users; from webmail to note-taking software, to digital wallets, and for any tool that handles sensitive communications.

title: LIF: Legitimate Intervention Framework
description:
LIF (Legitimate Intervention Framework) is an open-source Ethereum security research and tooling project maintained by Parametrig. It helps protocols design credible incident response before they are in crisis.


When exploits happen, outcomes are shaped by what follows, more than the vulnerability: who can act, under what authority, how quickly, and with what constraints.


In practice, emergency interventions already happen across Ethereum and its L2 ecosystem (pauses, upgrades, validator or bridge coordination, negotiations, recovery actions), but they are often improvised. That creates governance risk and legitimacy disputes exactly when systems are under maximum stress.


LIF turns incident response into a design problem. We provide a maintained dataset of exploit and intervention cases, a taxonomy that makes response actions comparable (scope, authority, timing, outcomes), and practical playbooks and templates that protocols can adopt to pre-commit to bounded emergency powers and auditable recovery procedures. The goal is to make emergency authority explicit, constrained, and reviewable.


This work also supports the next phase of crypto protection: making risk legible enough for insurance and recovery mechanisms to be priced and executed credibly. Protocols are not equally insurable. A protocol with clear circuit breakers, monitoring, and a bounded response plan should not be treated the same as one that has none. LIF helps the ecosystem standardize these guardrails so incident response improves and coverage boundaries become clearer over time.


Donations will fund LIF as a public good by:

  1. shipping a readiness and insurability toolkit that protocols can use to improve their incident response posture before an incident
  2. upgrading the dataset into a verification-grade release process (sources, confidence, changelogs)
  3. publishing adoptable incident response and emergency governance templates
  4. expanding L2 and cross-domain response case coverage
  5. building open tooling on lif-research.org to make precedent searchable and usable under time pressure.

title: mab.xyz - transaction guards
description:
This project is being developed by mab.xyz, a Web3 security company rooted in crypto security research from KTH Royal Institute of Technology. The intended users are Ethereum wallet teams, transaction simulation providers, smart contract wallet builders, and ultimately everyday blockchain users who rely on wallet previews to understand what a transaction will do before signing it.


What?

The project proposes Transaction Guard Contracts for Ethereum: a mechanism that turns simulated transaction outcomes into enforceable on-chain guarantees. Today, wallets can simulate a transaction and show the user expected effects such as token transfers or balance changes, but the blockchain only enforces the raw transaction input, not the displayed outcome. This project closes that gap by wrapping a transaction in a one-shot guard contract that checks whether the actual side effects match the simulated ones. If the outcome deviates beyond allowed tolerance, the entire transaction reverts.


Why?

The project addresses the simulation-execution gap, a major weakness in current Ethereum UX and security. A user may approve a swap, approval, lending action, or governance interaction based on a safe simulation, only for conditions to change before the transaction lands on-chain. That creates exposure to front-running, oracle manipulation, governance changes, upgradeable contract abuse, and other state-dependent attacks. Existing defenses such as slippage and deadlines only cover narrow cases. Transaction Guard Contracts aim to protect users by ensuring they receive what they approved, not merely what they were shown.


Where?

The solution is designed for the Ethereum ecosystem and broadly for DeFi, wallet infrastructure, account abstraction systems, and transaction simulation pipelines. It sits between wallet simulation and on-chain execution, making it relevant anywhere users interact with smart contracts under changing blockchain state. It also complements standards such as EIP-7730, which helps users understand what they are signing, by adding guarantees about what they will actually get.


How?

The flow has three steps: simulate the transaction, capture the important side effects, and encode them into a temporary guard contract that executes the original call and verifies the resulting balance or state changes atomically. The mechanism supports configurable tolerances, so it can allow small acceptable deviations such as AMM rounding or modest price movement while still blocking harmful divergences. Because verification happens on-chain, the model avoids extra off-chain trust during enforcement. In practice, this means a swap that was simulated to return around 2,000 USDC can be protected so that if manipulation reduces the result below an acceptable threshold, the transaction fails instead of silently succeeding with a bad outcome.


When?

This project is timely because Ethereum users increasingly depend on simulation-driven wallet UX, while MEV, adversarial reordering, proxy upgrades, and fast-changing protocol state make pre-signing previews less trustworthy on their own. As wallets become clearer about transaction intent, the next step is to guarantee execution integrity as well. Transaction Guard Contracts are positioned as that next layer: a practical security improvement for current Ethereum usage and a strong fit for the future of safer wallet infrastructure.

title: Canon Guard
description:
Multisig treasuries can't verify the off-chain data they depend on. Canon Guard moves it onchain so they can.


Safe's signing flow has a gap: transaction proposals live off-chain. Payloads can change between review and execution. Signers might approve different versions of the same transaction without realising it. External UIs and coordination layers become attack surfaces. Reviewer fatigue only makes the process worse.

What Canon Guard does

Canon Guard is an open-source security layer for Safe that moves all transaction intent onchain, removing the off-chain blind spots that put multisig treasuries at risk.

At the core are Actions: immutable onchain contracts that encode the exact call data and value of a Safe transaction. Once an Action is queued, it cannot be altered. Anyone can simulate it, fork-test, and verify that what signers approved is what will execute. No more trusting off-chain blobs.

Every transaction faces a mandatory time delay before execution. Pre-approved, low-risk operations (e.g. routine token transfers) take a short path. Novel or higher-risk proposals face longer delays, giving reviewers time to scrutinise and cancel.

Owners approve Safe transaction hashes directly onchain against specific payloads, creating a shared source of truth, clear audit trails, and coercion resistance through timelocks.

If something goes wrong, a designated trigger can restrict execution to an emergency caller only. Owners can still propose and approve, so governance continues, but outflows pause until the situation is resolved.

Design philosophy

Canon Guard assumes worst-case scenarios will happen. Three rules:

  1. Reusable vetting: routine operations are reviewed thoroughly once, then safely reused.
  2. Universal timelocks: every transaction faces a delay. No exceptions.
  3. Constrained delegation: DELEGATECALL is blocked (except for multisend batching), and all coordination happens onchain.

Why donate?

Canon Guard is a public good. It is fully open-source (MIT Licensed) and free to use. Donations support continued development, security audits, new chain deployments, and maintenance.

If your organisation uses a Safe, Canon Guard makes it harder for things to go wrong, and gives you real options when they do.

title: Zealynx Academy
description:
Zealynx Academy is a free, interactive platform to help Web3 founders build secure protocols and grow them into real businesses. No videos, no slides. You write every function yourself, guided by starter code and automated test suites. Visit the platform: https://academy.zealynx.io


Ethereum's security depends on a growing pipeline of skilled builders and auditors. Right now, most security education is either passive (watch and read) or locked behind expensive bootcamps. Zealynx Academy makes this education accessible to everyone, completely FREE, with no paywall and no premium tier.


Four things inside:


- Guides to fork DeFi protocols with awareness

- Security training to build safer Smart Contracts

- MBA-level knowledge to grow your protocol into a business

- Interactive guides to build your own AI Agents to help you grow your company


Build it before you fork it.


You rebuild the protocol from scratch. Guided. Line by line. Until your code matches the original.


Not to learn Solidity. To actually understand what you're about to fork. What you have, what you want to keep, what you want to change, what you want to throw out.


Our first module rebuilds Uniswap V2 from zero. 8 sections. 207 automated tests. You don't finish until every test passes. You can also find Compound V2 already, with more coming.


The security training.


You shadow-audit a past contest of a fork of what you just built.


Basin. ElasticSwap. Velodrome. Flux Finance. Canto v2. Five real protocol forks, 10,163 lines of Solidity, 46 documented bugs.


You see how other builders forked. What they kept. What they broke. What the attack surface looks like on the thing you're about to ship a version of.


When the time-boxed shadow audit ends, you get the full review and learnings. Security mindset built into the foundation, before you ever deploy.


The eMBA for Web3 Founders.


Tokenomics. Fundraising. Governance. Treasury. Regulatory. Go-to-market.


Because most of us are technical, and launching a protocol is much harder than we think we know. The eMBA handles everything we don't know we don't know.


Create your own AI Auditor Agent.


An interactive guide with multiple paths, each modeled after the most powerful existing AI auditor tools. Pick your path. Build your agent. Then benchmark it in the AI Auditor Arena against 118 real Code4rena bugs across 10 contests.


If you're shipping AI audit tools, this is where you find out if yours actually works.


The whole platform is gamified by design.


7 ranks from newcomer to sovereign. A public leaderboard. Lynx and badges earned through real work.


Because in Web3, your reputation is your resume. Zealynx Academy turns every lesson, every bug you find, every module you finish into a verifiable public track record.


Zealynx


The platform is built by Zealynx Security, a boutique smart contract audit firm with 40+ protocol audits under its belt. Community feedback and collaboration happen through our public GitHub repository (https://github.com/ZealynxSecurity/zealynx-academy-feedback) and the Academy Insiders Telegram group.


The platform code is not open source to protect educational integrity. Test solutions, challenge scaffolding, and Shadow Arena finding catalogs would lose their educational value if publicly available. This follows the same model used by Cyfrin Updraft, RareSkills, and Node Guardians.


How Funding Scales Our Impact


Every dollar goes toward people and content, not infrastructure markup. The platform stays free for all users regardless of funding level.


Under $5k: We cover infrastructure costs out of pocket and continue building modules solo.


$5k to $10k: We hire a part time security content creator to ship new modules faster. Priority: Lending/Borrowing, Bridge Security, Oracle Integration, Vault/Staking, and AI/MCP security, each built around real Ethereum exploits with actual vulnerable code.


$10k to $25k: We hire a part time developer to accelerate platform features (Exploit Archive, Krait AI integration for automated feedback on student code). We pay working auditors and protocol builders as guest tutors for free weekly live sessions covering building, auditing, and the business side of Web3 security.


$25k to $50k: We connect Academy directly with our Audit Grants program (grants.zealynx.io). We fund junior auditor stipends so top graduates can work on real Ethereum protocol audits, mentored by our senior team. We hire a content lead and fund Spanish and Portuguese translations.


$50k+: We build a dedicated team (developers, domain experts, marketing) and launch a paid Security Apprenticeship Pipeline: 3 month funded positions where graduates audit real Ethereum protocols alongside professionals. Goal: 20+ job ready security researchers per year feeding into the Ethereum ecosystem.


Follow us on Twitter (https://x.com/ZealynxSecurity) and join the Academy Insiders community to stay updated on our progress.

title: Safe Multisig Payload Report Action
description:
We MAXYZ are a service provider for DAOs, specialising in onchain operations. A big part of that is multisig transactions, especially in the form of building and reviewing Safe multisig payload JSONs.


While working for Balancer DAO, we have developed and battletested a reliable method to review such payloads: before posting them to the Safe UI, we PR them on GitHub. A JSON file lends itself perfectly for being reviewed as _code_, before looking at it in a human interface such as app.safe.global.


Besides having a chance to look at the payload line by line, we also have a GitHub workflow that reads the JSON, simulates it onchain and decodes it into human readable input. This gives considerably more information then even the Safe UI, given we can do things such as implement custom decodings and inject personal addresses for labelling.


We believe many other DAOs would benefit from this method. An experimental version is currently already being used in private by Ombrello Group; an EVM security service review service: https://ombrello.group/.


Continuing development on this project, taking it out of alpha and making it public is the goal here. Such a publicly accessible GitHub action would be a great addition to the public security tooling currently out there!


See the report live in production for example here: https://github.com/balancer/multisig-ops/pull/2768


A proof-of-concept repository can be found here: https://github.com/ombrello-group/payload-report-action
