title: Anticapture by blockful
description:
Anticapture: catching attacks before they drain your treasury

In March 2024 we found a way to drain about $150M from the ENS treasury (disclosure). Nothing in the code was broken. The problem sat one layer above it: a two-block gap between proposal creation and the vote snapshot, a timelock that couldn't cancel anything, and a handful of wallets large enough that someone could plausibly buy or borrow their way to quorum. We told ENS quietly, helped them design a 4-of-8 Security Council with veto power (forum thread), and only published the write-up once the fix was in. No funds moved. That's what governance security looks like when it works.



Anticapture is the platform we built around that kind of work. It reads governance activity onchain (delegations, voting power, proposal flow, treasury exposure) and turns it into something a DAO can actually act on, ideally before anything goes wrong.



Today we cover 11 DAOs, against 16 security indicators, sorted into 3 maturity stages, with a framework grounded in 30+ historical attacks (framework).


The layer no one is auditing

Smart contract audits look at code. Anticapture looks at the layer above: how decisions get made, who can make them, and what it would cost an attacker to take over. That layer is where the largest DAO losses have happened. Beanstalk lost $182M to a governance flash-loan in April 2022. Mango Markets lost $114M later that year in an oracle attack the attacker then ratified through a vote. Tornado Cash, Build Finance, Audius and others followed. Across documented incidents, governance and governance-adjacent attacks have cost the ecosystem well over $300M (a16z research).



None of these were code bugs, which is exactly why audits don't catch them. They're economic, behavioral, and structural. Almost no one is monitoring that surface continuously. We are.


What we do

Free and public on anticapture.com:


  • a dashboard with risk stages for every DAO we cover
  • real-time alerts on proposals, power shifts, and delegation changes
  • open research on how governance attacks actually unfold
  • the Anticapture Framework itself, which any DAO can use to grade itself


Commissioned work for DAOs that want to go deeper:


  • calldata review, where we check that what a proposal says it does is what it actually does onchain
  • full governance audits covering delegation concentration, timelock behavior, quorum economics, and upgrade paths
  • security upgrades and data monitoring as a service provider, working based on Anticapture indicators to reach a higher security stage 


Who we work with

We're an active delegate, grantee, or service provider with ENS, Uniswap, Arbitrum, Optimism, Scroll, and Superfluid (contributions). Our review of Shutter surfaced a path where roughly $100K worth of governance tokens could capture a treasury worth more than $3M (article). Compound, Nouns, Gitcoin, Obol and several other DAOs are continuously monitored on the dashboard.



Why this round, and why now

Treasuries worth millions, guarding protocols of billions, are being protected by voting systems that are hardly being checked. Delegation keeps concentrating. Quorum economics shift faster than most DAO ops teams can track. The Ethereum Security QF round exists because security work done before an exploit is the cheapest security work there is, and governance is the next obvious place for that work to land.




Our application fits several of the round's stated categories at once: security research and auditing, threat intelligence and on-chain investigation, security tooling and infrastructure, and security standards. It also fills a slot the round doesn't explicitly name yet, which is governance security itself.


What your support actually pays for

Anticapture is open source infrastructure for security. Governance security protects treasuries and protocol controls, but it also protects something quieter: the legitimacy of decentralized coordination. Concretely, money raised in this round goes to:


  • keeping the dashboard, alerts, and framework public and free
  • covering more DAOs and more L2 governance systems
  • deeper research into emerging attack vectors (AI-centric and not)
  • keeping our independent assessments independent



In quadratic funding every donor counts twice, once for the donation and once for the signal. If you think this work should keep happening, the cheapest way to say so is to show up.


Help us make resistance to governance capture the default, not the exception.


anticapture.com · blockful.io

title: EVM Chronicle
description:
EVM Chronicle is an EVM contract state research tool, currently focused on Ethereum, that helps people inspect real storage, mapping state, historical variable changes, execution flow, and code patterns, with the long-term goal of becoming an EVM search engine.


EVM Chronicle 4 Main Functions

1. Storage Explorer

Inspects real Ethereum storage, including slots, offsets, mappings, structs, arrays, and value history. It helps users see how contract state is actually stored and how it changes over time, especially for mapping variables that are usually difficult to inspect.


2. Transaction Tracer

Tracks execution flow, including variables read and variables changed. It helps users understand what a transaction actually did at the storage level, not just which logs were emitted or which functions were called.


3. Source Code Intelligence

Lets users inspect storage directly from source code and simulate functions in the same workflow. It helps users move from source to state to execution without needing separate tools or a local setup.


4. Contract Search

Searches contracts by string matching and code patterns. It helps users find contracts that contain specific code, logic structures, or vulnerability-related patterns, which is useful for research, auditing, and bug hunting.



Built For

> security researchers

> auditors

> bug bounty hunters

> protocol engineers

> advanced Web3 developers

> DEFI researchers

> people investigating strange contract behavior



Why it matters

Even today, understanding EVM storage values is still difficult, time consuming, and too manual, especially when it comes to mapping variables. My hope is that EVM Chronicle can reduce that gap, including for people without Solidity knowledge who still need to extract contract data and do meaningful analysis.



Next Milestones

1. Index from genesis and maintain realtime indexing

Expand EVM Chronicle from range-based indexing to full indexing from genesis to the latest block, and eventually maintain realtime indexing as each new block is produced.


2. Adopt Ethereum Layer 2s

Extend EVM Chronicle beyond Ethereum mainnet and bring the same storage, state, and execution visibility to Layer 2 networks.


3. Become an EVM search engine

Build EVM Chronicle toward an EVM search engine, where someone can search for a specific value, variable, mapping key, or code and immediately discover where it exists in a specific contract.



What the funding will be used for

1. Build full indexing infrastructure

Buy a powerful machine to index all Ethereum and Layer 2 contract variables and values from genesis to the latest block, and eventually maintain realtime indexing as each new block is produced.


2. Move to proper production servers

Pay for reliable servers to serve data with better connection quality and close to 100% uptime. Right now, the app is still running from my local machine through tunneling, which is far from ideal for long-term reliability.


3. Improve the search engine architecture

Hire a vector database expert to make the search layer smoother, faster, and more scalable, especially as EVM Chronicle moves closer to its long-term search engine vision.


4. Grow the project's presence

Hire someone focused on social and community growth to make the app feel more alive, reach more relevant people, and help the project gain the visibility it currently lacks.


If EVM Chronicle receives funding, it will be used in a clear order of priority. The first focus is making the product stronger and more reliable at the infrastructure level. After that, the goal is to improve search quality and then expand the project's reach.


Thank you for your time, and if this resonates with you, I would deeply appreciate your support.

title: Solidity-Wake: VS Code extension
description:
Solidity (Wake) is a VS Code extension for developing, testing, and securing Solidity smart contracts — powered by the Wake framework.


It brings a Remix-like experience into the editor: compile contracts, deploy them on a local node, interact with functions, fork mainnet or L2s, and work with proxy contracts — all without leaving VS Code. Real-time static analysis runs Wake's vulnerability detectors as you type, surfacing security issues inline and in a dedicated sidebar overview.



Features

- Local node testing — compile, deploy, and interact with contracts on an embedded Ethereum node directly in VS Code

- Mainnet & L2 forking — fork any EVM chain to test against real on-chain state and interact with deployed contracts

- Proxy contract support — native detection and interaction through proxy contracts

- Real-time vulnerability detection — Wake's detectors run on every keystroke, showing reentrancy, unsafe delegatecalls, and other issues inline as diagnostics

- Security overview sidebar — aggregated view of all detections across the project, filterable by severity and confidence

- Code navigation — go-to-definition, find references, hover documentation, contract outline, and document links across Solidity files

- Code lens — inline function selectors, reference counts, and detector annotations directly in the source

- Graph visualizations — interactive inheritance graphs, control flow graphs, and import dependency diagrams rendered in-editor

- Works with existing setups — compatible with Hardhat and Foundry projects, auto-imports Foundry remappings



Donation objectives

Solidity (Wake) is the most feature-rich open-source Solidity extension for VS Code — combining code intelligence, real-time security analysis, and interactive contract testing in one tool. The donation would fund expanding its capabilities and connecting it to Wake's upcoming AI infrastructure.

Deliverables

- Revm-based engine for Deploy & Interact — add Wake's built-in Rust EVM core as the primary engine for the Deploy & Interact UI alongside Anvil, making local node testing faster and self-contained with no external process required

- AI integration — bring-your-own-provider AI features powered by Wake's static analysis context: natural-language explanations of detected vulnerabilities with suggested fixes. Users connect their own API key (OpenAI, Anthropic, ...) — no vendor lock-in  

- AI-assisted fuzz test generation — generate Wake fuzz tests from contract code using static analysis context to produce meaningful flows and invariants

- Richer graph visualizations — cross-contract call graphs, token flow diagrams, and access control maps rendered interactively

- Ongoing maintenance — keep pace with VS Code API changes, Wake releases, new Solidity language features, and Foundry/Hardhat ecosystem updates

title: CORE3. The open risk layer for Web3
description:
The open‑source risk layer for Web3. Free for everyone.

Our goal is to boost transparency, accountability, and security – and to grow the Web3 cybersecurity market as a whole.

We already did this once

We built CER.live: open security ratings for 290 exchanges, trusted by CoinGecko as 20% of their exchange trust score. Used by millions. Free. CORE3 is the same idea applied to the whole web3 ecosystem - protocols, DeFi, chains, governance.


https://CORE3.io is live today. No paywall. 1,400+ projects analyzed and openly available.


The market still fails to answer one question

Audit badge - enough. Clean UI - enough. Stable yield - enough.


That is why weak, fragile, and negligent projects still attract capital.

Opacity is profitable.

The current system rewards projects that market security better than they practice it - and bad actors benefit directly from users not seeing what sits underneath.


As long as risk stays invisible, responsibility is optional and hype stays competitive.


What everyone can see now

Each project gets a Probability of Loss (0-100) built from six categories where failures actually happen: financial structure, governance, dependencies, operations, reputation, and technical stack.


Not an audit badge. Not a dashboard metric. A forward-looking signal built on open methodology - open for review, open for challenge, open for improvement by community.


0–20 > relatively stable.

20–50 > meaningful structural risk.

50+ > high likelihood of loss.


What we see across the market

We analyzed 1,400+ projects. Around 80% show structural risk signals. Even top-tier names are not automatically safe. Loss is not the exception - hidden risk is the norm.


The human layer on top of data

Numbers alone aren't enough. CORE3 adds Proof of Voice - a public expert layer: structured opinions on projects, verifiable track records, community challenge and refinement. So «I hope it's safe» becomes «I understand why it's risky». And that judgment is public, accountable, and improvable by anyone.


What your contribution does

Every dollar expands coverage.

More projects analyzed, more risks made visible before someone funds them.

Every project added to the open dataset is one fewer blind spot for the next person entering Web3.


In quadratic funding, the number of people who contribute matters as much as the amount. If you've ever lost money to a project that looked safe, or want to make sure fewer people do, this is the contribution that makes that outcome less likely.


Credibility

Built by Hacken Group: 8+ years in blockchain security. CER.live powers 20% of CoinGecko exchange trust scores across 290 exchanges. Active regulatory cooperationengagement with ADGM and EU Sandbox.


Dyma Budorin (CEO): Founder & CEO of CORE3, Co-founder and Executive Chairman of Hacken, CEO of Hacken Group. 8+ years in blockchain executive leadership. Previously senior manager at Deloitte.


Aimann Faiz (CBDO): former Head of BD at CoinGecko, the world's largest independent crypto data aggregator.


Roadmap

Q3 2026 — PoL API + Proof of Voice expert layer.

Q4 2026 — 5,000+ projects + community challenge program.

2027 — PoL becomes reference benchmark. Open governance.

title: Wake: Solidity static analysis and fuzzing framework
description:
Wake is a development framework for Solidity smart contracts that combines testing, fuzzing, static analysis, and IDE tooling in a single Python-based toolkit — helping developers write safer contracts, faster.



Features

- Testing framework based on pytest — write clean, readable tests with familiar Python tooling

- Property-based fuzzing — automatically generate diverse inputs to uncover hidden bugs

- Manually-guided fuzzing (MGF) — combine automated fuzzing with human insight to target specific contract behaviors and edge cases

- Rust EVM core — high-performance chain simulation via revm, with call tracing, coverage tracking, and mainnet forking built in

- Vulnerability detectors — catch reentrancy, unsafe delegatecalls, unchecked return values, and more out of the box

- Extensible static analysis — write custom detectors and printers in Python to enforce project-specific rules

- Rich code intelligence — fully typed intermediate representation of Solidity code with control flow graphs, cross-reference resolution, storage layout analysis, and state change tracking — a foundation ready to power AI-driven security tooling

- Deployments & mainnet interactions — send transactions and deploy contracts on major chains




Donation objectives

Wake's static analysis engine produces rich, structured representations of Solidity code — typed IR, control flow graphs, cross-references, storage layouts, and state change tracking. Today, this powers detectors and IDE features. The donations would fund exposing this intelligence to AI agents, unlocking a new class of AI-driven security and development tooling.


Deliverables

- MCP server for static analysis — expose Wake's code intelligence (definitions, references, type hierarchy, control flow, storage layout, state changes) as an MCP server, giving AI agents structured, queryable access to Solidity codebases instead of raw source text

- AI-native fuzzing interface — provide an agent-friendly API for autonomous fuzz testing: AI agents define flows, invariants, and test strategies, then launch and monitor fuzzing campaign outputs

- Agent-oriented documentation and examples — reference implementations showing AI agents using Wake's MCP tools for end-to-end security analysis: from code understanding through fuzz testing to vulnerability reporting

- Ongoing revm core maintenance — keep Wake's Rust EVM core up to date with revm releases and upcoming Ethereum hardforks, ensuring tests and fuzzing always run against the latest EVM semantics

- New vulnerability detectors — expand the built-in detector suite with coverage for additional vulnerability classes, including detectors for known Solidity compiler bugs that silently generate incorrect bytecode

title: Pharos Watch: Transparent Stablecoins Analytics
description:
Stablecoin failures are among the most systemic risks in the Ethereum ecosystem. When a stablecoin loses its peg, the damage ripples across DeFi protocols, liquidity pools, and user funds simultaneously, often across multiple chains and L2s at once. Most users never see it coming because the tools available to them only show price. They do not show structure.


Pharos is an open-source stablecoin security analytics platform built to change that. Where most dashboards tell you whether a peg is holding, Pharos tells you what is holding it up, how fragile the exit really is, and where the risk sits before the surface starts to crack.


The platform aggregates on-chain data from integrated APIs including DefiLlama, Curve, CoinGecko, and others, to produce a comprehensive security profile for every stablecoin it tracks. This includes collateral composition, custody risk, blacklist and censorship exposure, liquidity depth, redemption path analysis, and a proprietary Depeg Early Warning System (DEWS) that monitors stress signals in real time across all chains.

Pharos currently tracks over 150 stablecoins across all major chains and L2s, including non-USD pegged assets systematically overlooked by existing security tooling. It serves over 2,000 users ranging from individual researchers to protocol teams and treasury managers.


The platform's real-world impact is already measurable. Pharos flagged the USR depeg risk early before the exploit became public, demonstrating that its monitoring infrastructure can surface systemic risk before it becomes a crisis.


Pharos is free at its base layer and fully open source. It is infrastructure built on the conviction that stablecoin transparency is a prerequisite for a safer Ethereum ecosystem, and that the people who need it most should never have to pay to access it.

The stablecoin market has grown into a critical layer of Ethereum's monetary infrastructure. Pharos is built to keep it honest.

title: Open-Source Smart Contract Firewall
description:
If you're generous enough to donate, keep in mind that to unlock part of the quadratic-funding pool of TheDAO round, you will also need to donate to at least two other projects (minimum $1 each) — otherwise the algorithm will not recognize your donation. Thank you so much!


Moat is an open-source, decentralized pre-execution transaction-level firewall for smart contracts.


It is for any protocol team that wants to shrink their attack surface — especially teams shipping fast, teams too early-stage to afford the audit they should have before going to production, and teams trying to convince risk-averse LPs that their funds are safe.

Moat originated as an internal solution in response to that exact pressure: running a DeFi protocol where security was the core promise and needing a practical way to back it up.


The Solution

It sits in front of your critical functions — deposits, withdrawals, swaps, anything you choose — and emulates every incoming transaction before it touches your protocol. If the transaction violates a rule or an invariant defined by your team, it is blocked before execution. A timelock always activates on any rejection, providing the protocol team with a configurable window (e.g., 30 minutes) to do incident response — after which the user can proceed with pushing the transaction through.


Reality

Protocols keep getting hacked. The current responses are reactive: frontrun the attack transaction in the mempool, or pause the entire protocol after the fact. The race defenders rarely win. By then, funds are often already gone. Moat addresses the mitigation gap by enforcing the simple invariants the team already understands — protocol-level ones (reserve ratios, solvency, share-price bounds) and economic ones (per-user yield, profit caps) — before state changes occur.


The existing solutions are not enough:


- There is no permissively-licensed day-one firewall where the protocol team authors the rules and ships them in their own repo.

- Hypernative Firewall is closed-source, proprietary, and enterprise-priced — unavailable to most early teams.

- Forta Firewall and Ironblocks ship a custom-rule surface, but the products are built around vendor-managed detection — AI Attesters and compliance filters at Forta, Approved Patterns at Ironblocks — designed for L2s, rollups, and protocols subscribing to a catalog. Neither is a permissively-licensed primitive a lean team can drop in and run with its own simple rules.


Lean DeFi teams in 2026 — increasingly shipping with LLM-assisted audits and no firewall budget — are exactly the buyer with nothing to drop in today. Moat fills that gap. Open source, auditable, easy to use at day-one.


Architecture

It operates at the intersection of a thin on-chain enforcement layer and an off-chain validator:


- The on-chain layer is the modifier and the force-through. A single modifier added to the functions you choose to protect — `withdraw`, `deposit`, anything critical. Routes the call through the firewall, blocks it on the validator's verdict, but still opens a 30-minute force-through timelock. That is the entire on-chain surface — every rule runs in the off-chain validator below.

- The protocol team writes the rules. Two shapes, both natural to the engineers who designed the protocol. Pre/post-state invariants — the same Foundry/Echidna predicates already in your test suite: constant-product, share-price bounds, reserve ratios, solvency. Statistical bounds — limits on aggregate behavior proven via zk-coprocessor (Brevis): per-user yield caps, profit thresholds, TVL anomaly bands. The class of rules that catches the one address suddenly earning 1,000,000% APY while every other LP earns 10% exit, without any black-box ML. The CTO authors them, ships them in the repo, and can read them out loud to an LP.

- Self-hosted backend at v1. The rules that don't fit on-chain — the full invariant set under state emulation — run on a backend that the team hosts themselves. Early-stage protocols already retain a lot of operational control (admin keys, upgrade powers, the ability to pull liquidity), so a team-hosted validator does not move the centralization needle for v1. The on-chain force-through window keeps the user from ever being permanently censored, regardless.

- Moving to an AVS. As the protocol decentralizes and TVL grows, the validator moves to an EigenLayer / Symbiotic AVS. A set of independent operators runs the same emulation + predicate logic, BLS-aggregates the verdicts, and the team is no longer a trusted operator. This is what makes the firewall credible to LPs at the mature stage.

- Users are protected from both attackers and censorship. Every blocked transaction triggers a 30-minute timelock. After 30 minutes, the user can always push through.


Composability

Moat is the floor, not the ceiling. A team integrates it on day one and keeps it. As the protocol matures and TVL grows, enterprise tooling layers on top — Hypernative's threat intel, Forta's attester network, and custom monitoring. Moat persists underneath as the place where the protocol-specific, non-outsourceable rules live: the invariants only the team can write.


Milestones

Milestone 1 — ~10 ETH

On-chain modifier and force-through state machine, self-hosted off-chain validator with the rule runtime for both Foundry-style invariants and Brevis-proven statistical rules, basic rule template set. Implementation is well advanced — the grant covers the final stretch and security review before public release.

$300M+ lost to DeFi exploits in 2025 (DeFiLlama). Access control failures and code vulnerabilities account for the majority, exactly the class of attacks that pre-execution emulation catches. Any team with M1 deployed is no longer a soft target.


Milestone 2 — ~8 ETH

Decentralized AVS on EigenLayer / Symbiotic. Multiple independent operators, no single backend. Data-feed integrations (ChainSecurity, Chainlink, third-party threat intel), richer rule templates.

Removes the last trusted third party, which makes the firewall credible to LPs.


Milestone 3 — ~4 ETH

Preset rule library covering the most common exploits across lending, AMM, vaults, and staking. Pick a template, deploy, done.

~95% of teams covered out of the box.


Conclusion

It is a transaction-level circuit breaker that any team can drop in today. It is not a replacement for other tools or professional audits. As your protocol matures, grows TVL, and builds out its security practice, you layer those on top. Moat is the floor — something you can have from day one, before you have the budget or the team for anything else.

title: Verity: Formal Verification for Smart Contracts
description:
Who?

We’re LFG Labs, founded by Thomas and Ben.

Before Verity, we shipped security-focused products on Ethereum for the last 3 years. Here is a quick look at what we built in the last year:

  • Lucid: Gnosis Safe mobile signer built with Nexus Mutual, while doing so, we uncovered a high-severity vulnerability in Rabby Wallet. (Acquired by OpenCover)
  • SafeLens: Offline Safe transaction verifier. (EF-funded)
  • Private LLM: Local-first Ethereum assistant. (EF-funded)
  • Runes Bridge: Starknet-Bitcoin bridge for 1:1 redeemable USDC on Bitcoin. (Funded by Starkware)


What?

Verity is a formally verified smart contract compiler written in Lean 4. You write contracts in an embedded DSL, state what they should do, prove those properties hold, and compile to EVM bytecode.


It can be used in two main ways:

  • Modeling existing Solidity contracts and formally verifying them.
  • Writing new contracts with built-in proofs

It's already possible to use it, and we've worked with the best Ethereum protocols to formally verify production DeFi contracts with Verity:

  • Lido V3: solvency invariant of Staking Vaults
  • Safe: linked-list invariants of the owner list


The compiler itself is also fully formally verified, not just the contracts it produces. We're co-authoring a research paper on the framework, how it bridges Lean 4 and the EVM, and why we think formal verification is about to become practical at scale. Verity is fully open-source and MIT-licensed. You can read more about the approach here: https://lfglabs.dev/research/verity


Why

Why Formal Verification

Smart contract audits are human opinions frozen in time. An auditor reads your code, checks for known patterns, and writes a report, but the report is not a guarantee. Formal verification means writing down the exact rules your contract must follow, then producing a machine-checkable proof that those rules hold for every possible input and execution path within the model. That matters even more when frameworks could ship with insecure defaults that audits tend to miss. Formal verification catches them at the model level.


In Short: Formal verification gives you a real guarantee: if the assumptions match the deployed system, the proven properties hold for every possible input, no matter who's attacking.


Why It Matters Now

AI is getting better every day at finding vulnerabilities that humans and simple automated tools miss. Audits won't scale against adversaries that never sleep and improve weekly thanks to AI model advancements when a formal proof doesn't degrade over time. Once a property is proven, it holds permanently, no matter how sophisticated the attacker.


Why Verity

Most smart contract verification tools rely on bounded checks: they can only say they found no counterexample up to a depth. Verity produces unbounded, machine-checkable proofs. It also tackles two problems the ecosystem has long ignored. First, compiler risk: a proven contract can still be betrayed by an unverified compiler, so Verity’s toolchain is formally verified. Second, language limits: Solidity favors expressiveness over safety, so Verity’s embedded DSL is built for end-to-end guarantees. Verity is fully open-source and MIT-licensed, so anyone can inspect the prover, verify proofs, and build on it to make formal verification a common Ethereum security practice.


How will we use the funds?

Tier 1: <$10k (Maintenance)

  • Verity maintenance: Solidity parity, bugfixes, compiler improvements
  • Peer-reviewed paper on the Verity compiler
  • Formal proof of one ecosystem contract's invariants
  • All proofs open-source, verifiable with lake build


Tier 2: $10k–$30k (Foundation)

  • Full Solidity feature coverage and compiler stabilization
  • Formal proofs for additional contracts, published open-source
  • Reusable lemma library for common EVM patterns
  • Beginner docs, tutorials, and AI skill for writing proofs


Tier 3: $30k–$60k (Growth)

  • Research on a security-first language semantics cleaner than Solidity, designed for agents to write and humans to audit
  • Expand the benchmark to more protocols as training data for proof agents
  • Formal proofs of partner protocol invariants
  • Peer-reviewed paper on the benchmark
  • Workshop or talk at EthCC, Devcon, or similar


Tier 4: $60k–$100k (Scale)

  • Implement language features from Tier 3 research
  • Foundry and Hardhat integration
  • Research on reducing the human cost of proof, iteration by iteration
  • Onboard early teams to formal verification


Tier 5: $100k+ (Ecosystem impact)

  • Research on proving Yul-to-EVM compilation correct — today a proven contract can still be betrayed by the compiler
  • Vyper interoperability and Venom as an alternative compilation target
  • Formal specs for ERC standards (ERC-20, ERC-721, ERC-4337)
  • Verify the full signing chain: does the signed message match the executed transaction?
  • Redistribute part of the funding to independent researchers contributing to the benchmark
  • Roadmap for Verity as a credible alternative to Solidity

title: Blobscan
description:
🌐 Blobscan - Making Ethereum’s Blob Layer Transparent


Every day, rollups publish gigabytes of data into Ethereum blobs — the foundation of Ethereum's scaling strategy, securing billions of dollars in value.


But the blob layer is still largely invisible.


Unlike transactions or smart contract calls, blob data has no dedicated tooling for inspection or analysis. If unusual patterns emerge or something goes wrong in a rollup, there's no straightforward way for researchers or developers to investigate. A layer that can't be independently inspected can't be independently trusted.


Compounding this, blob data is ephemeral: Ethereum nodes prune it after 18 days by default, leaving historical data either gone entirely or locked behind centralized providers — with no guarantee any individual node retains it longer. As PeerDAS rolls out, nodes will store even less complete data — making independent archival increasingly critical.


Blobscan was created to change that.


🔍 What Blobscan Does


Blobscan is open-source infrastructure that permanently archives every Ethereum blob and makes it queryable by anyone.


Through a public explorer and API, it lets you:

  • Search blob data by versioned hash, KZG commitment, transaction hash, slot, or block number
  • Decode rollup batch contents — we integrate rollup-specific decoders so raw bytes become readable across multiple L2s
  • Analyze usage patterns with real-time dashboards covering fee markets, utilization rates, rollup leaderboards, and more
  • Access historical data programmatically via a free public API


Unlike general-purpose block explorers where blobs are an afterthought buried under layers of navigation, Blobscan is purpose-built for the blob layer.


🔐 Why This Matters for Security


Opacity is a risk. When critical infrastructure can't be independently inspected:

  • Anomalous rollup behavior goes undetected
  • Post-incident forensic analysis becomes impossible
  • The community loses the ability to verify what's actually happening on-chain


Blobscan makes this layer auditable. Security researchers can use it to inspect rollup batch submissions encoded in the blobs. Developers can use it to debug DA issues. Protocol teams can use it to validate client implementation and behavior after incidents.


📊 Blobscan Metrics


Blobscan isn't a proposal, it's running infrastructure with real users:

  • 4 networks supported (Ethereum, Sepolia, Hoodi, Gnosis)
  • 8+ TB archived
  • 32M+ blobs indexed
  • 20M+ transactions processed
  • 4K+ monthly active users
  • 5K+ monthly pageviews
  • 2M+ monthly API requests
  • 30 contributors, 65 forks and 99 stars on GitHub


🚀 What We're Building Next


Your donation directly helps us keep this critical infrastructure open, decentralized, and sustainable.


With your support, we will focus in the following directions:


1. Decentralized Storage (IPFS Migration)


We're moving blob archival from Google Cloud Storage to IPFS, enabling any community member to run their own IPFS node and help us replicating blob data. This removes Blobscan as a single point of failure and makes long-term preservation a shared, permissionless effort. We plan to develop a DAppNode package so node operators can contribute storage with one click.


2. Security Tooling & Anomaly Detection

We're building analytics and monitoring infrastructure to surface risks in real time. This includes anomaly detection for unusual blob usage patterns, APIs purpose-built for forensic investigation and post-incident analysis, and dashboards that give researchers and rollup teams continuous visibility into the health of the data availability layer.


3. Production-Grade Analytics

We're expanding our metrics layer with new blob-specific indicators: utilization rates, fee market trends, size distributions, rollup leaderboards, USD cost breakdowns, address-level analytics and more. All exposed via a public API and an interactive dashboard with flexible time windows and filtering.


4. Sustained Free Access

Infrastructure costs grow linearly with Ethereum usage. Your support keeps the core explorer and API free for researchers, developers, and the broader community — while we build towards long-term sustainability through optional paid tiers for high-volume users.


🌍  A Public Good for the Ecosystem


Blobscan is fully open-source (AGPL-3 / MIT). No paywalls. No gatekeeping. Core access will always be free.


Ethereum's future depends not just on scaling, but on keeping that scaling transparent and verifiable. That's what Blobscan is for.


By supporting Blobscan, you're helping ensure that as Ethereum scales, it doesn't do so in the dark.

title: DigiBastion: DNS, OpSec & Supply Chain Security
description:
DigiBastion is an open-source Web3 security project founded by Raiders (web3sec.news founder), an Ethereum Foundation grantee, SEAL Alliance contributor, and published MITRE AADAPT researcher. Built for Web3 protocols, developers, and users who need defense that goes far beyond smart contract audits.


DigiBastion is a full-stack defensive security platform built ground-up for the Web3 threat model. It covers:

  • DNS and domain security scanning across Ethereum mainnet and L2 protocols, currently in closed beta with direct outreach to protocol founders, developers, and heads of security (BETA)
  • Supply chain and JavaScript integrity monitoring for protocol frontends (WIP)
  • Phishing detection and active lookalike domain tracking (WIP)
  • Domain risk scoring browser extension for users (WIP)
  • Real-time threat intelligence feeds for protocols, researchers, and incident responders (LIVE)
  • Operational security guides, checklists, and quizzes for developers and everyday users (LIVE)


The DNS security scanner is currently operating in a structured closed beta. Rather than dumping findings publicly, we reach out directly to protocol teams, share findings privately, work with them to fix issues, and collect feedback before the tool goes fully public. This responsible disclosure approach ensures real fixes happen before attackers notice the same gaps.


Unlike generic security tools retrofitted for crypto, every component of DigiBastion was designed specifically for the attack surfaces draining Web3 users today: lookalike domains, DNS hijacks, malicious frontends, compromised dependencies, and supply chain poisoning.


The full platform is open source and publicly accessible at digibastion.com. The codebase is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Raiders0786/digibastion


Why?

Most losses in Web3 today don't come from novel smart contract exploits. They come from phishing, DNS hijacks, supply chain compromises, and malicious frontends. Yet the ecosystem remains heavily over-indexed on audits and under-invested in the continuous infrastructure-layer defense that actually protects users in real time.


Audits are snapshots. Attacks are continuous.


DigiBastion fills that gap as a public good. Through the closed beta responsible disclosure program, scanning top Ethereum and L2 protocols has already surfaced critical live findings shared directly with protocol teams:

  • Axelar: score 96
  • Lido: score 91
  • Chainlink: score 90
  • GMX: score 93
  • QuickSwap: score 90


The real-time threat intelligence feeds also serve a direct incident response function. When a DNS hijack or frontend compromise is suspected, responders need live data on domain status, lookalike activity, and infrastructure posture. DigiBastion provides exactly that, continuously updated and freely accessible.


Foundation work includes authoring the SEAL Alliance Domain and DNS Security Framework (frameworks.securityalliance.dev/infrastructure/domain-and-dns-security) and publishing supply chain attack TTPs to MITRE AADAPT (aadapt.mitre.org/techniques/ADT1195), establishing the research and standards credibility behind the tooling.


How?

DigiBastion runs as a continuously maintained open-source project. Current coverage includes 50+ top Ethereum and L2 protocols scanned regularly, threat intel feeds updated in real time, and a growing library of opsec resources used by developers and users across the ecosystem.


Running this at the level the ecosystem actually needs isn't cheap. Unlike a one-time audit or a static report, DigiBastion operates as live infrastructure across multiple interconnected systems that all require continuous funding to stay operational.


Infrastructure and Services:

  • DNS and domain scanning infrastructure running daily across 50+ protocols
  • Supply chain and JavaScript integrity monitoring with automated diff detection
  • Real-time threat intel scraping, aggregation, and feed generation
  • Database hosting and storage for historical findings, domain records, and threat data
  • API layer for researcher and incident responder access
  • Browser extension backend and update pipeline
  • Uptime monitoring, alerting, and redundancy across services


Research and Development:

  • Ongoing protocol coverage expansion across Ethereum L2s
  • New detection modules for emerging attack vectors including BGP hijacks, RPC poisoning, and frontend injection
  • Building a shared open DNS security data standard for the broader ecosystem
  • Integration work with existing security tooling and incident response workflows
  • Closed beta program management, responsible disclosure coordination, and protocol team engagement


Human Cost:

  • Continuous research, triage, and validation of findings
  • Threat intel curation and publishing
  • Community education content via Web3Sec News distributed to 10,000+ readers
  • Coordination with SEAL Alliance, MITRE, and ecosystem partners


Infrastructure and API costs alone run $400-600 per month. Add development, research, and human time across all active systems and the realistic number to maintain and meaningfully expand DigiBastion as a public good is $50,000 for 12 months.


This covers keeping all systems live, expanding protocol coverage across L2s, shipping the open DNS security data standard, maturing the closed beta into a publicly accessible tool, and ensuring threat intel feeds stay operational when the ecosystem needs them most including during active incidents.


This is not a one-time build. It is continuous defense infrastructure.


Active and live now. The closed beta is running with active protocol team engagement. Continuous monitoring runs daily. New findings, threat intel updates, and educational resources are published regularly at digibastion.com and distributed through Web3Sec News to a community of 10,000+ security-focused readers across Asia and beyond.


Donate to DigiBastion today.

You are not funding a whitepaper or a roadmap. You are sustaining live infrastructure that is actively finding critical vulnerabilities across the protocols you use right now. Every contribution keeps the scanners running, the threat feeds live, the closed beta moving toward public launch, and the ecosystem safer.


This is the defense layer Ethereum needs.

title: Walletbeat
description:
Walletbeat is an open-source public good dedicated to bringing transparency to the Ethereum wallet ecosystem. As L2BEAT has done for Layer 2s, Walletbeat does for wallets: providing objective, verifiable evaluations that help users make informed decisions.


The Ethereum wallet landscape lacks a neutral source of truth. Wallets compete on flashy features, not on Ethereum values, such as security, privacy, self-sovereignty, and transparency. Users have no easy way to know: does this wallet leak my personal information? Is it actually open source? Are my keys truly under my control? Walletbeat exists to answer these questions.


Walletbeat evaluates software wallets and hardware wallets across dozens of documented attributes following Ethereum values: security, privacy, self-sovereignty, transparency, and ecosystem. Every evaluation is backed by publicly reviewable data in our GitHub repository, cross-referenced against source code analysis (if publicly available) and data collected from wallet teams.


Walletbeat is committed to credible neutrality. We refuse funding from wallet-related entities. All contributor affiliations are disclosed. Our long-term governance goal is to become an independent DAO or foundation.


Walletbeat has received prior funding from the Ethereum Foundation, including a grant through the Pectra Proactive Grant Round and a larger grant as part of the EF's Trillion Dollar Security initiative.


Your funding supports continued evaluation work: filling data gaps across existing listings, onboarding new wallets, expanding hardware and embedded wallet coverage, and improving the evaluation framework. Every contribution helps keep Walletbeat comprehensive, current, and useful for Ethereum users.


Thank you for your support and for supporting public goods in Ethereum.

  • GitHub: github.com/walletbeat/walletbeat
  • Farcaster: @walletbeat & /walletbeat

title: The Red Guild: security as a public good
description:
The Red Guild is a public-goods security organization.

Since the beginning of 2023, we have worked full-time on the safety of the Ethereum ecosystem through open research, free training, advisories, tooling, and education. Our blog is a public record of recurring status updates, technical writeups, event reports, and shipped resources. Anyone can verify what we build and maintain. Today that work spans six active lines: Phishing Dojo, Damn Vulnerable DeFi, contributing with SEAL, education and awareness, security research and advisories, and open-source tooling.


We do not focus only on smart contracts because the threats go well beyond them. We steward Damn Vulnerable DeFi as a forever-free training ground and keep turning it into workshops and walkthroughs. We created, along with Patrick Collins, the first free and most complete smart contract security course, which to this day is the most viewed and recommended by the community. We built The Phishing Dojo (currently under maintenance) to train users against phishing and scams through realistic simulations, and continued improving it through beta releases, new wallet-signing and email challenges, account management, and progress tracking. We lead SEAL’s Security Frameworks work, publish technical advisories and research on off-chain and developer-security topics, and maintain practical public resources such as DevSecOops, devcontainer research, devcontainer-wizard and now exploring with transient/ephermal VMs in a world where having a 0day vulnerability has become cheaper. That body of work includes public investigations and guidance on Ethereum 7702 risks, malicious VSCode extensions, container escapes, npm supply-chain threats, "Why technical excellence fails" (whitehats not recognized as a critical infrastructure) and the One Time Pwnage / SLOVENLY COMET advisory on SMS interception attacks.


Our public impact is not only digital. We have mentored, judged, organized, and taught across Ethereum Argentina, Ethereum Uruguay, DeFi Security Summit, Devcon, Devconnect, ETHCC, and pop-up cities like muBuenos and Aleph/Crecimiento.


  • In Aleph, we organized the Security Day, a conference with original contents of its own, offered office-hours to startups, spoke about security as a public good, and hosted a Solidity & dApps week to onboard and improve builders skillsets.
  • At Devconnect, even after organizational restrictions and a rejected grant, we run a security awareness campaign: security challenges, a new Phishing Dojo beta, a QR threat analyzer, a live threat dashboard, and 3,500 printed OPSEC-while-traveling books distributed across the week (we still continue to receive requests for more, recently sent 200 more at EthCC sponsored by SEAL).
  • At Ekoparty, the biggest security conference in Latin America, we were invited to organize the blockchain security village, in which we onboarded members of the WebtrES community, sponsoring the booth, supporting its contents and installation, promoting CTFs and talks, bringing young people into hands-on security learning.
  • In Tandil, our public posts also show us organizing GEERS, a local web3 focused set of gatherings/conferences, helping energize local Ethereum community-building around Nodo Serrano.


We have also taken a very important role in many Ethereum-centered activities of course, two key examples are organizing the first iteration of the Ethereum Rangers program, and being champions at the One-trillion-dollar initiative first gathering, coordinating the Offchain layer, presenting insights and creating a blog-post later used by ethereum.org’s 1TS official report.


What matters now is continuity.

Our team ran out of funding on November 8, 2025, and kept going anyway: building, publishing, running the Devconnect awareness campaign, showing up for talks and workshops, and taking on community work because our commitment is to the ecosystem, not to a revenue model. We have no paywalls, no token, no closed access, and no sales funnel. Our public goods do not make money, but still require time, infrastructure, maintenance, logistics, and sustained research.


This round is not about helping us start.

It is about deciding whether work The Red Guild has delivered, maintained, and used in public can continue to exist. People across the ecosystem keep saying The Red Guild’s work matters. This is when words can become concrete support. Our funding on this round decides whether The Red Guild survives and continues producing independent top-quality security public goods for Ethereum.

title: scfuzzbench: smart contract fuzzer benchmark suite
description:
scfuzzbench is a benchmark suite for evaluating smart contract fuzzers.


Who

We are security researchers, protocol engineers, and open-source contributors focused on improving the safety of blockchain applications. The project is led by experienced practitioners in smart contract security and fuzz testing, with strong roots in real-world protocol auditing and vulnerability research. The core maintainer is Antonio Viggiano, and the project has received valuable contributions from Gustavo Grieco, alpharush, Rappie, and Alex The Entreprenerd.


What

scfuzzbench provides a standardized benchmark suite and methodology to measure the effectiveness of smart contract fuzzers, especially for stateful invariant testing, one of the most important techniques for discovering complex multi-transaction vulnerabilities in DeFi protocols and blockchain infrastructure. The platform allows researchers and tool builders to compare fuzzers using reproducible runs, shared datasets, transparent methodology, and publicly accessible results. As of now, we support Aave v4, Superform v2 periphery, Liquity v2 Governance, and Nerite as benchmark targets.


Why

Today, the blockchain ecosystem secures billions of dollars in assets, yet security tooling is still fragmented and difficult to compare fairly. Different fuzzers report results using different metrics, environments, and assumptions, making it hard for researchers, developers, and auditors to know which tools actually perform best. scfuzzbench solves this by creating an objective benchmark that drives scientific progress, improves transparency, and accelerates the discovery of vulnerabilities before attackers do.


Where

The project is fully open source and publicly accessible online at scfuzzbench.com, with benchmark definitions, methodology, and results available to the community. It is currently in the beta stage and is being constantly peer-reviewed before official benchmark results can be shared with the world.


How

Donations directly support cloud infrastructure for benchmark runs, expansion of benchmark datasets, integration of new fuzzing tools, reproducibility pipelines, result dashboards, and research collaborations with the broader blockchain security community.


When

Funding now will help us scale benchmark coverage in 2026, onboard additional open-source fuzzers, and establish scfuzzbench as the reference benchmark for smart contract security tooling.

By supporting scfuzzbench, donors help strengthen the security foundations of Web3 and protect users, protocols, and ecosystems from catastrophic vulnerabilities.

title: CypherTalk Podcast: Security Education for Ethereum

title: Etherform
description:
Etherform is an open-source security and DevSecOps toolkit of reusable GitHub Actions workflows for Foundry smart contract CI/CD. It is designed to help smart contract teams standardize and automate core development and deployment tasks through reusable workflows instead of rebuilding the same CI/CD setup in each repository.

title: Assertions.eth On-chain Transaction Guards for Ethereum
description:
Assertions (assertions.eth) is a public-good smart contract that brings test-driven development to on-chain transactions. Deployed at 0xA55e4707A94Ce4Aa647517ed9aD4084e4E5D1f3F on Ethereum mainnet, it provides a comprehensive suite of view-only assertion functions that can be composed into any batched transaction to enforce pre-conditions, post-conditions, and invariants, atomically on-chain.


Why it matters

High-stake on-chain operations (treasury transfers, protocol upgrades, permission changes, fund recoveries) are irreversible. Off-chain simulations (like Tenderly) can be rendered inaccurate by MEV, front-running, or state changes between simulation and execution. On-chain assertions are the only mechanism that guarantees conditions hold at the exact moment of execution. They are the last line of defense.


How it works

Assertion calls are batched alongside your actual operations in a DAO proposal, a Safe transaction batch (using Transaction Builder), or an EIP-7702 batched transaction. At execution time, each assertion verifies the live blockchain state (balances, return values, permissions, code hashes, timestamps, and more). If any single assertion fails, the entire transaction reverts. No partial execution, and no unexpected outcomes.


Capabilities:

  • Call-based assertions. Execute any view function on any contract and assert the return value (uint256, address, bool, bytes32, string, raw bytes).
  • Comparison operators. Equal, not equal, greater than, less than, greater/less or equal, approximate equality (within delta).
  • Tuple indexing. Assert specific return values from functions that return multiple values
  • Array length assertions. Validate dynamic array sizes.
  • Native balance assertions. Verify ETH balances of any address.
  • Block & chain assertions. Assert block number, timestamp, and chain ID.
  • Contract existence checks. Verify code presence and exact code hashes (critical for upgrade verification).
  • Custom error messages. Every assertion has an overloaded version with descriptive messages for debugging.


Where to use it:

  • Safe Transaction Builder. Batch assertions as additional transactions in your Safe multisig batch.
  • DAO proposals. Embed assertions directly in governance proposal action lists (Aragon, Governor, Compound, etc.).
  • EIP-7702 batches. Include assertions in Smart Account call batches for EOA-initiated multi-step operations.


Real-world impact

Assertions was used in TheDAO Security Fund reactivation to safely recover and distribute over 75,000 ETH (~$220M) in one of the largest on-chain fund movements in Ethereum history. The assertions verified final ETH balances across multiple safes, confirmed DAO token distributions, and validated contract whitelisting, ensuring every step of the complex multi-sig operation completed exactly as intended.


Assertions is fully open source (MIT license), free to use, and has no commercial components.

title: Self-Custodial Agent Authorization for Ethereum
description:
TLDR

Self-custodial authorization for agentic workflows that move capital onchain. Building a keystore layer: one signer registry anchored to Ethereum. Programmable permissions. Global revocation. Native account recovery. Works across every L2, no bridges, no redeployments per chain. GPL-3, open source.


The Problem

Wallets have always forced a trade-off: you can have security, or you can have self-custody. Not both.

  • One key controls everything. Lose it, the funds are gone. Expose it, there is no revocation, no fallback, no way to limit the damage. The only escape is handing control to a custodian.
  • No scope, no hierarchy. A $10 transfer and a $50M protocol deposit go through the exact same signing process. There is no way to assign different roles or permissions to different signers, the way a Google Workspace admin can grant an employee edit access without giving them ownership.
  • No native recovery for self-custodial accounts. Lose your keys and you lose your wallet. The infrastructure to attach guardians, rotate credentials, and recover access has never existed for accounts you fully own. Until now.
  • And it affects agentic workflows too. AI agents moving funds onchain have no way to operate under scoped, revocable permissions that live outside the agent. The same security gap that affects human wallet holders blocks every agentic workflow that touches onchain capital.


Functor introduces a security hierarchy for self-custodial wallets: multiple signers, programmable permissions, native recovery, and instant revocation, without giving up custody.


What We're Building

Functor is the keystore layer for Ethereum: a dedicated signer network with a single source of truth anchored to Ethereum, readable by any chain. It’s self-custodial authorization that agentic workflows need to move onchain capital: humans retain control, agents execute under scoped permissions.

The core idea is separating "who can act" from "where the assets are." Instead of each chain storing its own copy of who can sign, all chains reference one source of truth. This means:

  • Multiple signers per wallet. Add a passkey, a hardware key, a guardian. Each with its own permissions and scope.
  • Programmable permissions. Spend limits, time windows, contract restrictions, set once and enforced everywhere.
  • Native account recovery. Attach guardians and recover access the way you would reset a forgotten password, without trusting a custodian.
  • Global revocation. Rotate a compromised key once. It reflects across every chain instantly.


It works across all wallet types: smart contract wallets, EOAs, multisigs, and keystore-native wallets. Signature schemes can include passkeys, hardware keys, and other standards, so teams are not locked into a single signing method. 

Functor directly addresses 5 of 6 UX pain points identified in Ethereum's 1TS initiative:

  • Key management
  • Permission management
  • Fragmentation
  • Blind signing
  • Compromised web interfaces


Demo: ERC-7579 smart account with native multi-passkey recovery via Functor Keystore: https://www.loom.com/share/daf68134cd46458c965fbaad136cb28d

Docs: https://docs.functor.sh


Who Benefits

  • Power users and individuals: Add multiple devices as signers on one wallet. Lose your phone, revoke that signer, keep using your laptop. No seed phrase. No starting over.
  • Teams and asset managers: Assign different permissions per team member, set programmable execution rules, and maintain a clear audit trail across chains.
  • Agent wallets and agentic workflows: Give agents scoped permissions, set spending limits, restrict which contracts they can touch, and revoke access instantly if a key is compromised.
  • Wallet and smart account infrastructure: Any team building on ERC-7579 can integrate Functor to offer unified signer management and native recovery to their users, without per-chain redeployment.


How Funds Are Used

Security audit of the Functor Keystore. The protocol is fully open source and the audit is a prerequisite for public release, so the ecosystem can build on it reliably.

In QF, every unique donor increases the matching pool allocation. If this infrastructure matters to you, a small donation has real weight.

Thank you for supporting open-source Ethereum security.

title: Open-Source AI Security Triage by HackenProof
description:
Every Web3 project needs security review, but most can't afford it. A dedicated security engineer costs $150-300K/year. Professional triage services run $5-20K/month. The result: thousands of open-source protocols, DAOs, and public goods projects ship code with no systematic vulnerability review process.

Meanwhile, the tools that large security teams use internally — structured triage workflows, severity classification frameworks, duplicate detection, bounty management — remain locked behind enterprise contracts.

This leaves the most important part of the ecosystem — the open, permissionless, public goods layer — as the least protected.


What We Built

We built and open-sourced a complete AI-powered security triage system that any project can deploy for free. It consists of three components:

1. HackenProof MCP Server (Model Context Protocol)

An open-source server that connects AI assistants like Claude directly to bug bounty infrastructure. Any project team can:

  • Review vulnerability reports against their own codebase — the AI reads the security report and cross-references it with the project's actual source code to validate findings, locate affected code paths, and suggest fixes
  • Manage the full vulnerability lifecycle — from receiving a report to validating it, classifying severity, posting responses, and tracking resolution
  • Run batch operations — process dozens of reports across multiple programs simultaneously instead of one-by-one manual review

The server exposes 25+ structured tools covering report reading, state management, severity classification, commenting, label management, attachment handling, and authenticated screenshots. It supports both API key and session-based auth, runs as a Docker container, and can be self-hosted or used via our public endpoint.

This is not a wrapper around HackenProof's UI. It's a structured API layer that turns AI assistants into security triage agents — giving any team the operational capability that previously required a dedicated security operations center.

Source: https://docs.hackenproof.com/dashboard/mcp-server


2. Triage Skill — AI-Guided Vulnerability Assessment

A structured workflow that encodes professional triage methodology into a reusable AI skill. When a security report comes in, the skill guides the AI through:

  • Scope validation — is the reported target and version actually in scope for the program?
  • PoC verification — does the report include concrete proof of exploitation?
  • Duplicate detection — has this vulnerability already been reported?
  • Severity classification — what's the real impact, mapped to industry-standard severity levels?
  • Decision and response — what's the correct triage outcome, with a professional explanation for the reporter?

This encodes years of triage experience from handling 60,000+ vulnerability reports into a tool that any team can use immediately. A solo developer running a DeFi protocol gets the same triage quality as a team with a 10-person security department.


3. Bulk Triage Skill — Portfolio-Wide Security Monitoring

For teams managing multiple programs or protocols, the bulk triage skill:

  • Discovers all open reports across every program
  • Syncs with local codebases and blockchain explorers for validation
  • Analyzes each report and produces structured recommendations
  • Outputs everything for human review — no actions are taken without approval

This turns what would be days of manual review across multiple dashboards into a single command that produces a prioritized security status report.

Source: github.com/hackenproof-public/skills


Who This Is For

These tools are designed for exactly the teams that the Giveth Security Fund exists to support:

Open-source protocol teams — You have a codebase on GitHub and receive security reports, but don't have a dedicated triage person. Connect the MCP to Claude Code, open your repo, and ask the AI to validate incoming reports against your actual code.

DAOs and public goods builders — You run a bug bounty program but can't afford professional triage. The triage skill gives your contributors the same structured methodology used by professional security teams.

Small teams managing multiple projects — You maintain several contracts or applications and need to stay on top of security across all of them. The bulk triage skill scans everything at once and tells you where to focus.

Any Ethereum project — Connect the MCP, open your project in Claude Code, and say: "Fetch new reports and check each one against our codebase." The AI reads the report, reads your code, and tells you what's real, where it is, and how to fix it.


Why This Is a Public Good

It's fully open source. Skills, references, templates — all MIT licensed on GitHub. Fork it, modify it, run it yourself.

It removes the cost barrier. Professional security triage operations previously required either expensive staff or expensive service contracts. This makes the same capability available to any project with a GitHub repo and a Claude Code session.

It scales with the ecosystem. Every vulnerability report that passes through the system teaches the AI new attack patterns. A project that receives 50 reports doesn't just get 50 triage decisions — it gets a 50-pattern codebase scan that finds similar vulnerabilities the researchers didn't report.

It compounds. The triage skill encodes HackenProof's institutional knowledge from 60,000+ reports. Every project that uses it benefits from that accumulated experience without having to build it themselves.


What We're Building Next

  • Report Handoff Skill — standardized format for transferring triaged reports to client engineering teams with severity, bounty range, and remediation guidance
  • Codebase Security Review integration — deeper integration between bug bounty reports and local code analysis for pattern-based vulnerability scanning
  • Community skill contributions — opening the skill framework for other security teams to contribute their own triage methodologies


About HackenProof

HackenProof is a leading Web3 bug bounty and crowdsourced security platform with 70,000+ registered researchers, 60,000+ vulnerability reports processed, and $22M+ paid to whitehats across 350+ programs. We serve NEAR, Sui, Aptos, Celestia, OKX, MetaMask, Aurora, and hundreds of other projects.

We also produce a free YouTube podcast series on Web3 security — practitioner-led episodes covering real vulnerabilities, attack patterns, and defensive strategies, available to any developer, researcher, or founder worldwide.


What the Giveth Security Fund Enables

  • Onboard open-source and public goods Ethereum projects into professionally triaged bug bounty programs — subsidized or free for qualifying teams
  • Maintain and expand the open MCP server and skill library as free infrastructure for the community
  • Build new skills (report handoff, codebase review, automated pipeline) that further lower the barrier to running a responsible security program
  • Grow the security education podcast to reach more builders with the knowledge they need to ship securely

title: Nihilium
description:
Building the "Forgot My Password" Button for Web3

Imagine never losing access to your crypto wallet, encrypted files, or private data again, without trusting a custodian. That’s the gap Nihilium closes. For years Web3 has delivered self-custody for authorization, but recovery stayed stuck in the seed-phrase-in-a-drawer era.


Nihilium delivers the missing middle path: slashable conditional key release — a crypto-economic protocol that binds secrets to any NP-style condition (time-locks, ZKEmail, ZKPassport, signatures, oracles, etc.) so only the rightful owner can unseal them.


No one ever holds the private key in plaintext. Processors validate client-generated ZK proofs and decrypt only on valid conditions — or lose their entire staked reputation permanently. The result? Self-sovereign recovery that’s censorship-resistant, observable, and actually usable.


Why This Matters

Encrypted-by-default apps, private transactions, E2EE messaging, and medical-data “break-glass” access all become practical when recovery is reliable. We make the next billion users comfortable with true self-custody.


A picture saying a thousand words, a comparison graph on how nihilium carves out it's own category

Current state

This is not based on theory crafting, it works!

  • A full technical spec is live: https://www.nihilium.io/Nihilium_Whitepaper.pdf

  • An editor to build the conditions exists (editor.nihilium.io), demo: https://x.com/nihiliumio/status/2020942270011199535


Goals

  • Better SDK support & professionalize the codebase
  • Build out the on-chain registry and slashing capabilities
  • Onboarding processors

title: The Web3 OpSec Standard - W3OS
description:
What this project is

W3OS is an open-source operational security standard for web3 teams with the goal of making it easier for teams to set up and maintain effective security practices without requiring security expertise.

Most security failures in web3 don’t come from complex smart contract bugs, but from from operational security failures:

  • compromised multi-sig signers
  • misconfigured service permissions
  • phishing and social engineering
  • poor key management
  • vulnerable communications
  • malware infected devices


W3OS focuses on addressing these problems with practical, implementation-focused guidance.

GitHub: https://github.com/W3OSC/web3-opsec-standard

Why this matters

Operational security is one of the most common sources of failure, but industry guidance is not well standardized or easily actionable.


As a result, teams often:

Designed for failure

Humans make mistakes, processes break down over time, and controls fail. W3OS focuses on adding defense-in-depth with multiple layers of security controls to reduce the impact of eventual vulnerability.

Standard + tooling

W3OS is not just docs and guides. We also build tools that help teams enforce these practices and monitor for potential compromise.

Current progress

  • Initial version of the W3OS standard is live and publicly available
  • Extensive set of service configuration guides across commonly used platforms including X, Google, Github, Telegram

Each cohort, roughly 20 to 25 fellows execute security reviews alongside expert resident auditors. The fellowship remains one of the few structured, merit-based pathways into professional blockchain security that operates entirely as a public good.


Track record

We launched in late 2021 to help make DeFi more secure. Since then, yAudit has completed hundreds of security reviews for major DeFi protocols, securing over $2 billion in total value locked.


Expanding into zero-knowledge security

In 2024, we expanded into ZK security and research, driven by three converging trends: the SNARKification of the Ethereum protocol itself, the proliferation of ZK-powered networks, dApps, and cross-chain middleware, and the growing role of ZK in hardening Web2 through primitives like zkEmail and MPC-TLS ("zkTLS").
