title: Solidity Language Server
description:
👋 Hi, Solidity devs,

Solidity Language Server is an open-source public good language server that supports over 20+ LSP methods accross all text editors i.e. Vim, Neovim, Helix, Zed, VS Code / Cursor, Opencode, Claude Code and maintains low latency in largest solidity/foundry projects.


Our 2026 LSP benchmarks found that existing Solidity LSPs struggle with large projects and often break across different editors and AI tools. We built this Language Server at Asyncswap Labs to support our own development, and have since open-sourced it to fill a critical gap in smart contract developer tooling.


How can we contribute to Ethereum security?

Smart contract security doesn't start at audit time. It starts in the editor while developers are writing, navigating, and reviewing code.


We want solidity developers to jump to definitions, trace references, and reason about your contracts with confidence whether you're building, reviewing, or using AI-assisted tooling. Ship faster and catch mistakes before they hit the chain.


The Features

1. Diagnostics

Diagnostics show you Solidity warnings, lints, and errors.


2. Semantic Tokens

Semantic tokens allow your editor to understand what each symbol represents so it can apply the correct colors for your editor's theme.


3. Go to Definition / Declaration


The Go to Definition feature lets you or your AI agent jump to the location where a variable or user-defined type is declared.


4. Implementation

Have you ever tried to find where IERC20(token).transfer(...) is defined and landed on the interface function instead of the actual code? Go to Implementation skips the interface declaration and jumps straight to the contract that inherits it where the function body lives. This works when the contract inherits the IERC20 interface and overrides the method, which is how the LSP resolves the implementation location.


5. Hover

Hover surfaces everything you need to know about a symbol without leaving the line. Just hover over a function, variable, or contract to see NatSpec documentation, 4-byte selectors, storage layout locations, contract deployment costs, and function gas estimates — all inline.


6. References

Find References shows every usage of a variable, function, or user-defined type across your entire project contracts, tests, scripts, and library dependencies. This is more accurate than manual searching to understand how a symbol is used throughout your codebase.


7. Completion

Completion suggests types, variables, functions, and Solidity identifiers as you type — helping you write contracts faster and with fewer typos.


8. Signature Help

Signature Help shows parameter hints as you fill in function arguments, emit events, or access mappings. Triggered automatically when you type ( for functions and events, or [ for mapping lookups — so you always know what comes next.


9. Rename

Rename lets you rename variables, functions, parameters, contracts, aliases, and user-defined types — updating every reference across your project in one action.


10. Document Symbol

Document Symbols lists every symbol in a file — contracts, functions, variables, events, errors — in a nested hierarchy. Use it with your editor's outline view to quickly navigate large files.


11. Formating

Formatting keeps your Solidity code clean and consistent. You can format automatically on save or manually on demand.


12. Inlay Hint

Inlay Hints display parameter names inline at function call sites and event emissions — so you can read what each argument means without jumping to the definition.


13. CodeAction

Code Actions offer quick fixes right where you need them — like removing unused imports — with more actions being added over time.


14. Will Create Files

File Templates scaffold new Solidity contracts, tests, and scripts with the right boilerplate — so you can start writing code immediately.


15. Will Rename Files

File Rename automatically updates all import paths across your project when you rename a file — no broken imports to chase down.


16. Incoming / Outgoing Calls

Incoming Calls shows every place a function is called from across your project. Outgoing Calls shows every external call a function makes. Together, they let you trace the full call chain in either direction without reading through files manually.


Why now?

Solidity editor tooling is still below the standard required for security-critical software development. Many existing language servers — Juan Blanco's VS Code LSP, Nomic Foundation's LSP, and solc's built-in LSP — work inside narrow, editor-specific workflows but break down or degrade significantly in environments like Neovim, Vim, Helix, Zed, Emacs, and Sublime.


This matters because Solidity developers are increasingly moving toward other IDEs and AI coding assistants. AI tools like Claude Code and Opencode are beginning to consume language server infrastructure directly, without a traditional editor user interfaces. If Solidity language servers are breaking outside of one editor, they will no meet the needs of the broader ecosystem.


More importantly, the Solidity team has stated the Solc LSP is effectively abandoned as development ceased before it became stable, with no plans to revive it (solidity#16124). This leaves Ethereum without upstream ownership of a critical layer of Solidity LSP development tooling. Developers, reviewers, and AI systems rely on to understand smart contract code before it reaches production.


There is also a growing supply-chain security problem around developer tooling itself. Public reporting has shown that malicious editor extensions and packages can steal data, install backdoors, and target crypto developers specifically. Solidity LSP tooling must not only be fast and capable, but trustworthy in how it is built and distributed.


We believe language server infrastructure for Ethereum should be open-source, auditable, and verifiable, not another opaque attack surface in the developer workflow.


Why this project

Across benchmarks against the Solidity language servers currently known to us i.e. Nomicfoundation, Solc, Quang, and Juan Blanco, our results show stronger overall performance, broader feature support, and faster lsp responses. Our benchmarks are reproducible, and we welcome scrutiny and comparison from anyone building language tooling, because transparent measurement helps the entire ecosystem improve.


Who I am

My name is Meek Msaki. I am a software developer, educator, and founder building on Ethereum.


Over the last several years I have worked across smart contract development, developer education, and open-source tooling.


A few milestones from my journey:

- 2021: Graduated from the University of Minnesota fintech bootcamp

- 2022: First hackathon win at ETHGlobal

- 2023: Consulted with Extropy via Encode Club across 7+ blockchain cohorts covering Solidity, the EVM, zero-knowledge proofs, and Solana

- 2023: Attended the Science of Blockchain conference at Stanford

- 2024: Independent consulting at Lifeworld

- 2025-present: Co-founder at AsyncSwap Labs, working on AMM transaction ordering and swap intents


Alongside that work, I teach workshops and build open-source developer tools for Ethereum.

Relevant links:


- X: @msakiart

- Project: solidity-language-server

- Other project: huff.nvim, a Neovim plugin for developing Huff contracts


What funding will support

Support from this round will help fund any of these causes:

  1. continued feature development and maintenance
  2. performance and indexing improvements
  3. better code navigation, references, and analysis tooling
  4. stronger interoperability across editors and nontraditional clients
  5. continued AI-native LSP support currently available in OpenCode
  6. benchmark infrastructure and reproducibility
  7. testing, regression prevention, and release engineering
  8. security hardening, and verifiable distribution


Donation impact

Your support helps fund preventative security infrastructure for Ethereum.


Example impact levels:

- $1,000 supports maintenance, issue triage, and continual development

- $2,000 improves compatibility across Solidity versions, editors, and AI-native tooling

- $5,000 accelerates major features, performance, and other contributor-driven improvements

- $10,000+ hardening LSP security.


Community signals

Developers are already feeling the gap in Solidity tooling and the value of better editor support:

- “Actually it’s the only thing that made solidity usable on zed so thanks.” — clandestine.eth

- “my former colleagues will surely appreciate to have a better lsp.” — badfalafel

- “zed's bad solidity support always annoys me... if you'd like a contributor I'm happy to help” — kakashi


We need your support.

If you believe Ethereum security starts where smart contracts are written, in the editor, in code navigation, and in the tools developers and AI systems rely on to understand code, please support the Solidity Language Server.


Donate $1, $5, $100, $200 or $5,000 :). Any donation will make a huge difference. Thank you ❤️.

title: Transaction graph
description:
Project Overview

tx-graph is a transaction visualizer for EVM-compatible chains that converts a transaction hash into an interactive graph, making complex contract interactions easy to explore and understand.


What problem does it solve?

Transactions on EVM chains are difficult to trace and interpret, especially when they involve multiple contract interactions. While existing tracers provide low-level execution details, they require significant time and effort to piece together how contracts are connected and interact.


Solution

The solution is to combine tracer with a graph that maps out how contracts interact within a transaction.


Additional features

  • One click download all the contract codes that were executed in a transaciton
  • Foundry integration
  • A smart contract developer or a security engineer can execute a Foundry test and see the execution using this tool. This will help them quickly understand how a protocol is structured.


Existing Solutions

While existing tools such as tracerflow.xyz provide graph-based views of transaction traces, they are optimized for low-level execution detail rather than high-level understanding. By representing each function call as a separate node, they produce fragmented graphs that obscure the relationships between contracts. This limits their usefulness for quickly understanding transaction structure, highlighting the need for a more intuitive, contract-centric visualization approach.


In addition, existing solutions lack Foundry integration.


How does it aid security?

It aids security by helping developers and security researchers understand what the transaction did.

For example, Balancer hack in 2025 has over 1700 calls to contracts, involving almost 100 contracts. As you can imagine, this transaction is difficult to understand and time consuming to manually draw out on a white board.


tx-graph instantly graphs out the transaction, helping a security researcher quickly understand how an exploit was executed.


How does it aid Ethereum ecosystem?

The tool can also be used for educational purpose. If an user wants to learn how a protocol works, the user can paste a transaction hash that is relevant to the protocol to see how the protocol works.

It enables anyone to learn how protocols function by exploring real transactions,


Proof of Work

  • Website is hosted here
  • Example of Foundry integration
  • Graph of a hack with 2843 calls


Use of Funds

Funds will primarly cover infrastructure costs (database and RPC services). Remaining funds will support continued development and feature improvements. The project is currently maintained by myself.

With or without funding, I will continue developement as it serves as a core tool in my workflow.

title: PlankEVM
description:
Plank is a new smart contract language for the EVM. It aims to make writing secure contracts easier and more efficient by pushing more checks into the type system and eliminating the need for inline assembly.


Fixing the Ecosystem's Core Bottleneck

Plank is designed to alleviate the main bottleneck holding back other languages like Solidity & Vyper: the bandwidth of compiler engineers. Currently, any non-trivial extension to the language requires updates in the compiler itself. As a result, even relatively simple features widely requested by users can take years to be implemented, such as a generic ERC712 utility or more optimized storage packing.


Drawing inspiration from Zig & Rust, Plank empowers users to "help themselves" by providing a powerful & general purpose set of language primitives. This allows users to implement their own ideas and extensions without requiring deep compiler know-how.


Plank's Killer Feature: Comptime

Comptime is Plank's main differentiator. It allows smart contract developers to add code that only exists at compile time, enabling expressive static checks, code specialization and other functionality to be added by users without fear of bloating their final application.


Comptime enables features that are taken for granted in normal programming languages like Javascript, Python or Rust but are not possible in Solidity/Vyper:

  1. Generic Data Structures: Allows users to define and endlessly reuse data structures with different data types
  2. Custom Static Analysis: From math rounding bugs, to mixing of units, comptime allows developers to define their own static analysis & security checks via the type system, without additional gas costs. No janky extra tooling, no custom scripts, just Plank.
  3. Reusable Generic Optimizations: Today, when devs discover a compiler inefficiency, they are forced to rewrite the same patterns in inline assembly again and again. With Plank, such optimizations can be wrapped in reusable generic functions and shared as libraries, avoiding wasting time reauditing the same 10 assembly patterns.


How your contribution helps us

Any contribution you make will go towards:

  • Extending our runway, allowing us to continue working fulltime on the project (upon runway depletion we need to take time off to do paid work to replenish it before resuming)
  • Allowing us to host hackathons and other events to bolster adoption for the language and gather vital user feedback
  • Hire contractors or other contributors to accelerate our development

title: PRSpec Automated EIP Compliance Checker for Ethereum
description:
What is PRSpec?


PRSpec is an open-source tool that checks Ethereum client implementations

against EIP specifications using LLM-based semantic analysis. It doesn't

just compare text — it understands protocol intent and catches deviations

that manual review and traditional static analysis miss


What has PRSpec achieved?


Real-world impact:

Found a confirmed specification deviation in Nethermind's EIP-1559 implementation. A core developer acknowledged the FeeCollector property contradicts the mandatory fee burn mechanism

(https://github.com/NethermindEth/nethermind/issues/10522)


Ethereum Foundation engagement: The execution-specs team (#2 contributor) provided architectural guidance for improving PRSpec's spec extraction pipeline

(https://github.com/ethereum/execution-specs/issues/2212)


Production-ready foundation: 6 EIPs analyzed across 3 clients (go-ethereum, Nethermind, Besu) in Go, C#, and Java. 62 passing tests.

Full CI pipeline. MIT licensed.


Why does this need funding?


I built PRSpec entirely self-funded — investing personal savings into

title: Verifereum
description:
Mathematically Verified Ethereum Smart Contracts

Verifereum is an open-source project that brings mathematical rigour to Ethereum smart contract verification. Using the HOL4 theorem prover, we’re building tools to prove the correctness of smart contracts and eliminate entire classes of vulnerabilities.


Why Verifereum Matters

  • Beyond Traditional Auditing: While audits can find bugs, mathematical verification proves the absence of entire classes of vulnerabilities
  • High Stakes, Higher Standards: With billions of dollars secured by smart contracts, formal verification offers the strongest security guarantees possible
  • Perfect Fit: Ethereum’s deterministic execution model, where additionally code is expensive so applications are small, makes it an ideal candidate for formal verification


Technical Focus Areas

We’re currently working on three main tracks:

  1. EVM Base Layer
  • Refining our formal EVM specification
  • Implementing precompiles (ecRecover, etc.)
  • Optimizing execution in logic
  • Ensuring test suite compliance
  1. Decompilation Pipeline
  • Building Hoare/Separation logic for EVM bytecode
  • Creating verification examples
  • Developing decompilation automation
  1. Vyper Verification
  • Formalizing Vyper semantics
  • Implementing compiler frontend in logic
  • Building verification infrastructure


Our Approach

  • Foundation: Formal model of the EVM in HOL4 (Higher-Order Logic)
  • Methodology: Operational semantics via definitional interpreter
  • Validation: Complete EVM test suite compliance
  • Verification: Program logic for smart contract correctness proofs
  • Implementation: Focus on decompilation and compiler verification

title: Enscribe
description:
Enscribe replaces risky hex addresses with trusted, human-readable identities for smart contracts, wallets, and agents.


What


Enscribe provides identity infrastructure for onchain teams, powered by ENS.


Today most onchain Ethereum infrastructure including contracts, wallets, agents are identified via hex addresses. This creates significant security risk, as users must trust they are interacting with the correct contract or wallet.


Enscribe makes it easy for team to assign human-readable ENS names and associated metadata to their entire onchain infrastructure using .eth names or using DNS names, via DNS on ENS.


Enscribe provides the tooling teams need to design, deploy, and manage these namespaces in production, including multi-user workspaces, API access, and integrations with tools like Safe.


The end result of using Enscribe, is onchain identity for smart contracts and wallets. So instead of simply a hex address, users can view rich identity information using Enscribe, such as demonstrated below.


See in the Enscribe App here.


Why

Address spoofing and poisoning attacks are responsible for tens of millions of losses every year. These are preventable with proper onchain identities for contracts and wallets.


Enscribe reduces this risk by:

  • Replacing opaque hex addresses, with human-readable ENS names
  • Help standardise how protocols present their onchain presence
  • Make it easy for wallets, explorers and users to verify these assets
  • Provide identify workflows that teams can use to ensure they incorporate good identity hygene into their products and protocols


This makes the Ethereum ecosystem safer by default and reduces the attack surface for phishing and spoofing.


Where

Enscribe is built on Ethereum and integrates directly with ENS. Our app is available at app.enscribe.xyz, and we’re collaborating with the ENS DAO and other algiend projects to drive broad adoption.


We've already integrated with Safe, Ethereum Follow Protocol and Open Labels Initiative, and provide verification support via Etherscan, Blockscout and Sourcify.



We've also collaborated with a number of notable projects on their naming including Nouns, Cork, Liquity, Giveth, SSV Network, Superfluid and Kleros. You can learn more about some of our partnerships on our blog.


How


 - Over the past year, Enscribe has helped protocols including Nouns DAO, Liquity, Cork, Giveth, Based Nouns, and SSV Network adopt ENS-based naming for production smart contracts.

 - We launched and continued growing ENS Contract Naming Season, turning contract identity into a visible, incentivised ecosystem initiative.

 - We expanded Enscribe from a contract naming tool into identity infrastructure for onchain teams, covering contracts, wallets, multisigs, and agents.

 - We shipped richer identity tooling, including contract metadata, Name Explorer, and better ways to browse and understand namespaces.

 - We improved ecosystem visibility through integrations such as Blockscout contract identity scoring.

 - We published API documentation, community calls, and video tutorials to make ENS-based identity easier for developers and teams to adopt.

 - We continued shipping practical tooling including Safe support, batch naming, and developer workflows for Foundry and Hardhat.


Enscribe is also aligned with Vitalik's vision on low-risk DeFi.



When

During the coming months we want to:


 - Evolve Enscribe from contract naming into shared identity infrastructure for onchain teams.

 - Add approval workflows and roles/permissions for multi-user namespace management.

 - Expand support for smart accounts, multisigs, notifications, and autorenewals.

 - Make DNS-on-ENS easier with better DNSSEC import and onboarding for organisations using existing domains.

 - Support ENSv2 as the protocol evolves.

 - Deepen API, CLI, and agent workflows so teams can manage identity programmatically.

 - Improve management of full namespaces across contracts, wallets, and agents.

 - Keep growing Contract Naming Season and ecosystem integrations so named identity becomes a stronger default for projects.


How your funding can impact our roadmap

<$5k

- Cover core infrastructure costs to keep Enscribe reliable and publicly accessible


$5k–$10k

- Improve developer experience and core UX for importing managing on-chain namespaces

- Further streamline contract naming and ENS resolution performance


$10k–$25k

- Accelerate DNS -> ENS onboarding (DNSSEC imports, namespace setup)

- Improve support for modern wallet patterns (e.g. smart accounts)


$25k–$50k

- Build out monitoring, alerting, and reliability infrastructure for production use

- Improve activity tracking and operational visibility for teams managing namespaces


$50k+

- Accelerate delivery of production-ready team features (e.g. workflows, automation, access controls)

- Expand support for protocol teams managing multi-chain infrastructure


---


Our goal is to make ENS usable for real-world teams and organisations. As more protocols adopt ENS namespaces, users benefit from clearer, safer interactions across wallets and applications.


We're also continuing to contribute directly to the ENS protocol, by identifying ways in which we can support primary naming for all smart contracts on Ethereum.


Giveth contributions will the continued development of Enscribe and help us eliminate hex addresses from Ethereum UX. Making Ethereum safer for everyone!

title: Safe Multisig Transaction Hashes
description:
Who?

Anyone who doesn't want to get rekt signing a multisig transaction. This script is used across the Ethereum ecosystem - from small teams to blue-chip projects - to locally verify and simulate Safe transactions before signing.


What?

A powerful, local-first Bash CLI tool (just one file guys!) that strengthens the security and transparency of any Safe multisig operations (transactions and off-chain messages are supported). It lets you independently verify and simulate transactions before signing them. If Bybit had used it, DPRK would be about $1.5 billion poorer.


Why?

Because verifying what's shown on your hardware wallet is what keeps you safe. If you skip that step, you're trusting someone else's data, and guess what, that's how you get rekt (see Bybit or Radiant Capital).


Where?

Runs on any OS with Bash, or via Docker/Podman. You can execute it entirely locally with the right parameters and verify exactly what you're signing.


How?

The script reconstructs Safe transaction hashes by fetching transaction details from the Safe Transaction Service API and computing both domain and message hashes according to the EIP-712 standard. Using the --interactive mode, you can work completely offline - entering parameters manually and verifying hashes without relying on any external API.


Core capabilities:

  • Reproduces the exact transaction/message hashes computed by Safe smart contracts.
  • Supports all Safe multisig versions starting from 0.1.0.
  • Works across 35+ networks.
  • Supports manual parameter entry for standalone or unlogged transactions.
  • Supports nested Safes (computes both primary and nested Safe approval hashes).
  • Generates Safe-compatible EIP-712 message hashes from any input (off-chain messages).
  • Simulates locally the Safe transaction to produce execution traces and detect runtime issues before signing.
  • Warns about untrusted delegate calls, owner/threshold changes, and suspicious gas or refund settings etc.
  • Performs all cryptographic computations locally; only simulations require an RPC provider.


When?

Whenever you sign a Safe multisig transaction or message.

title: Echidna: A Fast Smart Contract Fuzzer
description:
Echidna is a Haskell program designed for fuzzing/property-based testing of Ethereum smart contracts. It uses sophisticated grammar-based fuzzing campaigns based on a contract ABI to falsify user-defined predicates or Solidity assertions.



Echidna was created 8 years ago and it was already used in a number of complex real-world fuzzing campaign, most of them are detailed here: https://github.com/perimetersec/public-fuzzing-campaigns-list.


Features


  • Generates inputs tailored to your actual code
  • Corpus collection, mutation and coverage guidance to find deeper bugs
  • Powered by Slither to extract useful information before the fuzzing campaign
  • Source code integration to identify which lines are covered after the fuzzing campaign
  • Interactive terminal UI, text-only or JSON output
  • Automatic test case minimization for quick triage
  • Seamless integration into the development workflow using Github actions.
  • Optimization mode: instead of break a binary property, which was also adopted by other fuzzers such as Medusa and Foundry.
  • Efficient on-chain fetching of state to test live contracts and source code fetching (using either Sourcify or Etherscan)


New features


In recent releases, Echidna gained a few more advanced features!


  • Automatic Foundry unit-test generation from each invariant/property failure, for quick debugging
  • Support of a large number of Foundry cheatcodes, provided by hevm
  • Optional symbolic execution for formal verification or exploration or finding counter-examples using hevm



Upcoming agentic capabilities

Echidna will have a fully integrated MCP that allows AI agents to inspect and direct fuzzing campaigns while they run. Agents such as Claude or Codex can be used to explore quickly or try to break specific invariants, using the preview build already available. This feature needs a good amount of experimentation and development to make sure agents can use it efficiently. This is one key features that will develop faster with the donations received in this round.


How the donations will be used


The donations collected in from this QF round will be used to make sure Echidna gets my full attention and I wont be needed to work on other projects full time. Every $8k donated allows a month of dedicated Echidna research and development, including money spent in dedicated VPS for large-scale fuzzing experimentation and access to frontier LLM agents. For the number of months funded, here are some expected deliverables: 


  • At least one minor release each 2 months (e.g. bug fixes)
  • At least one major release each 3 months (e.g. new and improved major features)
  • At least one blog post each 2 months, explaining an example/depth dive into a major feature (e.g. symbolic execution, LLM agent integration, etc).


Related projects

Echidna depends on a number of components, critically hevm and Slither. Additionally, the following tools use Echidna: Recon Invariant Testing Extension and scfuzzbench. Please consider supporting these related projects.

title: Act
description:
act is a formal specification language and verification framework for Ethereum smart contracts, and rigorous tool for ensuring smart contract safety. 


Originally developed as part of the Ethereum Foundation's formal verification efforts, act has found a permanent home at Argot, an independent non-profit organization that stewards critical Ethereum infrastructure. With Argot also being home to Solidity, act is well positioned to contribute to the specification of Core Solidity in the future.


At its core, act bridges the gap between human-readable specifications and EVM bytecode, proving their equivalence using hevm as its underlying execution engine. This makes it possible to formally verify that a contract's implementation does exactly what its specification says it should, across multiple smart contract languages, including Solidity and Vyper. Rather than relying on testing alone, act gives development teams a mathematically grounded way to reason about contract behavior, making it a powerful tool for high-assurance deployments. On top of that, the project has recently been enhanced with an output to the Lean prover, making verification usable across multiple platforms. 


Recent work:

Recent work has focused on building act's theoretical foundations from the ground up, formalizing its mathematical semantics and establishing proofs of type safety. With these foundations in place, the team launched its act v0.2.0 release: https://github.com/argotorg/act/releases/tag/v0.2.0


This release is an important milestone for the project, marking the transition from early-stage research to a tool that developers can begin to explore and build familiarity with. As work on Core Solidity matures the team will begin exploratory work to verify smart contracts written in Core Solidity. 


More info:

Github: https://github.com/argotorg/act

Documentation: https://argotorg.github.io/act/


How donations will be used:

100% of donated funds go directly to engineer salaries. act is public good infrastructure maintained by a small research and engineering team at Argot, a non-profit organization. Every contribution goes toward keeping this foundational formal verification tooling open, maintained, and accessible to the broader developer community. See the full roadmap here.


Related projects:

act depends on hevm (see Giveth profile). Please consider supporting this related project.

title: hevm
description:
Hevm is a specialized symbolic execution engine and testing framework for Ethereum smart contracts, serving as a cornerstone tool for smart contract security. 

Originally developed under the Ethereum Foundation, hevm has found a new home at Argot (argot.org), an independent non-profit organization dedicated to maintaining and developing open source infrastructure for the Ethereum ecosystem.


By enabling developers to perform rigorous analysis of contract behavior, uncover edge cases, and verify code properties through symbolic manipulation, hevm plays an essential role in ensuring the correctness and safety of smart contracts. 


This essentially means that hevm can try out all execution possibilities of your contract and see it can somehow violate some assertions you have. These assertions can be e.g. the total number of tokens must always be X, some value must never be greater than Y, some value must never overflow, etc.


In some sense, hevm is similar to a fuzzer, but instead of only trying with random values to trigger faults, it instead computes whether a fault is possible. If it is possible, it gives an example call to trigger the fault, and if it isn't possible, it mathematically proves it so, and tells the user the contract is safe.


Hevm can not only be used to find bugs in programs, but can also help to make sure that two programs behave equivalently from the outside. This may be advantageous when one may be more efficient (use less gas) to execute, but harder to reason about. This can be done via equivalence checking where hevm either proves that the behaviour of the two bytecodes is the same, or gives inputs where they differ.


Recent work:

Recent work has centered on hardening the tool through maintenance-focused releases, delivering meaningful improvements to performance, reliability, and usability. Already powering tools like Echidna, with symbolic execution now progressively integrated into both Echidna and the Solidity fuzzing pipeline, hevm is increasingly being positioned as a foundational execution engine at the core of the broader verification and testing ecosystem, with the team's focus going forward shifting toward deepening that role and enabling more tools to build on top of it.


More info:

See full documentation here: https://hevm.dev/

Check out the latest releases here: https://github.com/argotorg/hevm/releases


How the donations will be used:

100% of donated funds go directly to engineer salaries. hevm is public good infrastructure, maintained by a small team at Argot, a non-profit organization. Contributions fund the work needed to ship a browser-based version of hevm via WebAssembly, advance stateful invariant testing, and continue the deeper integration with Echidna that combines fuzzing and symbolic execution for broader path discovery. Every dollar donated goes toward keeping this critical, open-source tooling maintained and moving forward. See full roadmap here.



Related projects

hevm is being used by a number of projects, including Echidna (see Giveth profile) and act (see Giveth profile). Please consider supporting these related projects.

title: Sourcify
description:
Sourcify is an open-source, public-good smart contract verification service built on the principle that verified Ethereum contract datasets should be open, accessible, and owned by no single entity.


Originally part of the Ethereum Foundation and now stewarded by Argot, Sourcify has long been an advocate for security and open standards in the ecosystem.Its mission is straightforward but critical:


ensuring that the link between deployed bytecode and human-readable source code is verifiable by anyone, and that the verification infrastructure passes the walkaway test: no single actor's disappearance should compromise the integrity or availability of the data.


At a practical level, Sourcify makes Ethereum safer by giving users, developers, and tools the ability to inspect exactly what a smart contract does before interacting with it. When a contract is verified through Sourcify, its source code is publicly available and matched to its on-chain bytecode, making contract behavior transparent and independently confirmable. This transparency is foundational to a healthier ecosystem, and Sourcify reinforces it by operating as a credibly neutral public good rather than a commercial service.


The team has spent the past period building the technical foundations of a reliable and scalable verification service and currently supports contracts written in Solidity, Vyper, and Fe. As those foundations mature, focus is increasingly shifting toward outreach and community initiatives, including active participation in the Verifier Alliance, a collaborative effort to ensure verified contract data is consistently available across explorers and verifiers, and to publish this dataset as a shared, open resource for the entire ecosystem (you can also find more info under https://one-trillion-dollar-security.netlify.app/ under Communtiy).


Sourcify is also playing an active role in tackling one of Ethereum's most persistent UX and security failures: blind signing. For years, users confirming transactions have been confronted with raw, incomprehensible hex data, with no reliable way to confirm that what they are signing matches their actual intent. Sourcify is participating in the ERC-7730 Clear Signing working group and developing tooling and an SDK to help protocols publish human-readable transaction descriptors, ensuring that the infrastructure behind clear signing remains open, neutral, and verifiable. It is work that sits squarely at the intersection of open-source integrity, security, and real-world user protection.


How donations will be used:

100% of raised funds go directly toward the salaries of the three engineers maintaining Sourcify and delivering on its roadmap over the coming months. This includes completing the migration to API v2, expanding contract coverage through similarity verification across all supported chains, advancing the Verifier Alliance's open dataset with improved Parquet exports and data sanitization, and contributing development capacity to the ERC-7730 Clear Signing initiative, including SDK development and tooling for generating specification files. Funds also support ongoing collaboration with the broader Ethereum ecosystem, including ethereum-lists/chains maintenance and Solidity infrastructure work.

title: Colibri: Trustless Blockchain Data for Wallets and dApp
description:
Colibri removes RPC trust by verifying blockchain data locally with cryptographic proofs.

Colibri is a trustless, stateless, ultra-light Ethereum client that enables applications to verify blockchain data locally — without trusting RPC providers. It brings proof-based verification to mobile, web, IoT, and AI systems.



The Problem

Most applications access blockchain data through centralized RPC providers. While the blockchain itself is decentralized, the access layer is not.

A compromised RPC provider can manipulate, censor, or withhold data. Applications cannot verify responses, leading to risks such as incorrect balances, manipulated contract state, unsafe transaction simulations, and undetectable attack vectors. This problem becomes critical for wallets, DeFi applications, IoT devices, and autonomous systems.

In recent years, multiple sophisticated supply-chain attacks have proven that this is not a theoretical risk.

A malicious/compromised provider can:

  • Return fake balances or outdated state,
  • manipulate transaction data before signing to redirect assets to attacker-controlled addresses,
  • Manipulate smart contract reads (e.g., lending apps or governance votes),
  • Silence or censor certain accounts or regions.

For end users, this means:

  • Wallets showing false information,
  • Transactions being hijacked or front-run,
  • IoT devices granting unauthorized access,
  • AI systems making wrong autonomous decisions.

In addition, all blockchain interactions begin with reads. These reads expose user intent and metadata through centralized infrastructure, creating privacy risks that are not addressed today.



What Colibri Does

Colibri replaces trust with cryptographic verification.

It verifies:

  • execution data (balances, storage, logs, transaction outcomes)
  • consensus validity (ensuring data originates from the canonical chain)

This is done statelessly — without sync, without stored state, and without trusting any data source.

Colibri extends this into application-level security:

  • Verified Transaction Simulation
  • Transactions can be simulated locally based on proofs before signing, ensuring correctness and preventing manipulation between simulation and execution.
  • Agentic Scam Analysis
  • Verified data can be analyzed to detect inconsistencies or suspicious patterns before users or automated systems act on it.
  • Human-Readable Simulation Translation
  • Simulation results can be translated into understandable explanations, improving user awareness and decision-making.
  • Pragmatic Adaptive Privacy (PAP)
  • Colibri introduces a privacy-aware read layer that reduces metadata leakage and protects user intent during blockchain interactions.

Why this matters now

The last months have shown how fragile today’s Web3 security model still is. The Bybit hack alone caused losses of approximately $1.5 billion. Large npm supply-chain attacks targeted the JavaScript ecosystem and injected wallet-draining malware into widely used packages. The recent KelpDAO exploit caused roughly $292 million in losses and was not primarily a smart-contract bug, but an off-chain infrastructure failure involving compromised internal RPC infrastructure.


Across these incidents and related attacks, billions of dollars were lost because critical parts of the stack were trusted instead of verified: user interfaces, dependencies, transaction data, RPC responses, simulations, bridge verifiers, and off-chain infrastructure.


Not every attack can be prevented fully by local blockchain-data verification. Some would not be possible at all and many attack paths become much harder when every wallet and dApp verifies what it reads, verifies what it simulates, and verifies what the user is about to sign.


Colibri exists to make this verification practical.

Colibri’s architecture

  • C-based core: ultra-light, fast, portable, runs on mobile, web, and embedded devices
  • SDK bindings: JS/TS/WASM, Python, Dart/Flutter, Swift, and Kotlin/Java — making integration into wallets, browsers, or backend systems straightforward.
  • zk-proof aggregation: recursively aggregates sync committee transitions into a single compact proof, minimizing bandwidth and compute needs
  • Local Transaction simulation: Next to on-chain data verification, all transaction data can be simulated locally before signing based on proofs. (offered as SDK library function)

This means that even a sensor, phone, or AI agent can verify the Ethereum state independently — without syncing or trusting any third party.


[Video showing colibri in the standalone case as RPC node within Metamask]


[Proofer Infrastructure Dashboard]


Roadmap

Q2 2026 — Production Expansion & zk Baseline

Core Client

  • Production-ready Ethereum verifier (execution + consensus proofs) (completed)
  • Production-ready Gnosis support
  • MVP support for OP Stack (Optimism, Base)
  • Hardened verifier across platforms (mobile, web, embedded)

Prover Infrastructure (vRPC)

  • Production-ready prover architecture:
  • Local Prover / Hybrid Prover
  • Proxy Prover
  • vRPC (remote prover)
  • Packaged deployments for different environments (local, hosted, provider)
  • Proof delivery (execution + consensus) at scale

zk-Proofs (Consensus)

  • zk-consensus proofs production ready
  • Compression of sync committee transitions into single proofs

Multichain (Phase I)

  • Production support:
  • Ethereum mainnet
  • Gnosis
  • Testnets (Sepolia, Chiado)
  • MVP:
  • OP Stack (Optimism, Base)

Developer Ecosystem

  • Stable bindings: JS/TS, Python, Swift, Kotlin/Java, Dart/Flutter
  • Developer documentation (integration-first)
  • Reference integrations:
  • Wallet (verified reads + simulation)
  • dApp 

Deliverables

  • Trustless reads (balances, storage, logs,...) in production
  • Local transaction simulation on verified state
  • End-to-end: Request → Proof → Verification → Execution

Q3 2026 — Scaling, Privacy Layer &

Architecture Consolidation

Prover Infrastructure

  • Scaling of prover architecture across all types:
  • Local Prover (optimization for constrained environments)
  • Proxy Prover (delegation patterns, hybrid verification)
  • vRPC (remote prover, provider-facing)
  • Standardized deployment models (local, hybrid, provider-operated)
  • Historical proof support

Multichain (Phase II)

  • Additional L1s / L2s
  • Standardization of proof formats across chains

Privacy Layer (PAP)

  • PAP MVP (Pragmatic Adaptive Privacy)
  • Transport privacy strategies (multi-endpoint, routing)
  • Content privacy strategies (query shaping, batching)
  • Integration into client and bindings

Transaction Security

  • Concept and architecture of Transaction Security Agent
  • Pre-signature verification model
  • Simulation-based intent validation
  • Integration points (wallet, SDK)

Developer Ecosystem

  • Additional bindings: C++, Rust, Go
  • SDKs for wallet and IoT integration
  • Testnet environments and reproducible setups

Deliverables

  • Unified prover architecture (local / proxy / vRPC)
  • Privacy-aware, verifiable data access (PAP MVP)
  • Defined architecture for transaction security layer

Q4 2026 — Product Integration &

Ecosystem Rollout

zk-Proofs

  • zk-consensus proofs fully integrated (completed)
  • Stabilization and optimization of zk verification pipeline

Prover Infrastructure

  • Advanced batching and aggregation strategies
  • Cost-optimized proof generation
  • Mature deployment patterns across:
  • Local Prover
  • Proxy Prover
  • vRPC (provider-operated)

Multichain (Phase III)

  • Broad L1 / L2 coverage
  • Stable multi-chain abstraction

Transaction Security

  • Transaction Security Agent (MVP)
  • Integration into wallet environments
  • LLM-based transaction analysis
  • Detection of anomalies and unexpected behavior
  • Pre-signature verification pipeline

Ecosystem Integration

  • Integration into wallet stacks (e.g. Kohaku-like SDKs)
  • Integration into IoT / embedded prototypes

Privacy Layer (PAP)

  • Extended PAP capabilities
  • Configurable privacy profiles (T×C model)

Deliverables

  • First production-ready transaction security layer
  • Integrated zk-based verification pipeline
  • Multi-chain proof system in real applications

2027 — Adoption, Standardization &

New Verticals

Infrastructure & Network

  • Mature prover ecosystem (multiple independent operators)
  • vRPC as a deployable standard for RPC providers

Standardization

  • Contribution to Ethereum Statelessness roadmap
  • Alignment with client teams on proof formats
  • Open standards for proof delivery

Product Layer Expansion

  • Transaction Security Agent (production)
  • Advanced simulation analysis
  • Automated risk detection
  • Integration into wallets and dApps

Privacy (PAP)

  • Full PAP release
  • Privacy as default layer in SDKs

New Verticals

  • IoT SDKs (device integration, access control, payments)
  • AI agents (trustless data access + verifiable actions)

Real-World Adoption

  • Multiple production integrations:
  • Wallets
  • IoT systems
  • Web applications

Deliverables

  • Trustless data access as deployable standard
  • Privacy + verification combined at protocol layer
  • Adoption beyond early ecosystem (wallets → devices → agents)


Strategic Positioning

Trust Model

  • No reliance on RPC correctness
  • Proof-based verification for all data access

Architecture

  • Stateless client (no sync, no state)
  • Execution proofs + consensus proofs as primitives

Core Principle

  • Request → Proof → Verification → Execution

Target Environments

  • Mobile
  • Web
  • IoT / Embedded
  • AI Agents

Objective

  • Replace trusted RPC access with verifiable, privacy-aware infrastructure


The Future with Colibri

Applications can detect manipulated inputs, inconsistent state, or unexpected execution paths before any action is taken. This fundamentally reduces one of the largest attack surfaces in Web3 today. Also, read privacy is available while maintaining full verification. 


In Web3

Colibri directly improves the security and reliability of existing wallets and dApps.

Applications no longer rely on centralized RPC providers for critical reads. Balances, contract state, logs, and simulation results can be verified locally before being used.

Transaction simulations become provable instead of assumed. Users no longer sign based on UI representations or RPC responses, but on verified execution outcomes.

This closes one of the most critical gaps in Web3 today: the ability to manipulate data between read, simulation, and signing. Wallets and dApps can now detect inconsistencies or manipulated inputs before any transaction is executed.

In practice, this means:

  • safer wallet interactions
  • verifiable DeFi operations
  • reduced attack surface for frontends and bots
  • more reliable automation systems


Colibri can be integrated incrementally, acting as a drop-in verification layer without requiring new infrastructure or full nodes.


In IoT

Devices such as smart locks, meters, vehicles, and industrial systems can independently verify blockchain state.

They no longer rely on cloud services or gateways to interpret blockchain data. Instead, they validate permissions, payments, and state transitions locally, enabling secure machine-to-machine interactions without trusted intermediaries.


In AI and Agentic Systems

Autonomous agents increasingly act on blockchain data — executing trades, managing assets, or coordinating actions.

Colibri ensures that these systems operate only on verified inputs. Agents can validate state, simulate outcomes, and detect inconsistencies before acting.

This creates a foundation for reliable, autonomous systems that are resistant to manipulation, incorrect data, and hidden trust assumptions.


Across Systems

Colibri introduces a new standard: verification replaces trust at every interaction point.

Blockchain is no longer only trustless at the core — it becomes trustless at the edge, where applications, devices, and users actually interact with it.



Conclusion

Colibri transforms blockchain access from trust-based to proof-based.

It is a foundational layer that ensures correctness, security, and independence for applications interacting with blockchain systems.

It is the missing piece in Ethereum’s journey toward full statelessness and decentralization — an infrastructure layer that guarantees verifiable truth at every endpoint.

By making trustless verification possible on any device, Colibri expands the reach, security, and resilience of Web3 — ensuring that every wallet, every sensor, and every agent can independently verify the world it interacts with.


How we plan to use funding of the DAOfund security QF round

<$5k

  • Hardening of the verifier (execution + consensus proof validation)
  • Hardening and extension of existing bindings (Java/Kotlin, Swift, Dart/Flutter, Python, JS/WASM) and addition of new language support
  • Developer documentation and integration guides (wallet / dApp integration)
  • Integration examples (verified reads, transaction simulation on verified state)

$5k–$10k

  • Performance improvements (verification latency on mobile/web)
  • Extension of verifier infrastructure (vRPC, proxy verifier, hybrid and local verifier modes)
  • Foundations for Pragmatic Adaptive Privacy (PAP) for verifiable, privacy-preserving reads
  • Testing against real attack scenarios (manipulated RPC data, incomplete or inconsistent state)

$10k–$25k

  • Production-ready integration patterns for wallets and dApps (verification-first architecture)
  • Integration of Pragmatic Adaptive Privacy (PAP) for verifiable, privacy-preserving reads
  • Local Transaction simulation and evaluation 
  • vRPC (Verifyable RPC) specification and reference implementation

$25k–$50k

  • Expansion to additional EVM L1/L2 networks
  • Robust prover infrastructure (vRPC, hybrid/local/proxy)
  • Deeper integrations (wallet SDKs, IoT and agent environments)
  • Foundation for Transaction Security Agent (AI based Transaction simulation and evaluation)

$50k+

  • End-to-end proof-based access stack (data + proofs as default, replacing RPC trust)
  • Full integration of Pragmatic Adaptive Privacy (PAP):
  • transport privacy (multi-provider routing, unlinkable requests)
  • content privacy (aggregation and abstraction of reads)
  • Privacy Abstraction Layer (PAL) for developers (privacy without breaking verification)
  • Advanced transaction security layer:
  • simulation on verified state
  • detection of manipulated calldata and malicious patterns
  • Human understandable Txs
  • Standardization of proof-based interfaces for wallets, dApps, and agents

Core principle across all tiers

The goal is to remove RPC trust as a security assumption by making proof-based verification practical in real applications—especially wallets, where most attacks occur today. Adding privacy for read access without compromising verification on protocol level.

title: Vero, a multi-node validator client
description:
Vero is a multi-node validator client designed to protect validators from client bugs. It does this by cross-checking the blockchain state across multiple client implementations before submitting attestations.



How does Vero help Ethereum?

Voting for an incorrect chain can have disastrous for Ethereum validators – in the worst case, all of their staked ETH can get slashed. By using Vero, Ethereum validators can avoid voting for an incorrect chain by getting a sort of "second opinion" before they attest.



What is Vero's goal?

The short-term goal is to protect as many validators as possible from client bugs.

The long-term goal is to protect all of Ethereum from the potentially catastrophic consequences of client bugs. To reach this goal, we need about 35-40% of the network to run Vero (or equivalent) setups.



Is Vero production-ready?

Yes, Vero is production-ready! Vero is already making thousands of validators more resilient to client bugs, across both Ethereum and Gnosis Chain.



What is coming up for Vero?

As a validator client, Vero needs to stay up-to-date with the latest network upgrades. We have added support for the Fusaka network upgrade in 2025, and have started working on the upcoming Glamsterdam network upgrade that is expected to ship in 2026.


Besides network upgrades we also regularly ship new features and optimizations, see Vero's changelog.



How will funds be used?

  • <$50k: support ongoing development and adoption-boosting efforts (talks, workshops, support)
  • $50k - $100k: hire another contributor to actively work on the project
  • $100k+: hire a full-time contributor dedicated to the project



Where can I find out more?

Check out the talks on Vero from EthCC 2025 , Lido's Node Operator Community Call or EthStaker's Community Call .


For a more hands-on session you can check out the Vero workshop from Dappcon 2025.


Learn more about Vero in the introductory blog article or in the official docs!

title: Recon Invariant Testing Extension & Framework
description:
Over 1300 downloads, the most used Stateful Fuzzing Smart Contract Testing Framework!


The Recon Extension allows you to quickly scaffold and run Invariant Testing with Echidna, Medusa and Halmos.


Leveraging the Chimera Framework, the extension makes you write Foundry tests, which can then be run with other specialized tools.


When a property breaks, you can immediately debug it using Foundry, making the best out of all tools.


## Features


The Recon extension is a VS Code extension that streamlines smart contract testing by providing:


- **One-click setup**: Automatically install and configure [Chimera](https://github.com/Recon-Fuzz/chimera) templates

- **Integrated fuzzing**: Run [Echidna](https://github.com/crytic/echidna), [Medusa](https://github.com/crytic/medusa) and [Halmos](https://github.com/a16z/halmos) directly from VS Code

- **Contract explorer**: Browse and select target contracts and functions

- **Fuzzer integration**: Quick access to fuzzing tools directly through the extension

- **Coverage visualization**: View and analyze code coverage from fuzzers

- **Test generation**: Generate Foundry unit tests from call sequences that break properties found by the fuzzer

- **Log to Foundry Repro converter**: Convert Echidna and Medusa logs to Foundry test reproductions with customizable VM options

- **Link Libraries (Experimental)**: Automatically detect and configure library dependencies for Echidna and Medusa

- **Mock/TargetFunctions generation**: Easily create mock contracts and target functions for testing

- **CodeLens integration**: Run tests and modify function behaviors directly in the editor


## Upcoming Features


  • A new Rust fuzzer, an exact copy of Echidna, 10 times faster than Echidna
  • Our AI Fuzzing Framework, Automations and Prompts, 40 times faster than manual work

title: Unruggable
description:
Unruggable is a research and development firm building the verified web through high-impact contributions to ENS. Unruggable created and maintains Unruggable Gateways, a core component of ENSv2, critical to scaling ENS including on Namechain and across all Ethereum L2s. Our work is consistently focused on the future of ENS, including supporting the development of secure ENS name resolution on L2s and crosschain identity relying upon next generation interop solutions.


What We’re Building

Recently, we have been working with the Ethereum Foundation and Wonderland on the development of an onchain registry of chain identifiers and chain-specific metadata. The registry allows chains to get a unique ENS subname of on.eth, such as base.on.eth, where the ERC-7930 chain identifier can be found, along with the CAIP-2 chain ID and other metadata about the chain.


Unruggable is also developing Unruggable Gateways, a key infrastructure for scaling ENS, including Namechain, Basenames, and subname services. We are also advancing research in crosschain identity, ensuring ENS adoption across L2s and unifying onchain identity records across multiple blockchains.


Our Focus Areas

  • Unruggable Gateways: Maintain and expand L2 verifiers, add support for new L2s, and manage the open-source repository.
  • Crosschain Identity: Enable ENS names to function seamlessly across chains using ERC-7786, OP Superchain interop, and other Ethereum-wide standards.
  • Secure ENS Resolution: Improve the integrity of ENS name resolution by incorporating verified onchain metadata, ensuring reliable access to identity records.


By building scalable, secure, and interoperable ENS infrastructure, we aim to establish ENS as the foundation of onchain identity, enabling seamless interactions across the Ethereum ecosystem.

title: EIPsInsight
description:
Project Overview

Every change to Ethereum begins as an EIP, but the process that takes it from idea to implementation has long relied on fragmented tools, manual coordination, and limited visibility. EIPsInsight was built to fix this, bringing structure, transparency, and data-driven coordination to Ethereum’s governance process. 

Today, EIPsInsight is already embedded in EIP’s core workflows. Its PR Board is used weekly by EIP Editors to manage proposals and generate agendas, while its analytics page has informed editor selection and surfaced critical issues in open PRs. The project was also selected as a grant recipient of Ethereum Foundation ESP grant Q2 2025 , with deliverables 

  • real-time upgrade tracking, 
  • EIPs monthly insights, 
  • Proposals lifecycle analytics, 
  • contributor education resources, 
  • the EIP Creator Tool, and 
  • customizable status notifications was completed on time. That track record is not a claim. It is a commit history.


The Problem Statement

With the introduction of EIP-4844, Ethereum now operates a live blob fee market powering rollups, but without public tooling to monitor cost efficiency, detect congestion, or assess economic risks. This creates blind spots for both governance and infrastructure operators.

What we are building next

The next chapter of EIPsInsight is Rollup Cost Insight (BlobLens) - an open-source extension for blob economics analytics that closes the two largest gaps in Ethereum's L2 observability layer - visibility into the economics and risks introduced by EIP-4844 and the emerging blob fee market.


Gap 1: No open per-rollup DA cost-efficiency scoring. No public tool computes cost per byte actually used, blob fullness ratios, amortized DA cost per L2 transaction, or blob coordination opportunity scores across rollups. Rollup Cost Insight will build this: a self-hostable efficiency scoring engine updated every epoch, a public rollup leaderboard that any researcher or operator can query.


Gap 2: No live blob fee market health layer. No public system classifies the current market regime, forecasts congestion from excess_blob_gas accumulation, or pushes threshold alerts to rollup operators. Rollup Cost Insight will build this: a real-time regime classifier (undersaturated / healthy / congested / spike), a 4–12 slot congestion forecast, and a webhook alert system for rollup teams.


Both modules connect back to EIPsInsight's governance layer. By connecting protocol governance with live economic data, EIPsInsight ensures that Ethereum’s future BPO upgrades are informed, observable, and accountable. The same public-goods ethos that has driven every line of EIPsInsight since day one.


Why your donation matters

Quadratic funding means breadth of support matters as much as amount. A donation of any size - $5, $10, $50 signals that the Ethereum community values this work and multiplies the matching pool allocation toward it.


EIPsInsight does not have a token. It does not have venture backing. It does not have a protocol treasury. It is funded by grants and community support, built in public, and given away free. The PR Board that EIP Editors use every week, the Editor Analytics that inform governance appointments, all of it runs on this model.


Built as a public good, EIPsInsight strengthens both governance security and rollup ecosystem resilience ensuring Ethereum can scale with clarity, coordination, and trust.


If you have ever submitted an EIP, relied on an ERC, used a rollup, or cared about Ethereum's governance being done right, this is the infrastructure that supports it. Help us keep it running and help us build what comes next.

title: DeFiScan
description:
DeFiScan is a research framework and analytics dashboard offering comprehensive and unbiased insights into the decentralisation level of EVM DeFi applications. DeFiScan categorizes projects according to their decentralization stages and single-point-of-failure vulnerabilities, providing verifiable insights into DeFi protocol maturity and risks.

DeFiScan promotes transparency, education, self-policing, and informed decision-making in DeFi.


DeFiScan has been created by The DeFi Collective, a non-profit association whose goal is to promote genuinely decentralised DeFi protocols and is behind a whole range of initiatives to support those protocols:

  • The Collective helps protocols to bootstrap liquidity for the hardest assets. It has already secured donations for liquidity-driving positions to achieve this goal and is actively seeking additional ones.
  • The decentralisation of public infrastructure is an active field of research, and understanding the drivers of security, reliability, and efficiency is crucial to protecting users and their funds. We conduct and support research that furthers the understanding of this field.
  • Developing and promoting a self-policing framework for DeFi protocols, such as DeFiScan.


DeFiScan is our flagship project.

We already covered more than 50% TVL of the entire DeFi landscape, failing to reach our 90% by the end of 2025.

This is due to the fact that we are actively working on a second version of our framework that enables live monitoring of TVL at risks, and bring more granularity into centralization risks.


Our goal is to reach 90% TVL coverage by Q3 2026, and to update DeFiScan’s framework by Q2.


Your funding will greatly contribute to this mission!


Website: deficollective.org

Public Good Dashboard & Framework: defiscan.info

Public Repository: MIT Licence - GitHub - https://github.com/deficollective/defiscan / https://github.com/deficollective/defi-disco


Team Information

Our team consists of 9 crypto natives and experienced professionals in blockchain technology, DeFi, software development, law and regulation, policy, and community engagement.

Board members include:

TokenBrice: A key figure in the DeFi community, and an integral part of The DeFi Collective.

title: SEAL 911
description:
SEAL 911 is a nonprofit dedicated to safeguarding the blockchain and crypto ecosystem. In an industry plagued with scams, malware, and security flaws, SEAL 911 steps in to provide critical protection for users, developers, and projects in danger. With your support, we can secure more wallets, protect valuable funds, and make crypto a safer space for all.


We founded SEAL 911 in response to the increasing need for organized security in the crypto space. Since its inception, we've handled over 12,200 security tickets, managing high-stakes incidents like the Curve exploit and countless phishing attempts. Our focus is on collaboration, innovation, and rapid response—ensuring that whenever a security threat arises, the community has a trusted ally to turn to.


Our Impact in 2024


The need for SEAL 911 has never been more urgent. In 2024, our team of 28 passionate volunteers has achieved outstanding results:

  • +1,500 tickets handled to resolve security incidents.
  • 75+ war rooms actively managed to mitigate ongoing exploits.
  • 150,000+ phishing domains blocked to protect users.
  • Incident Resolution Log
  • ~$75M USD saved through phishing prevention, smart contract rescues, and other critical actions.

We’ve tackled some of the most dangerous threats in the crypto space, including:

  1. Phishing attacks
  2. Private key leaks
  3. Malware infections
  4. Social media account hijacks
  5. Smart contract hacks
  6. Pig Butchering scams (Sha Zhu Pan)
  7. Vulnerability disclosures
  8. Phishing URL reports
  9. Frontrunning and wallet rescues by white hats
  10. Domain hijacks


Despite these successes, the road ahead is long. The security landscape in crypto still lags behind where it needs to be, and SEAL 911 is here to fill that gap.


How SEAL 911 Works


  • Emergency Response: Through the SEAL 911 Telegram bot, we offer instant support during security crises.
  • White Hat Support: We work closely with white hats to rescue funds, disclose vulnerabilities, and secure protocols.
  • Proactive Measures: We’re constantly blocking phishing domains and developing best practices for war rooms, building a safer crypto environment.


Why We Need Your Help


Every SEAL 911 member is a volunteer, and while we work tirelessly with limited resources, the demand for our expertise keeps growing. To expand and continue our efforts, we need your help. Your support will allow us to:

  • Scale up our phishing prevention systems.
  • Build better tools to detect and respond to threats.
  • Provide financial support to volunteers and white hats.
  • Educate and raise awareness on how to avoid risks.


By donating to SEAL 911, you're investing in the future of crypto security. Together, we can protect users, projects, and protocols from the dangers that threaten our industry.

title: Vyper
description:

Vyper is an open-source project maintained by a core team of experienced web3 engineers and a number of volunteer contributors. We collaborate extensively with partners across the EVM toolchain, infrastructure, and security ecosystems. 


Vyper aims to become the leading choice for smart contract development by offering:

  • Superior developer experience through pythonic syntax and extensive tooling

title: WebHash
description:
Webhash is a decentralized web deployment and verification infrastructure designed to reduce critical security risks in the Ethereum ecosystem.


Today, a significant portion of Web3 projects still rely on centralized hosting, exposing users to risks such as DNS hijacking, frontend tampering, phishing attacks, and silent code modifications. These vulnerabilities have been repeatedly exploited to compromise wallets and drain user funds.


Webhash addresses this by enabling verifiable, immutable, and tamper-resistant web deployments using IPFS and blockchain-based ownership.



Core Security Contributions


1. Immutable Frontend Deployment (IPFS)

Webhash deploys websites to IPFS using content-addressed storage (CIDs), ensuring that once deployed, the frontend cannot be altered without changing its hash. This eliminates risks of silent code injection and unauthorized modifications.


2. Verifiable Ownership & Integrity (On-chain)

Each website is linked to an on-chain record (Base), providing a transparent and immutable mapping between ownership and deployed content. This allows users and tools to verify that a website is authentic and has not been tampered with.


3. Protection Against Phishing & Frontend Attacks

By combining ENS/DNS resolution with IPFS content verification, Webhash enables a model where users can cryptographically verify the authenticity of a website, significantly reducing phishing risks.


4. Decentralized Hosting (No Single Point of Failure)

Webhash removes reliance on centralized servers and CDNs, reducing exposure to outages, censorship, and infrastructure-level attacks.


5. Supply Chain Security for Web3 Applications

Webhash ensures that deployed frontend code remains consistent from deployment to user access, addressing one of the weakest links in Web3 security: the frontend supply chain.



Why This Matters


Many of the largest exploits in Web3 have not originated from smart contract vulnerabilities, but from compromised frontends and infrastructure.


Webhash shifts trust from centralized infrastructure to cryptographic guarantees, enabling a safer interaction layer between users and decentralized protocols.


Adoption & Developer Accessibility


To ensure these security guarantees are widely adopted, Webhash provides:


No-code interface

A user-friendly interface that allows non-technical users to deploy immutable, verifiable websites without needing to understand IPFS or blockchain infrastructure. This lowers the barrier to adopting secure, decentralized hosting.


Developer platform (pro.webhash.com)

A Vercel-like deployment platform that enables developers to push applications directly from Git repositories to IPFS-backed infrastructure. This ensures that even modern frontend workflows can benefit from verifiable and tamper-resistant deployments without changing developer habits.


By combining strong security guarantees with accessible tooling, Webhash accelerates the adoption of safer web infrastructure across the Ethereum ecosystem.



Vision


Webhash aims to become a standard layer for secure, verifiable web delivery in Web3, ensuring that users can interact with Ethereum applications without relying on blind trust in centralized hosting.

title: Blockscout Open-Source Block Explorer
description:
Open-source block explorers are a vital public good

This redundancy is vital, but it is not Blockscout's mission. Our mission is to provide a first-class, open-source, decentralized explorer for all users. An explorer built by and for the community that can provide everything users, developers, and projects need to successfully explore and develop on a chain.

title: Militereum
description:

What chains and wallets does Militereum support?

Militereum is chain-agnostic (supporting L2s such as Optimism and Arbitrum) and works with every EVM-compatible crypto wallet, including browser-based and native desktop wallets.

This project is a success if our users are prevented from getting phished/drained/rugged at least once.

Features
